items.text: משנת הפתיחה: דיני השקיה במועד ובשביעית
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may irrigate a beit hashelachin (thirsty field) on Chol HaMoed and during the Sabbatical year from a spring, whether it first emerged or not, but not from rainwater or pond water. It also prohibits making depressions around vines and records a dispute between Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah and the Sages regarding constructing a water channel.
items.desc: המשנה מתירה להשקות בית השלחין ממעיין, בין חדש בין ישן, אך אוסרת להשקות ממי גשמים או קילון. כמו כן, אוסרת לעשות עוגיות לגפנים, ומביאה מחלוקת בין רבי אלעזר בן עזריה לחכמים לגבי עשיית אמה חדשה. בהמשך מפרטת המשנה פעולות מותרות לצורכי רבים.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that one may irrigate a beit hashelachin (thirsty field) on Chol HaMoed and during the Sabbatical year from a spring, whether it first emerged or not, but not from rainwater or pond water.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת בדין השקיית בית השלחין במועד ובשביעית, ומפרטת אילו מקורות מים מותרים ואסורים.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah prohibits making depressions around vines and records a dispute between Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah and the Sages regarding constructing a water channel.
sub.desc: המשנה מביאה איסור עשיית עוגיות לגפנים ומחלוקת בין רבי אלעזר בן עזריה לחכמים בעניין עשיית אמה במועד ובשביעית.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists additional permitted activities: repairing water channels in public domain, roads, streets, mikva'ot, all public needs, marking graves, and going out to inspect kil'ayim (mixed seeds).
sub.desc: המשנה מפרטת פעולות מותרות לצורכי רבים במועד, כגון תיקון קלקולי מים, דרכים, רחובות, מקוואות, ציון קברים ויציאה על הכלאיים.

items.text: קושיית הגמרא על כפל המקרים במשנה
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's redundancy
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah needs to mention both a spring that first emerged and one that did not, since the latter is more lenient. It explains that without the explicit mention of the latter, one might have thought that only a spring that first emerged permits irrigation of a beit hashelachin, but not a beit haba'al (rain-fed field), while a spring that did not first emerge might permit even a beit haba'al. The Mishnah therefore teaches that both types of springs permit only a beit hashelachin.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אם מותר להשקות ממעיין שיצא בתחילה (שעלול להתמוטט), כל שכן ממעיין שלא יצא בתחילה. ומתרצת שהמשנה נצרכה כדי שלא נטעה להתיר גם בית הבעל ממעיין ישן.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah needs to mention both a spring that first emerged and one that did not, since the latter is more lenient.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אם מותר להשקות ממעיין שיצא בתחילה, שסיכוי להתמוטטות גדול יותר, כל שכן ממעיין שלא יצא בתחילה?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that without the explicit mention of the latter, one might have thought that only a spring that first emerged permits irrigation of a beit hashelachin, but not a beit haba'al (rain-fed field), while a spring that did not first emerge might permit even a beit haba'al.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת שהמשנה נצרכה כדי שלא נטעה להתיר גם בית הבעל ממעיין שלא יצא בתחילה.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah therefore teaches that both types of springs permit only a beit hashelachin.

items.text: בירור לשוני: פירוש 'בית השלחין' ו'בית הבעל'
items.text_en: Proof of the meaning of beit hashelachin and beit haba'al
items.desc_en: The Gemara proves that 'beit hashelachin' means a thirsty field, citing the verse 'And you were faint and weary' (Deut. 25:18) and its Aramaic translation. It then proves that 'beit haba'al' means a settled field, citing the verse 'For as a young man marries a virgin' (Isaiah 62:5) and its Aramaic translation.
items.desc: הגמרא מבארת ש'בית השלחין' לשון צמא, ו'בית הבעל' לשון ישוב, על פי פסוקים ותרגומיהם.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know that 'בית השלחין' (beit hashelachin) means a thirsty field, and answers by citing the verse 'ואתה עיף ויגע' (Deut. 25:18) and its Aramaic translation where 'עיף' is rendered as 'משלהי' (thirsty).
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מהיכן נלמד שהמונח 'בית השלחין' פירושו צמא, ומביאה ראיה מהפסוק 'ואתה עייף ויגע' שמתורגם 'ואת משלהי ולאי'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know that 'בית הבעל' (beit haba'al) means a settled field, and answers by citing the verse 'כי יבעל בחור בתולה' (Isaiah 62:5) and its Aramaic translation where 'יבעל' is rendered as 'מתותב' (settles).
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מהיכן נלמד שהמונח 'בית הבעל' פירושו ישוב, ומביאה ראיה מהפסוק 'כי יבעל בחור בתולה' שמתורגם 'כמה דמיתותב עולם עם בתולתא יתיתבון בגוויך בניך'.

items.text: Identifying the Tanna of the Mishnah: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
items.text_en: Identifying the Tanna of the Mishnah: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna that permits only to prevent loss (pesida) but not for profit (harvacha), and even for loss does not allow exertion. Rav Huna answers that it is Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, who in a baraita permits drawing water from tree to tree but not irrigating the entire field.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna who permits only to prevent loss (פסידא) but not for profit (הרווחה), and even for loss does not allow exertion.
Rav Huna answers that it is Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, citing a baraita where he permits drawing water from tree to tree but not irrigating the entire field.

items.text: Rejection and alternative identification: Rabbi Yehudah
items.text_en: Rejection and alternative identification: Rabbi Yehudah
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects Rav Huna's answer, arguing that Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov only prohibits profit, not exertion for loss. Rav Pappa then identifies the Tanna as Rabbi Yehudah, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehudah permits irrigation only for a beit hashelachin that has become parched (charevah), unlike Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov only prohibits profit (הרווחה), not exertion for loss (טירחא במקום פסידא), so Rav Huna's identification is insufficient.

Rav Pappa identifies the Tanna as Rabbi Yehudah, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehudah permits irrigation only for a beit hashelachin that has become parched (charevah), unlike Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah.

items.text: Clarification of 'charevah' and Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah's position
items.text_en: Clarification of 'charevah' and Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'charevah' means: if literally destroyed, why irrigate it? Abaye explains it means a field that has become parched from this spring but has another spring. The Gemara then clarifies that Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah prohibits irrigation even from a spring that first emerged, whether the field's spring is parched or not. It questions whether Rabbi Yehudah's leniency applies only to a spring that first emerged.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'חָרְבָה' (parched field) means: if it is literally destroyed, why would one irrigate it?
Abaye explains that 'חָרְבָה' means a field that has become parched from its original spring but has another spring available.

sub.text: Gemara's clarification of Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah's position
sub.text_en: Gemara's clarification of Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah's position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah prohibits irrigation even from a spring that first emerged, whether the field's spring is parched or not.

sub.text: Gemara's question about Rabbi Yehudah's position
sub.text_en: Gemara's question about Rabbi Yehudah's position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yehudah's leniency applies only to a spring that first emerged, or also to other cases.

items.text: Clarifying the Mishnah's dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Clarifying the Mishnah's dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a contradiction in the Mishnah by explaining that Rabbi Yehuda permits irrigation only for a field that requires watering (בית השלחין), not for a rain-fed field (בית הבעל), regardless of whether the spring is new or old. The Mishnah's mention of a new spring is only to highlight Rabbi Meir's lenient position.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a concern: perhaps one might come to neglect the irrigation channel (אינופולי), and therefore even a new spring should be permitted for a rain-fed field (בית הבעל).

The Gemara resolves: the Mishnah must be attributed to Rabbi Yehuda, who permits irrigation only for a field that requires watering (בית השלחין), not for a rain-fed field (בית הבעל); the mention of a new spring is only to highlight Rabbi Meir's lenient position.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbah and Rav Yosef on the Sabbath labor category
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbah and Rav Yosef on the Sabbath labor category
items.desc_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef debate whether weeding and watering on Shabbat is prohibited because of plowing (חורש) or sowing (זורע). Each argues that his own reasoning is more logical: Rabbah compares it to loosening the soil, Rav Yosef to promoting growth.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a dispute: Rabbah says weeding and watering on Shabbat is prohibited because of plowing (חורש), Rav Yosef says because of sowing (זורע).
Rabbah argues his view is more logical: just as plowing loosens the soil, so too weeding loosens the soil.
Rav Yosef argues his view is more logical: just as sowing promotes growth, so too watering promotes growth.

items.text: Abaye's objection and the principle of multiple liabilities
items.text_en: Abaye's objection and the principle of multiple liabilities
items.desc_en: Abaye challenges both Rabbah and Rav Yosef: each implies that only one category applies, but Rav Kahana's ruling shows that one action can incur two liabilities. The Gemara concludes that the objection stands (קשיא).

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects to both Rabbah and Rav Yosef: each implies that only one category of liability applies, but the other is excluded.
The Gemara cites Rav Kahana's ruling that one who prunes and needs the wood is liable for two violations, showing that multiple liabilities can apply to a single action.
The Gemara concludes that the objection stands (קשיא) and is unresolved.

items.text: Rav Yosef's challenge from kilayim and the resolution
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's challenge from kilayim and the resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef challenges Rabbah from a baraita about weeding kilayim, which is prohibited due to sowing (זורע), not plowing. Rabbah initially answers that it is due to maintaining (מקיים), but the Gemara resolves that the entire baraita follows Rabbi Akiva, who derives the prohibition of maintaining kilayim from the verse.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef challenges Rabbah from a baraita that one who weeds or covers kilayim is flogged, arguing that if the prohibition is due to plowing (as Rabbah holds), plowing in kilayim is not biblically prohibited.
Rabbah answers that the prohibition is due to maintaining (מקיים) the kilayim, not plowing.
The Gemara objects that the baraita's continuation — Rabbi Akiva says 'even one who maintains' — implies the first Tanna does not hold the prohibition is due to maintaining.

The Gemara resolves that the entire baraita follows Rabbi Akiva, and the phrase 'what is the reason' explains that the first Tanna's ruling is also due to maintaining, as Rabbi Akiva explicitly states.

sub.text: Supporting baraita for Rabbi Akiva's reasoning
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita for Rabbi Akiva's reasoning
sub.desc_en: A baraita explains Rabbi Akiva's source: from the verse 'שָׂדְךָ לֹא תִזְרַע כִּלְאָיִם' (you shall not sow your field with mixed seeds) one derives only sowing, but maintaining is derived from the extended phrase 'כִּלְאַיִם שָׂדְךָ לֹא' (mixed seeds of your field — not).

items.text: The Mishnah's ruling on the Sabbatical year and its resolution
items.text_en: The Mishnah's ruling on the Sabbatical year and its resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the Mishnah permits irrigation during the Sabbatical year (שביעית) if it involves plowing or sowing. Abaye answers that the Mishnah refers to the post-exilic Sabbatical year, following Rabbi's opinion that the biblical prohibition applies only when the Jubilee is observed. Rava offers an alternative: even according to the Rabbis, the Torah only prohibited the primary labors (אבות), not secondary ones.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the Mishnah permits irrigation during the Sabbatical year (שביעית) if it involves plowing or sowing.
Abaye answers that the Mishnah refers to the post-exilic Sabbatical year, following Rabbi's opinion that the biblical prohibition applies only when the Jubilee is observed.
Rava offers an alternative: even according to the Rabbis, the Torah only prohibited the primary labors (אבות), not secondary ones.

items.text: Opening question: Why did the Torah list explicit labors at all?
items.text_en: Opening question: Why did the Torah list explicit labors at all?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah separately singled out pruning and harvesting in the Sabbatical year verse, since these are already subsumed under the general categories of sowing and reaping. It answers that the Torah thereby teaches that one is liable for 'derived' labors (תולדות) but not for other distinct categories.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that the Torah did not forbid derived labors (תולדות) and cites the verse about the Sabbatical year.
The Gemara asks why the Torah wrote pruning and harvesting separately, since they are already included in sowing and reaping.
The Gemara answers that the Torah wrote these to teach that one is liable for these derived labors (תולדות) but not for other distinct categories.

items.text: Baraita expands the prohibition to many agricultural labors
items.text_en: Baraita expands the prohibition to many agricultural labors
items.desc_en: A baraita challenges the previous answer by deriving from the verse 'your field you shall not sow' and 'your vineyard you shall not prune' that all field and vineyard labors are forbidden, including weeding, hoeing, trimming, and fertilizing. The Gemara concludes that these extensions are rabbinic, with the verse serving merely as a support (אסמכתא).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that expands the prohibition from the verse to include all field and vineyard labors.
The baraita derives from the verse that all agricultural labors in field and vineyard are forbidden, including weeding, hoeing, trimming, and fertilizing.
The baraita further derives that even indirect labors like watering and making basins are forbidden, using the principle of היקש (analogy) from sowing.
The Gemara resolves that these extensions are only rabbinic, and the verse serves merely as an אסמכתא (support).

items.text: Distinction between two types of loosening (קישוש)
items.text_en: Distinction between two types of loosening (קישוש)
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty: isn't loosening the soil (קישוש) forbidden in the Sabbatical year, based on the verse 'you shall let it rest and abandon it'? Rav Ukva bar Chama answers that there are two types of loosening: one that strengthens trees (forbidden) and one that merely closes cracks (permitted).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether loosening the soil (קישוש) is permitted in the Sabbatical year, citing the verse that commands to let it rest and abandon it.
Rav Ukva bar Chama resolves the difficulty by distinguishing two types of loosening: one that strengthens trees (forbidden) and one that merely closes cracks (permitted).

items.text: Dispute about liability for plowing in the Sabbatical year
items.text_en: Dispute about liability for plowing in the Sabbatical year
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar dispute whether one who plows during the Sabbatical year is lashed. One holds he is liable, the other not. The Gemara suggests the dispute hinges on a principle of Rabbi Avin citing Rabbi Ila: where a general rule is stated in a positive command and a specific rule in a negative command, we do not apply the hermeneutic of 'general, specific, general'. The positions are clarified: one holds liable consistently, the other exempts because derived labors (תולדות) are not punishable by lashes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar regarding whether one who plows during the Sabbatical year is lashed.

The Gemara suggests that the dispute hinges on a principle of Rabbi Avin citing Rabbi Ila: where a general rule is stated in a positive command and a specific rule in a negative command, we do not apply the hermeneutic of 'general, specific, general'.
The Gemara clarifies: the one who says he is liable rejects Rabbi Avin's principle, while the one who says he is not liable accepts it.

The Gemara rejects the previous analysis, stating that everyone rejects Rabbi Avin's principle; the one who exempts holds that derived labors (תולדות) are not punishable by lashes, based on the verses specifying pruning and harvesting.

items.text: Repeat of baraita to confirm the rabbinic status
items.text_en: Repeat of baraita to confirm the rabbinic status
items.desc_en: The Gemara recites the same baraita as earlier, re-emphasizing that the extensive list of forbidden labors—including hoeing, pruning, fertilizing, and watering—is derived from the verse's expansive language. It concludes again that these are rabbinic prohibitions, with the verse serving merely as a mnemonic support (אסמכתא).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the earlier conclusion by citing a baraita that lists many forbidden labors in the seventh year, implying they are Torah-level prohibitions.
The baraita continues, deriving from the verse's repetition that pruning, thinning, and trimming branches are also forbidden.
The baraita adds that fertilizing, clearing stones, dusting, and smoking trees are also forbidden, again derived from the verse's inclusive language.

The baraita considers whether one might think watering under olive trees, hoeing under vines, filling cracks, and making basins are forbidden, and then excludes them by citing the verse's specific wording.
The baraita explains that the specific mention of 'sowing' (זריעה) serves as a paradigm (היקש) to include all similar field and vineyard labors.
The Gemara resolves the challenge by stating that all these prohibitions are rabbinic (מדרבנן), and the verse serves only as a mnemonic support (אסמכתא בעלמא).

items.text: Rav Dimi's initial confusion
items.text_en: Rav Dimi's initial confusion
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports a tradition that one might think he is liable for lashes for violating the additional days (תוספת), but the Talmud exempts him, yet he does not know what the additional days refer to.

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports that one might think lashes apply for violating the additional days (תוספת), but the Talmud exempts him, and he does not know what the additional days refer to.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's interpretation: plowing
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's interpretation: plowing
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar explains that the 'additional days' refer to plowing (חרישה) that is derived from a general-principle-particular-general hermeneutic, and the Torah exempts one from lashes for it, asking why the particulars would otherwise be needed.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar identifies the 'additional days' as plowing (חרישה) derived from a general-principle-particular-general hermeneutic, and states that the Torah exempts one from lashes for it.
The Gemara asks why the Torah would list all the particulars if the general principle already covers plowing.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's interpretation: days added before Rosh Hashanah
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's interpretation: days added before Rosh Hashanah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that the 'additional days' are the days added by the Sages before Rosh Hashanah of the Sabbatical year, derived from the verse 'in plowing and in harvest you shall rest', and the Torah exempts one from lashes for violating them.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that the 'additional days' are the days added by the Sages before Rosh Hashanah of the Sabbatical year, derived from the verse 'in plowing and in harvest you shall rest', and the Torah exempts one from lashes for violating them.

items.text: Mishnah on plowing limits before the Sabbatical year
items.text_en: Mishnah on plowing limits before the Sabbatical year
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah that discusses until when one may plow in a tree field and a white field before the Sabbatical year, with disputes between Beit Shammai, Beit Hillel, and Rabbi Shimon.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the Mishnah that defines the 'days before the New Year' by citing the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding plowing in a tree field before the Sabbatical year.
The Mishnah continues with the rule for plowing a white field (non-tree field) before the Sabbatical year, until the moisture is gone and as long as people plant vegetables.

Rabbi Shimon objects that the previous rule gives each person a subjective measure, and instead sets fixed limits: white field until Passover, tree field until Atzeret, with Beit Hillel agreeing on Passover.

items.text: Rabban Gamliel and his court abolished the two periods
items.text_en: Rabban Gamliel and his court abolished the two periods
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi reports in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi citing Bar Kappara that Rabban Gamliel and his court voted on these two periods (the additional days) and abolished them.

sub.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi in the name of Bar Kappara
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi in the name of Bar Kappara
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi reports that Rabban Gamliel and his court voted on the two periods (the additional days before Rosh Hashanah) and abolished them.

items.text: Question on the authority to abolish earlier enactments
items.text_en: Question on the authority to abolish earlier enactments
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks Rabbi Avahu (or Resh Lakish asks Rabbi Yochanan) how Rabban Gamliel's court could abolish the enactment of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, given the rule that a court cannot overturn another court's ruling unless greater in wisdom and number. The answer is that they stipulated at the outset that anyone who wishes to abolish may do so.

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira's question to Rabbi Avahu
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's question to Rabbi Avahu
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks Rabbi Avahu how Rabban Gamliel's court could abolish the enactment of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, given the rule that a court cannot overturn another court's ruling unless greater in wisdom and number.
Rabbi Avahu answers that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel stipulated at the outset that anyone who wishes to abolish their enactment may do so.

items.text: Objection: these are halakhot from Sinai
items.text_en: Objection: these are halakhot from Sinai
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that these additional days are not mere enactments but halakhot from Sinai (הלכה למשה מסיני), citing Rabbi Asi's tradition about ten saplings, willow, and water libation. Rabbi Yitzchak explains that the halakha from Sinai applies only to thirty days before Rosh Hashanah, while the Sages added from Passover and Shavuot, and they stipulated that anyone may abolish.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the additional days are not mere enactments but a הלכה למשה מסיני (halakha from Sinai), citing Rabbi Asi's tradition about ten saplings, willow, and water libation.
Rabbi Yitzchak explains that the halakha from Sinai applies only to thirty days before Rosh Hashanah, while the Sages added from Passover and Shavuot, and they stipulated that anyone may abolish.

items.text: Further objection: these are from verses
items.text_en: Further objection: these are from verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that these additional days are not halakhot but derived from verses, citing the Mishnah where Rabbi Akiva interprets 'in plowing and in harvest you shall rest' as referring to plowing of the eve of the Sabbatical year.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that these additional days are not הלכה למשה מסיני (halakha from Sinai) but are derived from verses.

The Gemara cites the Mishnah where Rabbi Akiva interprets the verse 'בחריש ובקציר תשבות' (in plowing and in harvest you shall rest) as referring to plowing of the eve of the Sabbatical year, showing these are from verses.

items.text: Debate on the source of the prohibition: halakha vs. verses
items.text_en: Debate on the source of the prohibition: halakha vs. verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially suggests that the prohibition of watering during Chol HaMoed is based on a halakha leMoshe miSinai for a young field and verses for an old field. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak refines this: the halakha permits a young field, implying an old field is prohibited by verses. The Gemara questions this logic and concludes that the halakha follows Rabbi Yishmael and the verses follow Rabbi Akiva.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak refines the earlier suggestion: the halakha leMoshe miSinai permits watering a young field (יַלְדָּה), while the verses prohibit an old field (זְקֵינָה).
The Gemara objects: if the halakha permits a young field, does it not automatically follow that an old field is prohibited by the same halakha, making the verses redundant?
The Gemara resolves: the halakha applies to Rabbi Yishmael's position (permitting a young field), while the verses apply to Rabbi Akiva's position (prohibiting an old field).

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's alternative: a gezeirah shavah
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's alternative: a gezeirah shavah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan argues that Rabban Gamliel and his court derived the prohibition from a gezeirah shavah comparing 'Shabbat' in the context of Chol HaMoed to Shabbat Bereishit, where the day itself is prohibited but the surrounding days are permitted.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that Rabban Gamliel and his court derived the prohibition from the Torah.
The Gemara asks for the reasoning behind Rabbi Yochanan's statement.

Rabbi Yochanan explains that Rabban Gamliel derived a גזירה שוה (verbal analogy) from the word 'שבת' (Shabbat) in the context of Chol HaMoed to Shabbat Bereishit, where the day itself is prohibited but the surrounding days are permitted.

items.text: Rav Ashi's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi objects: how can a gezeirah shavah override a halakha or a verse? He resolves that Rabban Gamliel and his court followed Rabbi Yishmael's view that the halakha applies only when the Temple stands, similar to the water libation ceremony, but not when the Temple is destroyed.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi objects: how can a גזירה שוה (verbal analogy) override a הלכה (binding law) or a verse?

Rav Ashi resolves that Rabban Gamliel and his court followed Rabbi Yishmael's view that the הלכה applies only when the Temple stands, like the water libation ceremony, but not when the Temple is destroyed.

items.text: Debate on watering with rainwater and kilon water
items.text_en: Debate on watering with rainwater and kilon water
items.desc_en: The Mishnah prohibits watering with rainwater and kilon water. The Gemara questions the reason for rainwater, and Rabbi Ila and Rav Ashi offer explanations: a decree against rainwater due to kilon water, or that rainwater itself can lead to kilon water. They then debate based on Rabbi Zeira's ruling about rivers drawing from ponds.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why rainwater is prohibited, since it does not involve extra labor like kilon water.
Rabbi Ila in the name of Rabbi Yochanan explains that rainwater is prohibited as a decree (גזירה) lest one come to use kilon water.
Rav Ashi offers an alternative explanation: rainwater itself can lead to the use of kilon water (since rainwater collects in ponds that become like kilon).
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Ila and Rav Ashi disagree based on Rabbi Zeira's ruling that rivers drawing from ponds are permitted for irrigation on חול המועד (the intermediate festival days).

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's ruling and Rabbi Yirmeyah's challenge
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's ruling and Rabbi Yirmeyah's challenge
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Zeira's ruling that rivers drawing from ponds may be used for irrigation during Chol HaMoed. Rabbi Yirmeyah challenges this from the Mishnah's prohibition of rainwater and kilon water. Rabbi Zeira responds that Babylonian ponds are like non-stop flowing water.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira cites Shmuel's ruling that rivers drawing water from ponds may be used for irrigation during Chol HaMoed.
Rabbi Yirmeyah challenges Rabbi Zeira by citing the Mishnah's prohibition of rainwater and kilon water for irrigation during Chol HaMoed.
Rabbi Zeira responds that Babylonian ponds are like non-stop flowing water, thus permitted.

items.text: Baraita on pits and pools, and Rav Pappa and Rav Ashi's conditions
items.text_en: Baraita on pits and pools, and Rav Pappa and Rav Ashi's conditions
items.desc_en: A baraita states that pits and pools filled before Yom Tov may not be used during Chol HaMoed, unless a water channel passes between them. Rav Pappa adds that this applies only if most of the field drinks from that channel; Rav Ashi permits even if not, as the water will eventually be absorbed.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that pits and pools filled before Yom Tov may not be used for irrigation during Chol HaMoed.
The baraita adds that if a water channel passes between them, irrigation is permitted.
Rav Pappa limits the permission to a case where most of the field drinks from that channel.
Rav Ashi permits even without a majority, reasoning that the water will eventually be absorbed over two or three days.

items.text: Baraita on a dripping pool and its conditions
items.text_en: Baraita on a dripping pool and its conditions
items.desc_en: A baraita permits watering from a pool that drips from one irrigated field to another. The Gemara questions that such a pool might stop dripping. Rabbi Yirmeyah explains it is still dripping, and Abaye adds that the original spring must not have ceased.

sub.desc_en: A baraita permits watering from a dripping pool from one irrigated field to another.
The Gemara objects that such a pool might stop dripping, making the watering forbidden.
Rabbi Yirmeyah answers that the pool is still dripping, so the watering is permitted.
Abaye adds the condition that the original spring must not have ceased, ensuring the pool's water source is continuous.

items.text: Additional rulings: Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya, Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon, and the story of Ravina and Rabbah Tosefa'ah
items.text_en: Additional rulings: Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya, Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon, and the story of Ravina and Rabbah Tosefa'ah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya prohibits drawing water from a lower bed to water a higher one; Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon extends this even within a single bed. A baraita permits watering vegetables for eating but not for beautification. Ravina and Rabbah Tosefa'ah encounter a man watering during Chol HaMoed; Rabbah wants to excommunicate him, but Ravina cites the baraita permitting watering for eating. Rabbah clarifies that 'madlin' refers to drawing water, not watering vegetables.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya prohibiting drawing water from a lower bed to water a higher one, and Rabbi Elazar bar Shimon extends this even within a single bed.
A baraita permits watering vegetables for eating but prohibits watering for beautification.
Rabbah Tosefa'ah, seeing a man watering during Chol HaMoed, asks Ravina to excommunicate him.
Ravina cites the baraita permitting watering vegetables for eating, implying the man's action is permitted.
Rabbah Tosefa'ah clarifies that 'madlin' in the baraita refers to drawing water, not watering vegetables, thus the man's action may still be prohibited.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Delaying and the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Meir
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Delaying and the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Meir
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who delays (prunes) vines may do so for his own and for the poor's vines according to Rabbi Yehuda, while Rabbi Meir permits only for his own. The Gemara begins by clarifying the meaning of 'madlin' as 'shalofei' (removing branches).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's term 'madlin' means removing branches (שלופי).
The Gemara cites a baraita that one who prunes vines may prune his own and the poor's vines according to Rabbi Yehuda, while Rabbi Meir permits only his own.

items.text: Gemara's question and resolution about watering vegetables
items.text_en: Gemara's question and resolution about watering vegetables
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's leniency by citing a baraita that permits watering vegetables during Chol HaMoed. The response is simply 'If it is taught, it is taught,' accepting the baraita without further analysis.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the Mishnah's leniency by citing a baraita that permits watering vegetables during Chol HaMoed for eating.
The Gemara responds by accepting the baraita without further analysis, effectively resolving the challenge.

items.text: The prohibition of making 'ugiyot' (support-beds) for vines
items.text_en: The prohibition of making 'ugiyot' (support-beds) for vines
items.desc_en: The Mishnah prohibits making 'ugiyot' for vines. Rav Yehuda explains this as 'bankei' (support-beds). A baraita confirms this. The Gemara then notes a contradiction: Rav Yehuda permitted the people of Bar Tzeitai to make such beds. The resolution distinguishes between new and old vines.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the prohibition of making 'עוגיות' (support-beds) for vines.
The Gemara asks what 'עוגיות' means.
Rav Yehuda explains that 'עוגיות' are 'בנכי' (support-beds).
A baraita confirms that 'עוגיות' are beds at the roots of olive trees and vines.
The Gemara objects that Rav Yehuda himself permitted the people of Bar Tzeitai to make such beds for their vineyards.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: the prohibition applies to new vines, while the permission applies to old vines.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's prohibition of making a water channel
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's prohibition of making a water channel
items.desc_en: The Mishnah cites Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya who prohibits making a water channel (amma) during Chol HaMoed and also during the Sabbatical year. The Gemara questions the reason for the Sabbatical year prohibition, since it is not a time of mourning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's ruling of Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya prohibiting making a water channel during Chol HaMoed and the Sabbatical year, and questions the reason for the Sabbatical year prohibition.

items.text: Debate between Rabbi Zeira and Rabbi Abba bar Memel on the reason for the Sabbatical prohibition
items.text_en: Debate between Rabbi Zeira and Rabbi Abba bar Memel on the reason for the Sabbatical prohibition
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira and Rabbi Abba bar Memel dispute the reason: one says it appears like one is 'oder' (clearing a field), the other says it prepares the banks for planting. The Gemara explores the practical differences between these reasons, considering cases where water follows or where one removes soil.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute between Rabbi Zeira and Rabbi Abba bar Memel regarding the reason for the Sabbatical prohibition of making a water channel (אמה): one says it appears like one is 'oder' (clearing a field), the other says it prepares the banks for planting.

The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two reasons, and answers that if water follows the digging, the 'preparing banks' reason applies but the 'appears like oder' reason does not.

The Gemara objects that even for the 'appears like oder' reason, one should also worry about the 'preparing banks' reason, and resolves that when one removes soil and throws it outside, the 'preparing banks' reason does not apply, but the 'appears like oder' reason does.

The Gemara objects that for the 'preparing banks' reason, one should also worry about the 'appears like oder' reason, and resolves that even an 'oder' (one who clears a field) places the removed soil in its place, so the appearance is not problematic.

items.text: Amemar's teaching and the contradiction in Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's rulings
items.text_en: Amemar's teaching and the contradiction in Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's rulings
items.desc_en: Amemar teaches the reason as 'appears like one who clears' and raises a contradiction from another Mishnah where Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya permits making a manure pile unless one deepens three handbreadths. The Gemara resolves this with two answers: either he deepened, or the manure itself testifies.

sub.desc_en: Amemar teaches the reason for the prohibition as 'appears like one who clears' (נראה כעודר), and raises a contradiction between Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's rulings.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya permits making a manure pile unless one deepens three handbreadths, contradicting his earlier strict position.

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira and Rabbi Abba bar Memel's answers
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira and Rabbi Abba bar Memel's answers
sub.desc_en: Two Amoraim resolve the contradiction: one says the case is where he deepened the pile, and the other says the manure itself testifies that he is not clearing the field.

items.text: Repairing a damaged water channel and the measurement dilemma
items.text_en: Repairing a damaged water channel and the measurement dilemma
items.desc_en: The Mishnah permits repairing a 'mekulkelet' (damaged) water channel. Rabbi Abba explains: if it was one handbreadth deep, one may deepen it to six. The Gemara questions the limits: a half-handbreadth to three is trivial, two to twelve is too much work. It then asks about two to seven, leaving the question unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah permits repairing a damaged water channel during חול המועד (the intermediate festival days).
The Gemara asks what 'mekulkelet' (damaged) means in this context.
Rabbi Abba explains that a damaged channel is one that was one handbreadth deep, and one may deepen it to six handbreadths.
The Gemara questions the limits: a half-handbreadth deepened to three is trivial and not worth discussing.
The Gemara questions whether two handbreadths deepened to twelve is too much work and therefore forbidden.
The Gemara asks about the intermediate case of two handbreadths deepened to seven, debating whether the extra handbreadth of depth constitutes excessive labor.
The question remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Permissibility of digging channels for public use
items.text_en: Permissibility of digging channels for public use
items.desc_en: Abaye, Rabbi Yirmeya, and Rav Ashi permitted digging or clearing channels for public water supply. Rav Ashi reasons that since many drink from it, it is considered a public need, and the Mishnah permits all public needs during Chol HaMoed.

sub.desc_en: Abaye permitted the people of Bar Hamdakh to clear a channel (digging out a waterway for public use).
Rabbi Yirmeya permitted the people of Sachuta to dig a blocked channel (to restore water flow).
Rav Ashi permitted the people of Mata Machseya to clear the Burinitz canal (to restore its flow).
Rav Ashi explains that since many drink from it, it is considered a public need, and the Mishnah permits all public needs during Chol HaMoed.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may clear (חטיטה) water channels in the public domain during Chol HaMoed, but not dig (חפירה) them.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that during Chol HaMoed one may clear (חטיטה) water channels in the public domain but not dig (חפירה) them.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's distinction
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's distinction
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov citing Rabbi Yochanan limits the Mishnah to when the public does not need the water, but if needed, even digging is permitted. The Gemara challenges this with a baraita and resolves the contradictions by reinterpreting the baraita to distinguish between cases of need.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov in the name of Rabbi Yochanan limits the Mishnah's allowance of digging (חפירה) to cases where the public does not need the water, but if the public needs it, even digging is permitted.

The Gemara objects: Is digging really permitted when the public needs water? It cites a baraita that permits only clearing (חטיטה) of public pits, not digging (חפירה), implying that even when the public needs water, digging is forbidden.
The Gemara initially answers that the baraita refers to a case where the public does not need the water, so digging is forbidden.

The Gemara objects further: If the baraita is about a case where the public does not need water, then by analogy, for an individual who does not need water, even clearing (חטיטה) should be forbidden, but another baraita permits clearing for an individual who does not need water.

The Gemara considers the opposite interpretation: if the baraita is about a case where the individual needs water, then by analogy, for the public who need water, digging should be permitted, but another baraita forbids digging for the public even when they need water.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by reinterpreting the first baraita: it permits clearing for an individual who needs water, and all the more so for the public who need water (even digging is permitted); it forbids digging for the public who do not need water, and all the more so for an individual who does not need water (even clearing is forbidden).

items.text: Rav Ashi's proof from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's proof from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi argues that the Mishnah's phrase 'all public needs' includes digging. The Gemara initially deflects by citing other public needs, but then concludes that the Mishnah indeed supports Rav Ashi.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi argues that the Mishnah's phrase 'all public needs' (עושין כל צורכי רבים) implies digging (חפירה) is included.
The Gemara deflects, suggesting the Mishnah's 'all' refers to other public needs like clearing roads, fixing streets, and measuring mikva'ot.
A baraita adds that if they fail to do these repairs, blood is accounted against them, citing the verse 'והיה עליך דמים'.
The Gemara concludes that since the Mishnah already explicitly lists those other needs, the word 'all' must indeed come to include digging (חפירה), confirming Rav Ashi's proof.

items.text: Source for marking graves
items.text_en: Source for marking graves
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi finds a hint for marking graves from the verse about seeing a bone and building a marker. Ravina questions how this could be known before Ezekiel, and Rav Ashi explains that it was a tradition later supported by a verse.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that graves are marked.
Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi cites a verse from Ezekiel as a hint for marking graves.
Ravina asks Rav Ashi: before Ezekiel, who said this?
Rav Ashi answers that it was a tradition (גמרא) later supported by a verse, as with Rav Chisda's teaching about Ezekiel.

items.text: Various sources for the obligation to mark graves and remove obstacles
items.text_en: Various sources for the obligation to mark graves and remove obstacles
items.desc_en: Multiple Amoraim offer different verses as sources for marking graves and removing obstacles: Rabbi Avahu from 'and the impure shall call out impure', Abaye from 'do not place a stumbling block', and others. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi adds that one who marks paths merits seeing God's salvation.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu derives the obligation to mark graves from the verse 'וְטָמֵא טָמֵא יִקְרָא' (the impure shall call out 'impure'), explaining that impurity itself calls out to warn people to keep away.
The Gemara objects that the verse 'וְטָמֵא טָמֵא יִקְרָא' is already needed for the halacha that a person must announce their own impurity so the public can pray for mercy.
The Gemara resolves that the doubled wording 'וְטָמֵא טָמֵא' (impure, impure) teaches both obligations: announcing impurity and marking graves.
Abaye derives the obligation from 'וְלִפְנֵי עִוֵּר לֹא תִתֵּן מִכְשׁוֹל' (do not place a stumbling block before the blind), and Rav Pappa from 'סֹלּוּ סֹלּוּ פַּנּוּ דָרֶךְ' (clear the way).

Rav Chinana cites 'הָרִימוּ מִכְשׁוֹל מִדֶּרֶךְ עַמִּי' (remove the stumbling block from My people's path), and Rabbi Yehoshua bar Rav Idi cites 'וְהוֹדַעְתָּ לָהֶם אֶת הַדֶּרֶךְ' (make known to them the way).

Mar Zutra cites 'וְהִזַּרְתֶּם אֶת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מִטּוּמְאָתָם' (warn the children of Israel from their impurity), and Rav Ashi cites 'וּשְׁמַרְתֶּם אֶת מִשְׁמַרְתִּי' (guard My charge) to mean make a safeguard for My charge.
Ravina cites 'וְשָׂם דֶּרֶךְ אַרְאֶנּוּ בְּיֵשַׁע אֱלֹהִים' (and sets a path, I will show him the salvation of God).
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi adds that one who marks paths merits seeing God's salvation, interpreting 'וְשָׂם' (and sets) as 'וְשָׁם' (and places a marker).

items.text: Anecdote about Rabbi Yannai's student
items.text_en: Anecdote about Rabbi Yannai's student
items.desc_en: The daf ends with a brief story about Rabbi Yannai's student who would challenge him daily but refrained on the Shabbat of the festival.

sub.desc_en: The gemara relates that Rabbi Yannai had a student who would challenge him daily but refrained from doing so on the Shabbat of the festival.

items.text: Opening verse citation
items.text_en: Opening verse citation
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse from Psalms to support the practice of marking graves.

items.text: Baraita on marking graves
items.text_en: Baraita on marking graves
items.desc_en: A baraita lists which corpse parts require marking (e.g., spine, skull, majority of structure or count) and which do not (e.g., an olive's bulk, a barley-sized bone). It also discusses marking for uncertain graves (ספיקות) like סככות, פרעות, and בית הפרס, and rules about placing markers to avoid causing impurity.

items.text: Question on an olive's bulk and Rav Pappa's answer
items.text_en: Question on an olive's bulk and Rav Pappa's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why an olive's bulk of a corpse is not marked, since it imparts impurity in a tent. Rav Pappa answers that the baraita deals with a precisely measured olive's bulk (מצומצם) which will eventually decay, so it is better to risk temporary loss of teruma and sacrifices than permanent loss.

items.text: Explanation of ספיקות: סככות, פרעות, and בית הפרס
items.text_en: Explanation of ספיקות: סככות, פרעות, and בית הפרס
items.desc_en: The Gemara defines the uncertain grave types: סככות (a tree overhanging the ground), פרעות (protruding stones from a fence), and בית הפרס (a field plowed over a grave, which creates a hundred cubits of impurity). It cites a mishnah about the measure of בית הפרס.

items.text: Question on בית הפרס impurity and Rav Pappa's resolution
items.text_en: Question on בית הפרס impurity and Rav Pappa's resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether בית הפרס imparts impurity in a tent, citing Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel that one may sift and walk through it, and Rav Yehuda bar Ami citing Ulla that a trodden בית הפרס is pure. Rav Pappa resolves the contradiction: one case is a field where a grave was lost (מטמא באוהל), the other where a grave was plowed (טהור).

items.text: Clarification of three types of בית הפרס
items.text_en: Clarification of three types of בית הפרס
items.desc_en: The Gemara confirms that a field plowed over a grave is indeed called בית הפרס, citing a mishnah listing three types: a field where a grave was lost, a field where a grave was plowed, and a field of mourners (שדה בוכין). It explains that שדה בוכין is where they eulogize the dead, and Avimi says the reason is due to despair of the owners (יאוש בעלים).

items.text: Discussion on marking a plowed field and Rav Pappa's distinction
items.text_en: Discussion on marking a plowed field and Rav Pappa's distinction
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a field plowed over a grave requires marking, citing a baraita about finding a marked field with trees indicating a plowed grave. Rabbi Yehuda requires an elder or student to interpret. Rav Pappa explains the baraita refers to a field where a grave was lost and was marked. The Gemara then asks about the possibility of trees inside and grave outside, and Ulla answers that the trees stand on the borders.

items.text: Gemara's question and answer about marking trees
items.text_en: Gemara's question and answer about marking trees
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the concern about marking trees is that impurity might be inside the tree while the trees are outside, and answers that it refers to intertwined trees. Alternatively, it cites the principle that markers are not moved far from the impurity to avoid wasting land.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the concern about marking trees is that impurity might be inside the tree while the trees are outside.
The Gemara answers that the case involves intertwined trees, where the impurity is inside the cluster.
The Gemara offers an alternative answer, citing the principle that markers are not moved far from the impurity to avoid wasting land of Israel.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's requirement and Abaye's inference
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's requirement and Abaye's inference
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda requires that an elder or student be present when marking graves because not everyone is knowledgeable. Abaye infers from this that a Torah scholar in a town is responsible for all communal matters.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda requires that a sage or student be present when marking graves, because not everyone is knowledgeable in the matter.
Abaye infers from Rabbi Yehuda's statement that a Torah scholar (צורבא מרבנן) present in a town bears responsibility for all communal matters.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's ruling on marked stones and Rav Pappa's resolution
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's ruling on marked stones and Rav Pappa's resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that if one finds a marked stone, the area under it is impure; if two stones with lime between them, the area between is impure. The Gemara objects with a baraita that mentions a plowed strip (חורש) between stones. Rav Pappa resolves the contradiction by explaining that the case is where lime is spread on the tops of the stones and drips down; if there is a plowed strip, the lime is attributed to the plowing and the area is pure.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that a single marked stone renders the area under it impure, while two stones with lime between them render the area between impure, but without lime the area is pure.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that mentions a plowed strip (חורש) as a condition for purity between two stones, contradicting Rav Yehuda's ruling.

Rav Pappa resolves the contradiction by explaining that the case involves lime spread on the tops of the stones dripping down; if there is a plowed strip, the lime is attributed to the plowing and the area is pure, otherwise it is from the stones and impure.

items.text: Rabbi Asi's ruling on multiple marked stones
items.text_en: Rabbi Asi's ruling on multiple marked stones
items.desc_en: Rabbi Asi rules that if one marked stone is found, it is impure but the whole field is pure; with two or three, they are impure but the field is pure; with four, they are pure but the whole field is impure. This is because markers are not moved far from the impurity to avoid wasting land.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Asi rules that one, two, or three marked stones are impure but the field is pure, while four marked stones are pure but the entire field is impure.
Mar's principle is cited: markers are not moved far from the impurity to avoid wasting land of Israel, explaining why four stones mark the entire field as impure.

items.text: Gemara's question on going out for kilayim during Chol HaMoed
items.text_en: Gemara's question on going out for kilayim during Chol HaMoed
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the court goes out to inspect kilayim during Chol HaMoed. The Gemara questions why this is done during Chol HaMoed when the Mishnah in Shekalim says announcements about kilayim are made on the first of Adar. Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina offer two resolutions: one distinguishes between early and late crops, the other between seeds and vegetables.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the court goes out to inspect kilayim (mixed species) during Chol HaMoed.
The Gemara questions why the court goes out for kilayim during Chol HaMoed, citing a contradiction from the Mishnah in Shekalim that announcements about kilayim are made on the first of Adar.
The Gemara cites a baraita that on the fifteenth of Adar the court goes out to inspect kilayim, reinforcing the contradiction with the Mishnah's statement about Chol HaMoed.

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina offer two resolutions: one distinguishes between early crops (בכיר) and late crops (אפיל), and the other distinguishes between seeds (זרעים) and vegetables (ירקות).

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's distinction regarding recognizable buds
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's distinction regarding recognizable buds
items.desc_en: Rabbi Asi quotes Rabbi Yochanan that the earlier announcement about kilayim applies only when the bud is not yet recognizable, but if the bud is recognizable, the court goes out during Chol HaMoed.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Asi quotes Rabbi Yochanan resolving the contradiction by distinguishing between cases where the bud is not yet recognizable (the earlier announcement suffices) and where it is recognizable (the court goes out during Chol HaMoed).

items.text: Reason for going out during Chol HaMoed and source of wages
items.text_en: Reason for going out during Chol HaMoed and source of wages
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the inspection is specifically during Chol HaMoed. Rabbi Yochanan explains it is because laborers are cheaper then. Rav Zevid or Rav Mesharshiya infer that the wages are paid from the Temple treasury chamber, otherwise there would be no benefit. Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak cites a Mishnah to define the wage limit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the inspection for kilayim is specifically performed during חול המועד (Chol HaMoed, the intermediate days of a festival).
Rabbi Yochanan explains that the inspection is done during חול המועד because laborers are cheaper (שכר פעולה דמוזלי גבן) at that time.

sub.text: Rav Zevid or Rav Mesharshiya's inference
sub.text_en: Rav Zevid or Rav Mesharshiya's inference
sub.desc_en: Rav Zevid (or alternatively Rav Mesharshiya) infers from this that the wages for the inspectors are paid from the Temple treasury chamber (תרומת הלשכה), not from private funds.

sub.text: Rav Zevid or Rav Mesharshiya's reasoning
sub.text_en: Rav Zevid or Rav Mesharshiya's reasoning
sub.desc_en: He explains that if the wages came from private funds, there would be no financial benefit to the public from the cheaper labor, since the laborers could demand any amount.
The Gemara asks what the maximum wage limit is for the inspectors.
Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak answers by citing a Mishnah that defines the wage limit as 'every se'ah that has in it' (the standard rate for such work).

items.text: Weeding dispute and the enactment of declaring the entire field ownerless
items.text_en: Weeding dispute and the enactment of declaring the entire field ownerless
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a contradiction between the Mishnah, which permits weeding only a quarter-kav of another species, and a baraita that requires declaring the entire field ownerless. It explains that the Mishnah reflects the earlier practice before the enactment, while the baraita describes the later enactment. The baraita details the historical progression: initially, weeds were uprooted and fed to animals, then left on paths, and finally the entire field was declared ownerless to prevent landowner joy.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's ruling that one may remove a quarter-kav of another species, and then challenges it with a baraita that requires declaring the entire field ownerless.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that the Mishnah reflects the practice before the enactment, while the baraita describes the practice after the enactment.
The baraita details the historical progression: initially weeds were uprooted and fed to animals, then left on paths, and finally the entire field was declared ownerless to prevent landowner joy.

items.text: Mishnah: Irrigation and planting restrictions
items.text_en: Mishnah: Irrigation and planting restrictions
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute between Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov and the Sages. Rabbi Eliezer permits drawing water from tree to tree but not irrigating the entire field, and prohibits watering seeds that were not watered before the festival. The Sages permit both actions.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov permits drawing water from tree to tree but prohibits irrigating the entire field and watering seeds not watered before the festival.
The Sages permit both drawing water from tree to tree and watering seeds that were not watered before the festival.

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying irrigation rules and the case of a parched field
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying irrigation rules and the case of a parched field
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda distinguishes between a field that was previously watered (permitted) and one that was not (prohibited), and adds that a 'parched field' (שדה מטוננת) is permitted. A baraita supports this. Ravina deduces that one may flood a field during Chol HaMoed, comparing it to a parched field which is permitted because it prevents cracking.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that a parched field (שדה מטוננת) is permitted for irrigation during Chol HaMoed.
A baraita supports Rav Yehuda, distinguishing between seeds that were watered before the festival (permitted) and those that were not (prohibited), and adds that a parched field is permitted.
The baraita reiterates that a parched field is permitted, and notes that the Sages permit both a parched field and a dry field (שדה גריד) during Chol HaMoed.

Ravina deduces that flooding a field (תרביצא) is permitted during Chol HaMoed, reasoning that just as a dry field (שדה גריד) is permitted because it prevents cracking, so too flooding prevents cracking.

items.text: Dispute about irrigating a white field (שדה לבן) during the Sabbatical year and Chol HaMoed
items.text_en: Dispute about irrigating a white field (שדה לבן) during the Sabbatical year and Chol HaMoed
items.desc_en: A baraita prohibits irrigating a white field during Chol HaMoed but permits it during the Sabbatical year. Another baraita permits it in both. Rav Huna resolves the contradiction by attributing the first to Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov and the second to the Sages. A third baraita permits irrigating a white field before the Sabbatical year to produce vegetables during the Sabbatical, and even during the Sabbatical to produce vegetables after it.

sub.desc_en: A baraita rules that one may irrigate a white field (שדה לבן) during the Sabbatical year but not during Chol HaMoed.
The Gemara objects by citing a contradictory baraita that permits irrigating a white field both during Chol HaMoed and the Sabbatical year.
Rav Huna resolves the contradiction by attributing the first baraita to Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov and the second to the Sages.
A third baraita permits irrigating a white field before the Sabbatical year to produce vegetables during it, and even during the Sabbatical year to produce vegetables after it.

items.text: Mishnah: Trapping pests and repairing fences
items.text_en: Mishnah: Trapping pests and repairing fences
items.desc_en: The Mishnah permits trapping the 'ishut' (a blind creature) and mice in an orchard or white field in the usual manner during Chol HaMoed and the Sabbatical year. The Sages distinguish: in an orchard, one may trap in the usual manner; in a white field, only in an unusual manner. Additionally, one may repair a breach in a fence during Chol HaMoed, and during the Sabbatical year one may build it in the usual manner.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may trap the 'ishut' (a blind creature) and mice in an orchard or white field in the usual manner during Chol HaMoed and the Sabbatical year.
The Sages distinguish: in an orchard one may trap in the usual manner, but in a white field only in an unusual manner.
The Mishnah adds that one may repair a breach in a fence during Chol HaMoed, and during the Sabbatical year one may build it in the usual manner.

items.text: Gemara: Identifying the 'ishut'
items.text_en: Gemara: Identifying the 'ishut'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that 'ishut' is a creature without eyes, citing a verse from Psalms: 'Like a snail that melts away as it goes, like a stillborn of a woman that never saw the sun.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the creature 'אישות' (ishut) is.
Rav Yehuda defines 'אישות' as a creature without eyes.

sub.text: Rava bar Yishmael or Rav Yeimar bar Shelemia's scriptural support
sub.text_en: Rava bar Yishmael or Rav Yeimar bar Shelemia's scriptural support
sub.desc_en: Rava bar Yishmael (or alternatively Rav Yeimar bar Shelemia) cites a verse from Psalms (58:9) that describes a creature like a snail and a stillborn that never saw the sun, supporting Rav Yehuda's definition.

items.text: Baraita: Trapping and destroying ant holes
items.text_en: Baraita: Trapping and destroying ant holes
items.desc_en: A baraita permits trapping the 'ishut' and mice in both white and orchard fields in the usual manner, and also permits destroying ant holes. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel explains the method: one brings dirt from one hole and places it into another, causing the ants to choke each other. Rav Yeimar bar Shelemia adds in the name of Abaye that this method is only effective when the holes are on opposite sides of a river with no bridge, no camel, and no ford.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that one may trap the 'ishut' and mice in both white and orchard fields in the usual manner, and may destroy ant holes.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel explains the method: one brings dirt from one hole and places it into another, causing the ants to choke each other.

sub.text: Rav Yeimar bar Shelemia in the name of Abaye
sub.text_en: Rav Yeimar bar Shelemia in the name of Abaye
sub.desc_en: Rav Yeimar bar Shelemia adds in the name of Abaye that this method is only effective when the holes are on opposite sides of a river with no bridge, no camel, and no ford.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Distance for trapping
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Distance for trapping
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may trap animals from a field up to a parasang away.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the maximum distance for trapping animals during חול המועד (the intermediate festival days) is up to a parasang.

items.text: Baraitot on trapping methods and location
items.text_en: Baraitot on trapping methods and location
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between an orchard and a white field, and a baraita explains the methods. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar adds a caveat about a white field near the city versus near an orchard.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda states the rule: in an orchard one may trap in the usual manner, but in a white field one must trap in an unusual manner.
A baraita explains the two methods: the usual method is digging a pit and hanging a net; the unusual method is driving a spit and striking with an axe to loosen the soil from underneath.

Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar adds a caveat: the unusual method applies only to a white field near the city, but for a white field near an orchard even the usual method is forbidden lest animals escape and destroy the trees.

items.text: Repairing a breach in the wall
items.text_en: Repairing a breach in the wall
items.desc_en: The Mishnah permits repairing a breach during the festival. Rav Yosef describes the method, and a baraita adds that one uses a pebble but not mortar. Rav Chisda distinguishes between a garden wall and a courtyard wall.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may repair a breach (פרצה) during the festival.
Rav Yosef explains that the repair is done with הוצא (branches) and דפנא (palm branches).
A baraita adds that one binds the breach with a pebble (צרור) but does not plaster with mortar (טיט).
Rav Chisda distinguishes: the restriction applies only to a garden wall (כותל הגינה), but a courtyard wall (כותל החצר) may be built in the usual manner.

items.text: Gemara's challenge to Rav Chisda from a wall leaning into public domain
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge to Rav Chisda from a wall leaning into public domain
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to refute Rav Chisda with a baraita about a wall leaning into public domain, which is demolished and rebuilt normally due to danger. Rav Chisda distinguishes between demolishing and building. The Gemara objects that one could just demolish without rebuilding, but Rav Chisda explains that would deter demolition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to support Rav Chisda's position by citing a baraita about a wall leaning into the public domain, which is demolished and rebuilt normally due to danger.
An alternative version presents the baraita as a refutation of Rav Chisda, arguing that only danger permits building normally, not other cases.
Rav Chisda distinguishes the cases: there one demolishes and rebuilds, here one only builds without demolishing.
The Gemara objects that one could simply demolish without rebuilding, but Rav Chisda explains that would deter people from demolishing.

items.text: Rav Ashi's proof from the Mishnah in Shevi'it
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's proof from the Mishnah in Shevi'it
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi proves Rav Chisda's distinction from a Mishnah in Shevi'it that permits building a garden wall normally in the seventh year, implying it is not considered agricultural work.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi opens by asserting that the Mishnah in Shevi'it supports Rav Chisda's distinction, citing its ruling that in the seventh year one builds a garden wall normally.
The Gemara questions which type of wall the Mishnah refers to, noting that if it were a courtyard wall the ruling would be obvious.
Rav Ashi answers that the Mishnah must refer to a garden wall, and even though it appears to be protecting fruit, it is permitted — proving Rav Chisda's point.

items.text: Mishnah: Examining skin blemishes on Chol HaMoed
items.text_en: Mishnah: Examining skin blemishes on Chol HaMoed
items.desc_en: The Mishnah records a dispute: Rabbi Meir permits examining blemishes only to be lenient, while the Sages forbid both lenient and stringent examinations.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Meir permits examining skin blemishes on Chol HaMoed only to be lenient (להקל), not to be stringent (להחמיר).
The Sages forbid examining blemishes entirely on Chol HaMoed, whether for leniency or stringency.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yossi, and Rava's resolution
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yossi, and Rava's resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita presents Rabbi Yossi's view forbidding both lenient and stringent examinations. Rabbi distinguishes between a confined person and a confirmed leper. Rava clarifies that all agree a pure person is not examined, and the dispute is only about the first confinement.

sub.desc_en: A baraita presents the dispute between Rabbi Meir (who permits lenient examination) and Rabbi Yossi (who forbids both lenient and stringent examination, arguing that leniency leads to stringency).
Rabbi (Judah the Prince) resolves the dispute: Rabbi Meir's lenient view applies to a confined person (מוסגר), while Rabbi Yossi's stringent view applies to a confirmed leper (מוחלט).
Rava clarifies that all agree a pure person is not examined, and the dispute is only about the first confinement (הסגר ראשון).

items.text: Dispute about the kohen's role in declaring purity
items.text_en: Dispute about the kohen's role in declaring purity
items.desc_en: Two opinions are presented: one holds that the declaration depends on the kohen (if pure he says 'tahor', if impure he remains silent), the other derives from the verse 'to purify him or to defile him' that the kohen must explicitly declare both.

sub.text: Stam's presentation of the first opinion
sub.text_en: Stam's presentation of the first opinion
sub.desc_en: The first opinion holds that the declaration depends on the kohen: if pure he says 'tahor', if impure he remains silent.

sub.text: Stam's presentation of the second opinion
sub.text_en: Stam's presentation of the second opinion
sub.desc_en: The second opinion derives from the verse 'to purify him or to defile him' that the kohen must explicitly declare both.

items.text: Rabbi's ruling on Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Meir
items.text_en: Rabbi's ruling on Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Meir
items.desc_en: Rabbi stated that Rabbi Yosei's words apply to a muchlat and Rabbi Meir's to a musgar, but a baraita states the opposite. The Gemara resolves this by saying there are Tannaim who differ in their interpretation of Rabbi's view: one holds that communal honor is more important, the other that his wife's honor is more important.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports Rabbi's ruling that Rabbi Yosei's words apply to a muchlat (confirmed leper) and Rabbi Meir's to a musgar (quarantined leper).
The Gemara objects that a baraita states the opposite assignment of opinions.

The Gemara resolves that there are Tannaim who differ in interpreting Rabbi's view: one holds that communal honor (צוותא דעלמא) is more important, the other that his wife's honor (צוותא דאשתו) is more important.

items.text: Permissibility of marital relations for a muchlat
items.text_en: Permissibility of marital relations for a muchlat
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a muchlat is permitted marital relations, and answers yes, citing a baraita that derives from 'and he shall dwell outside his tent' that he is forbidden marital relations, with 'tent' referring to his wife. Rabbi Yehuda limits this to days of counting, not days of his floccosity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a muchlat (confirmed leper) is permitted marital relations.
The Gemara answers yes, citing a supporting baraita.
The baraita derives from the verse 'and he shall dwell outside his tent' that a leper is forbidden marital relations, interpreting 'tent' as his wife.
Rabbi Yehuda limits the prohibition of marital relations to the days of counting (ימי ספירו), not the days of his floccosity (ימי חלוטו).

items.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's kal vachomer and the dispute
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's kal vachomer and the dispute
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda argues that if he is forbidden during the seven days of counting, then certainly during days of floccosity. Rabbi Chiyya testified before Rabbi that King Yotam was born to Uzziah during his days of floccosity, and Rabbi agreed. The dispute is whether the Torah's explicit prohibition during counting implies a kal vachomer for floccosity, or whether what is revealed is revealed and what is not is not.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's statement
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda's statement
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda states a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument): if the metzora is forbidden during the seven days of counting, then certainly he is forbidden during the days of floccosity.
Rabbi Chiyya testifies before Rabbi that King Yotam was born to Uzziah during his days of floccosity, and Rabbi agrees, supporting the kal vachomer.

The Gemara explains the dispute: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda holds that the Torah's explicit prohibition during counting implies a kal vachomer for floccosity, while the first opinion holds that what is revealed is revealed and what is not is not.

items.text: The kohen's discretion in inspection
items.text_en: The kohen's discretion in inspection
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the matter depends on the kohen, and answers yes, citing a baraita that derives from 'and on the day of being seen' that there are days you see and days you do not see.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the matter of inspection depends on the kohen's discretion.
The Gemara answers affirmatively and cites a baraita as support.
The baraita derives from the verse 'וּבְיוֹם הֵרָאוֹת בּוֹ' (and on the day of being seen) that there are days when the kohen sees and days when he does not see, implying discretion.

items.text: Delaying inspection for a groom or festival
items.text_en: Delaying inspection for a groom or festival
items.desc_en: From this it is said: a groom who develops a lesion is given seven days of the wedding feast, and similarly for a festival, according to Rabbi Yehuda. Rabbi says he does not need this, as the verse 'and the kohen shall command and they shall clear the house' shows that if we delay for a mundane matter, certainly for a mitzvah. Abaye and Rava dispute what is between them: Abaye says it is a matter of interpreting verses, Rava says it is a matter of mundane vs. mitzvah. Rabbi Yehuda does not learn from there because it is a novelty.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that a groom who develops a lesion is given seven days of the wedding feast, and similarly for a festival, according to Rabbi Yehuda.

Rabbi says the groom does not need this delay, reasoning from the verse 'וְצִוָּה הַכֹּהֵן וּפִנּוּ אֶת הַבַּיִת' (the kohen shall command and they shall clear the house): if we delay for a mundane matter, certainly for a mitzvah.
The gemara asks what is the practical difference between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi.
Abaye says the difference is in how they interpret the verses.
Rava says the difference is whether the matter is mundane or a mitzvah.
The gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda does not learn from the verse because the law of clearing the house is a novelty (חידוש) and cannot be used for a קל וחומר (a fortiori) argument.

items.text: Gemara's justification for the extra verse
items.text_en: Gemara's justification for the extra verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Torah needed both the phrase 'on the day it appears' and 'the priest shall command' regarding a house with tzara'at. Rabbi argues that each phrase teaches a different leniency: one for a mitzvah matter)Skip, the other for non-body impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Torah needed both phrases, since wood and stones are not inherently susceptible to טומאה (ritual impurity).

Rabbi explains that each phrase is necessary: 'וּבְיוֹם הֵרָאוֹת בּוֹ' teaches leniency for a מצוה (commandment) matter, while 'וְצִוָּה הַכֹּהֵן' teaches leniency for non-body impurity, and without both, one might mistakenly restrict the leniency.

items.text: Derivation of 'some days you see, some days you do not'
items.text_en: Derivation of 'some days you see, some days you do not'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the derivation from the extra 'and on the day' that there are days when the priest sees the plague and days when he does not. Abaye and Rava each offer their own derivation from the verse.

sub.desc_en: Mar states the principle that there are days when the priest sees the plague and days when he does not.
The Gemara asks: what is the scriptural basis for this principle?
Abaye derives the principle from the extra 'וּבְיוֹם' (and on the day) in the verse, implying that some days are excluded.
Rava derives the same principle from the entire extra phrase 'וּבְיוֹם' being superfluous, indicating a limitation.
The Gemara objects that Abaye's derivation is needed to teach that inspection is done by day and not by night.

The Gemara explains that Rava derives 'by day and not by night' from the phrase 'לְכׇל מַרְאֵה עֵינֵי הַכֹּהֵן' (to all the sight of the priest's eyes), and Abaye uses that phrase to exclude a priest blind in one eye.

The Gemara confirms that Rava also needs that verse for the exclusion of a blind priest, and then derives 'by day and not by night' from the verse 'כְּנֶגַע נִרְאָה לִי בַּבָּיִת' (like a plague appeared to me in the house), with 'לִי' (to me) excluding light.

The Gemara objects that Abaye might have thought the exclusion of light applies only to impurity not of the body, but for bodily impurity even light would be valid, so the extra verse teaches otherwise.

items.text: Debate over the source for 'by day and not at night'
items.text_en: Debate over the source for 'by day and not at night'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Abaye and Rava derive the rule that inspection is by day and not at night. Abaye uses the extra 'and on the day' for this, while Rava derives it from 'for every appearance of the priest's eyes'. The Gemara resolves the differences and shows that both agree on the final derivation from 'like a plague seen to me in the house'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the rule 'there is a day you see and a day you do not see' is derived from the verse.
Abaye explains that the extra 'וּבְיוֹם' (and on the day) teaches that there is a day you see and a day you do not see.
Rava argues that the entire phrase 'וּבְיוֹם' is superfluous, teaching the same distinction.
The Gemara objects that Abaye needs the extra 'וּבְיוֹם' to teach 'by day and not at night', not the day distinction.

The Gemara explains that Rava derives 'by day and not at night' from 'לְכׇל מַרְאֵה עֵינֵי הַכֹּהֵן' (for every appearance of the priest's eyes), while Abaye uses that verse to exclude a blind person in one eye.
The Gemara asks how Rava derives 'by day and not at night' if he uses 'לְכׇל מַרְאֵה עֵינֵי הַכֹּהֵן' for the blind person.

The Gemara answers that Rava derives 'by day and not at night' from 'כְּנֶגַע נִרְאָה לִי בַּבָּיִת' (like a plague seen to me in the house), and Abaye explains that without the extra verse, one might have thought that bodily impurity is also inspected at night.

items.text: Mishnah: Debate on gathering parents' bones
items.text_en: Mishnah: Debate on gathering parents' bones
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei. Rabbi Meir permits gathering the bones of one's parents because it is a joy for him, while Rabbi Yosei says it is mourning for him.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with Rabbi Meir's ruling that one may gather the bones of one's parents because it is a joy for him.
Rabbi Yosei counters that gathering the bones is an act of mourning for him.

items.text: Mishnah: Prohibition on eulogizing within thirty days before a festival
items.text_en: Mishnah: Prohibition on eulogizing within thirty days before a festival
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not stir up mourning for his deceased nor eulogize him within thirty days before a festival.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the prohibition on stirring up mourning or eulogizing within thirty days before a festival.

items.text: Gemara: Contradiction on mourning for bones
items.text_en: Gemara: Contradiction on mourning for bones
