items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita that says one who gathers his parents' bones mourns for them the entire day. Abaye resolves that the Mishnah means the joy of the festival overrides the mourning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita that says one who gathers his parents' bones mourns for them the entire day, implying mourning is required, while the Mishnah says it is a joy.
Rav Chisda adds that even if the bones are tied in his sheet, the mourning applies.
Abaye resolves the contradiction by explaining that the Mishnah means the joy of the festival overrides the mourning, so the gathering is a joy, not a mourning.

items.text: Gemara: Explanation of the thirty-day prohibition
items.text_en: Gemara: Explanation of the thirty-day prohibition
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the terms 'stir up' and the reason for thirty days. Rav Kahana citing Rav Yehuda citing Rav tells a story of a man who lost his travel funds to a eulogizer, leading to the decree.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks the meaning of the Mishnah's phrase 'לֹא יְעַרְעֵר עַל מֵתוֹ' (one shall not stir up [mourning] for his dead).
Rav explains that 'stirring up' refers to when a eulogizer in the West would say 'let all the bitter-hearted weep with him.'
The Gemara asks why the Mishnah specifies a thirty-day prohibition before the festival.

sub.text: Rav Kahana citing Rav Yehuda citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Kahana citing Rav Yehuda citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana in the name of Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav tells a story of a man who lost his travel funds to a eulogizer, leading to the decree of thirty days.

items.text: Shmuel's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Shmuel's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Shmuel offers a different explanation for the thirty-day period, though the text cuts off.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel begins to offer an alternative explanation for the thirty-day period, though the text cuts off.

items.text: Transition from previous daf
items.text_en: Transition from previous daf
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the reason for the thirty-day mourning period: the deceased is not forgotten from the heart for thirty days. It then asks what practical difference this makes, and answers that it matters for one who performs the mourning for free.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the reason for the thirty-day mourning period: the deceased is not forgotten from the heart for thirty days.
The Gemara asks what practical difference this reason makes.
The Gemara answers that the difference applies to one who performs the mourning for free (without payment).

items.text: Mishnah: Digging graves and making coffins
items.text_en: Mishnah: Digging graves and making coffins
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not dig burial niches or graves during Chol HaMoed, but one may finish preparing existing niches. One may make a grave enclosure and a coffin with the deceased in the courtyard. Rabbi Yehuda prohibits making a coffin unless the boards were prepared beforehand.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one may not dig burial niches or graves during Chol HaMoed, but may finish existing ones, and permits making a grave enclosure and a coffin with the deceased present; Rabbi Yehuda forbids making a coffin unless the boards were prepared beforehand.

items.text: Gemara: Definition of כוכין and קברים
items.text_en: Gemara: Definition of כוכין and קברים
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what are כוכין and what are קברים. Rav Yehuda explains: כוכין are dug out (caves), while קברים are built (structures). A baraita supports this distinction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what are the definitions of 'כוכין' (niches) and 'קברים' (graves) mentioned in the Mishnah.
Rav Yehuda explains that 'כוכין' are dug out (caves) while 'קברים' are built (structures).
A baraita is cited that supports Rav Yehuda's distinction between 'כוכין' and 'קברים'.

items.text: Gemara: How to finish a niche
items.text_en: Gemara: How to finish a niche
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the Mishnah's phrase 'but they may finish the niches.' Rav Yehuda says this means if the niche was too long, one may shorten it. A baraita teaches that one may lengthen and widen it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how one performs the act of 'finishing' (מחנכין) the niches mentioned in the Mishnah.
Rav Yehuda answers that if the niche was too long, one may shorten it.
A baraita teaches that one may also lengthen and widen the niche, expanding on Rav Yehuda's statement.

items.text: Gemara: Definition of נברכת
items.text_en: Gemara: Definition of נברכת
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is a נברכת. Rav Yehuda says it is a בקיע (a type of grave enclosure). A contradiction is raised from a baraita that mentions both נברכת and בקיע. Abaye, or alternatively Rav Kahana, resolves this by saying they refer to two different types: גיהא and בר גיהא.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what a נברכת (grave enclosure) is.
Rav Yehuda answers that a נברכת is a בקיע (a type of grave enclosure).
The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita that mentions both נברכת and בקיע as distinct terms.
Abaye, or alternatively Rav Kahana, resolves the contradiction by explaining that נברכת and בקיע refer to two different types of grave enclosures: גיהא and בר גיהא.

items.text: Gemara: Making a coffin with the deceased
items.text_en: Gemara: Making a coffin with the deceased
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that teaches one may do all needs of the deceased: cut his hair, wash his garment, and make a coffin from boards that were sawed before the festival. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds that one may even bring wood and saw it discreetly inside his house.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that one may perform all needs of the deceased, including cutting hair, washing garments, and making a coffin from boards sawed before the festival.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds that one may even bring wood and saw it discreetly inside his house.

items.text: Mishnah: Prohibition on marrying during Chol HaMoed
items.text_en: Mishnah: Prohibition on marrying during Chol HaMoed
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not marry women during Chol HaMoed, neither virgins nor widows, nor perform levirate marriage, because it is a joy for him. However, he may remarry his divorced wife. A woman may do her adornments during the festival. Rabbi Yehuda says she may not apply eye shadow because it is disfiguring. A layperson may sew normally, but a craftsman uses a cross-stitch. They may string beds; Rabbi Yose says they may tighten them.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating the prohibition on marrying during Chol HaMoed, including virgins, widows, and levirate marriage, because it is a joy for the groom.
The Mishnah adds an exception: a man may remarry his divorced wife during Chol HaMoed.
The Mishnah permits a woman to apply her adornments during the festival.
Rabbi Yehuda prohibits applying eye shadow because it is disfiguring.
The Mishnah rules that a layperson may sew normally, but a craftsman uses a cross-stitch.
The Mishnah permits stringing beds during Chol HaMoed.
Rabbi Yose says they may tighten the beds.

items.text: Gemara: Reasons for the marriage prohibition
items.text_en: Gemara: Reasons for the marriage prohibition
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: since it is a joy for him, what is the problem? Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel, and similarly Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Oshaya, and some say Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Chanina, answer: because one may not mix one joy with another joy. Rabbah bar Rav Huna says: because he would abandon the joy of the festival and engage in the joy of his wife.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why marriage is prohibited during the festival if it is a joy for the groom.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel, and others
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel, and others
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel, and similarly Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Oshaya or Rabbi Chanina, answer that one may not mix one joy (marriage) with another joy (the festival).
Rabbah bar Rav Huna gives a different reason: because the groom would abandon the joy of the festival and engage in the joy of his wife.

items.text: Gemara: Abaye's clarification and Rav's proof
items.text_en: Gemara: Abaye's clarification and Rav's proof
items.desc_en: Abaye says to Rav Yosef that the statement of Rabbah bar Rav Huna is actually from Rav, as Rav Daniel bar Katina said in the name of Rav: from where is it derived that one may not marry during Chol HaMoed? As it is stated: 'And you shall rejoice in your festival' — in your festival, not in your wife.

sub.desc_en: Abaye tells Rav Yosef that the statement of Rabbah bar Rav Huna is actually from Rav.

sub.text: Rav Daniel bar Katina citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Daniel bar Katina citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Daniel bar Katina reports in the name of Rav that the prohibition against marrying during Chol HaMoed is derived from the verse 'ושמחת בחגך' (and you shall rejoice in your festival), implying 'in your festival' and not 'in your wife'.

items.text: Gemara: Additional reasons from Ulla and Rabbi Yitzchak
items.text_en: Gemara: Additional reasons from Ulla and Rabbi Yitzchak
items.desc_en: Ulla says the reason is because of the trouble (involved in the wedding). Rabbi Yitzchak the smith says it is because of the neglect of procreation (since one might be too busy to fulfill the mitzvah during the festival).

sub.desc_en: Ulla gives the reason for the prohibition of marrying during the festival: because of the trouble (הטורח) involved in the wedding preparations.
Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha gives an alternative reason: because of the neglect of procreation (ביטול פריה ורביה), as one might be too busy to fulfill the mitzvah during the festival.

items.text: Gemara: Challenge from a baraita
items.text_en: Gemara: Challenge from a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that lists all those who are forbidden to marry during Chol HaMoed, implying a challenge to the earlier reasons.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that lists all those who are forbidden to marry during Chol HaMoed, challenging the earlier reasons given for the prohibition.

items.text: Resolving the contradiction about marrying on the eve of a festival
items.text_en: Resolving the contradiction about marrying on the eve of a festival
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah permits marrying on the eve of a festival, which contradicts all three explanations for the prohibition of marrying on the eve of Shabbat. It resolves each: for the reason of joy, the main joy is only one day; for the reason of burden, the main burden is only one day; for the reason of neglecting procreation, one does not delay for one day.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah permits marrying on the eve of a festival, which contradicts all three explanations for the prohibition of marrying on the eve of Shabbat.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction for the reason of joy: the main joy is only one day.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction for the reasons of burden and neglecting procreation: the main burden is only one day, and one does not delay procreation for one day.

items.text: Deriving the prohibition of mixing joy with joy from Solomon's dedication
items.text_en: Deriving the prohibition of mixing joy with joy from Solomon's dedication
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that one does not mix joy with joy, citing Solomon's fourteen-day dedication (seven for the Temple and seven for Sukkot). If mixing were permitted, he should have waited until Sukkot and done seven for each. Rejecting suggestions that he could have delayed or left a small part unfinished, the Gemara concludes from the redundant phrase 'seven days and seven days' that they were separate.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that one does not mix joy with joy, citing Solomon's fourteen-day dedication.
The Gemara objects that perhaps one does not delay but only acts when the opportunity arises, so Solomon could have left a small part unfinished.
The Gemara rejects leaving a part of the Temple building unfinished, but suggests leaving the 'cubit of the raven's nest' (אמה כליא עורב).
The Gemara rejects that too as part of the building's need, and concludes from the redundant phrase 'seven days and seven days' that the two celebrations were separate.

items.text: The story of Yom Kippur not observed and the Bat Kol
items.text_en: The story of Yom Kippur not observed and the Bat Kol
items.desc_en: Rabbi Parnakh quoting Rabbi Yochanan relates that in that year Israel did not observe Yom Kippur, and they feared they were liable for destruction. A Bat Kol assured them they were all destined for the World to Come. The Gemara explains their reasoning: a kal vachomer from the Tabernacle (where an individual sacrifice overrides Shabbat) to the Temple (with a communal sacrifice and Yom Kippur under karet). It then questions why they worried, since the Tabernacle's case involved God's needs while here it is human needs; but they could have eaten and drunk? The answer: there is no joy without eating and drinking.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Parnakh in the name of Rabbi Yochanan relates that in a certain year Israel did not observe Yom Kippur, and they feared destruction, but a Bat Kol (heavenly voice) assured them they are all destined for the World to Come.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the kal vachomer
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the kal vachomer
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that they derived a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument): if the Tabernacle, whose sanctity is not eternal, and an individual sacrifice overrides Shabbat under penalty of stoning, then the Temple, whose sanctity is eternal, with a communal sacrifice on Yom Kippur under penalty of כרת (excision), certainly overrides the prohibition.

The Gemara objects: why were they worried? In the Tabernacle the sacrifice was for God's needs (צורך גבוה), but here it is for human needs (צורך הדיוט); they could have eaten and drunk without violating Yom Kippur.
The Gemara resolves: there is no joy without eating and drinking, so the celebration required consumption, which conflicted with Yom Kippur.

items.text: Deriving that the Tabernacle and Temple override Shabbat and Yom Kippur
items.text_en: Deriving that the Tabernacle and Temple override Shabbat and Yom Kippur
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks the source that the Tabernacle overrides Shabbat, citing verses about the dedication days. It rejects the possibility that the days were only those suitable for sacrifices, using a second verse to establish that all days were consecutive. Similarly, it derives that the Temple overrides Yom Kippur from the verse 'fourteen days' and a gezerah shavah of 'day' from the Tabernacle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that the Tabernacle overrides Shabbat, and proposes a verse about the dedication days, but immediately objects that the verse might refer only to days suitable for sacrifices.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cites the verse 'on the eleventh day' to prove that all eleven days were consecutive, using a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from 'day'.
The Gemara objects that the eleventh day might still refer only to days suitable for sacrifices, and cites another verse about the twelfth day to reinforce the argument.
The Gemara objects that the same doubt applies to the second verse, but then resolves that two verses would be superfluous if they only taught the same point.

The Gemara asks for the source that the Temple overrides Yom Kippur, proposes the verse 'fourteen days', objects that it might refer only to suitable days, and resolves with a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) of 'day' from the Tabernacle.

items.text: The Bat Kol and the forgiveness for David
items.text_en: The Bat Kol and the forgiveness for David
items.desc_en: The Bat Kol assured them all were destined for the World to Come. The Gemara explains the verse 'on the eighth day he sent the people away' — they found their wives pure, enjoyed the Divine Presence, and each wife conceived a male child. The Bat Kol's message is repeated. The Gemara then asks about the phrase 'to David His servant' and relates that when Solomon tried to bring the Ark into the Temple, the gates stuck together. After twenty-four songs and 'Lift up your heads', he was not answered until he said 'Remember the kindnesses of David Your servant'. Then the enemies of David were shamed, and all knew that God had forgiven David's sin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita from Tachlifa that quotes the verse about Solomon sending the people away on the eighth day, establishing the basis for the Bat Kol's message.

The Gemara interprets each phrase of the verse: 'to their tents' means they found their wives pure, 'rejoicing' means they enjoyed the Divine Presence, 'good of heart' means each wife conceived a male child, and 'all the goodness' refers to the Bat Kol's assurance.
The Gemara asks: regarding Israel, the forgiveness for Yom Kippur is understandable, but what specific goodness was done for David His servant?
Rav Yehuda citing Rav relates that when Solomon sought to bring the Ark into the Temple, the gates stuck together; he recited twenty-four songs and 'Lift up your heads' but was not answered.
Once Solomon said 'Remember the kindnesses of David Your servant', he was immediately answered; the enemies of David were shamed, and all knew that God had forgiven David's sin.

items.text: The law of a student taking leave from his teacher and the contradiction resolved
items.text_en: The law of a student taking leave from his teacher and the contradiction resolved
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yonatan ben Asmai and Rabbi Yehuda ben Gerim learned the section on vows from Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and took leave at night. In the morning they returned to take leave again. Rabbi Shimon asked why, and they taught him that a student who stays overnight in the same city must take leave again, as derived from the verses about Solomon sending the people on the eighth and twenty-third days. Rabbi Shimon then sent his son to them for a blessing. The son found them resolving a contradiction between verses about planning one's path: one verse says 'weigh the path of your feet' and another says 'do not weigh the path of life'. They answered that the former refers to a mitzvah that can be done by others.

sub.desc_en: The narrative opens: Rabbi Yonatan ben Asmai and Rabbi Yehuda ben Gerim studied the section on vows with Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, took leave at night, but returned in the morning to take leave again, prompting Rabbi Shimon's question.

sub.text: Rabbi Yonatan ben Asmai and Rabbi Yehuda ben Gerim
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yonatan ben Asmai and Rabbi Yehuda ben Gerim
sub.desc_en: They answer Rabbi Shimon's question by citing his own teaching: a student who stays overnight in the same city must take leave of his teacher again, derived from the verses about Solomon sending the people on the eighth and twenty-third days.
Rabbi Shimon sends his son to these men for a blessing, and the son finds them resolving a contradiction between verses.

sub.text: Rabbi Yonatan ben Asmai and Rabbi Yehuda ben Gerim
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yonatan ben Asmai and Rabbi Yehuda ben Gerim
sub.desc_en: They resolve the contradiction: one verse ('weigh the path of your feet') refers to a מצוה (commandment) that can be performed by others, while the other ('do not weigh the path of life') refers to one that cannot.

items.text: Resolving the contradiction between verses on Torah's value
items.text_en: Resolving the contradiction between verses on Torah's value
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: one verse says all your desires are not equal to Torah, implying heavenly desires are equal; another says all desires are not equal, even heavenly ones. The resolution distinguishes between a mitzvah that can be done by others and one that cannot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a mitzvah that cannot be performed by others (which is superior to heavenly desires) and one that can.

items.text: Blessings for a mourner and their interpretation
items.text_en: Blessings for a mourner and their interpretation
items.desc_en: Rav's son visits the Sages for a blessing; they give him a series of seemingly negative statements. His father interprets each as a blessing: e.g., 'you will sow and not reap' means you will have children who do not die; 'your house will be destroyed' refers to this world as a temporary dwelling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between two verses about the value of Torah: one implies that heavenly objects are comparable, the other that nothing is.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: one verse refers to a mitzvah that can be performed through others, the other to a mitzvah that cannot.
The Sages ask Rav's son why he has come, and he explains that his father sent him to receive a blessing.
The Sages give Rav's son a series of statements that sound like curses: you will sow and not reap, enter and not exit, etc.
Rav's son returns to his father and complains that the Sages not only failed to bless him but actually distressed him.

sub.text: Rav's interpretation of the first two statements
sub.text_en: Rav's interpretation of the first two statements
sub.desc_en: Rav asks what was said and then interprets each statement as a blessing: 'sow and not reap' means you will have children who do not die, etc.

sub.text: Rav's interpretation of the third statement
sub.text_en: Rav's interpretation of the third statement
sub.desc_en: Rav interprets 'your house will be destroyed and your guest will dwell' as referring to this world as a temporary dwelling and the next world as the permanent home, citing a verse.

sub.text: Rav's interpretation of the remaining statements
sub.text_en: Rav's interpretation of the remaining statements
sub.desc_en: Rav interprets 'your table will be confused' as referring to sons and daughters, and 'may you not see a new year' as meaning your wife will not die and you will not need to remarry.

items.text: Blessing of not being ashamed
items.text_en: Blessing of not being ashamed
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta visits Rav for a blessing; Rav blesses him that he should not shame others nor be shamed. His father explains that this is the same blessing God gave Israel in the verse about not being ashamed.

sub.text: Narrative: Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta visits Rav
sub.text_en: Narrative: Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta visits Rav
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta takes leave of Rav, and his father tells him to go back for a blessing; Rav blesses him that he should not shame nor be shamed, but Rabbi Shimon dismisses it as mere words.

sub.text: Father of Rabbi Shimon explains the blessing
sub.text_en: Father of Rabbi Shimon explains the blessing
sub.desc_en: His father explains that Rav's blessing is the same blessing God gave Israel in the verse 'וְלֹא יֵבוֹשׁוּ עַמִּי לְעוֹלָם' (and My people shall never be ashamed).

items.text: Women's adornments during the festival
items.text_en: Women's adornments during the festival
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states a woman may adorn herself during the festival. The Gemara specifies these adornments: applying eye shadow, rouge, and removing hair. Rav Huna bar Chinana limits this to young women, but Rav Chisda objects, saying even old women may adorn themselves, citing a folk saying.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states a woman may adorn herself during the festival, and a baraita specifies the adornments: applying eye shadow, rouge, and removing hair from her face or lower body.
Rav Huna bar Chinana, sitting before Rav Chisda, limits the allowance to a young woman (ילדה), but not an old woman (זקנה).

Rav Chisda objects emphatically, saying even an old woman, even one standing at her grave, may adorn herself, citing a folk saying that a sixty-year-old runs to the sound of music like a six-year-old.

items.text: Dispute about plastering with lime and its resolution
items.text_en: Dispute about plastering with lime and its resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda prohibits a woman from plastering her face with lime during the festival because it is degrading, but allows it if she can remove it during the festival. The Gemara questions this logic, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda says a gentile is repaid because he is distressed, but the Sages say he will be happy later. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves that in festival laws, all are distressed now and happy later.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda rules that a woman may not plaster her face with lime during the festival because it is degrading.
A baraita adds that Rabbi Yehuda concedes regarding lime that can be removed during the festival, because although she is distressed now, she will be happy later.
The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yehuda actually holds the principle that present distress is outweighed by future happiness.
A baraita is cited where Rabbi Yehuda says a gentile is repaid immediately because he is distressed, but the Sages object that he will be happy later.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves that in the laws of the festival, all are distressed now and happy later, so Rabbi Yehuda's position is consistent.

items.text: Alternative resolution: a gentile is always distressed
items.text_en: Alternative resolution: a gentile is always distressed
items.desc_en: Ravina offers an alternative resolution: a gentile is always distressed regarding repayment, so Rabbi Yehuda's logic stands.

sub.desc_en: Ravina resolves the contradiction by asserting that a gentile is always distressed regarding repayment, so Rabbi Yehuda's logic that distress now leads to joy later does not apply.

items.text: Plastering with lime for young women and the identity of 'shemen hamor'
items.text_en: Plastering with lime for young women and the identity of 'shemen hamor'
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda teaches that girls who have reached puberty but not age are plastered with lime; the poor use lime, the rich use flour, and princesses use 'shemen hamor'. The Gemara debates the meaning of 'shemen hamor': some say it is stacte, others say it is olive oil that has not reached a third of its growth. A baraita supports the latter, explaining it removes hair and softens skin.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda teaches that girls who have reached puberty but not age are plastered with lime (poor), flour (rich), or shemen hamor (princesses), citing the verse about Esther's beauty treatments.

The Gemara asks what 'shemen hamor' is, and two Amoraim offer competing identifications: Rav Huna bar Chiyya says it is stacte, Rav Yirmeya bar Ami says it is olive oil that has not reached a third of its growth.
A baraita citing Rabbi Yehuda supports Rav Yirmeya bar Ami's view, identifying 'anpikinun' as olive oil that has not reached a third, and explaining that it removes hair and softens the skin.

items.text: Rav Bibi's practice and Rav Nachman's comment
items.text_en: Rav Bibi's practice and Rav Nachman's comment
items.desc_en: Rav Bibi plastered his daughter limb by limb, spending 400 zuz. A gentile neighbor did the same to his daughter all at once, and she died, leading the gentile to blame Rav Bibi. Rav Nachman comments that Rav Bibi drinks beer, so his daughters need plastering, but we who do not drink beer do not need it.

sub.desc_en: The narrative opens by describing that Rav Bibi had a daughter and plastered her limb by limb, spending 400 zuz.
A gentile neighbor also had a daughter, plastered her all at once, and she died, leading the gentile to blame Rav Bibi.
Rav Nachman explains that Rav Bibi drinks beer, so his daughters need plastering, but we who do not drink beer do not need it.

items.text: Definition of amateur vs. professional sewing
items.text_en: Definition of amateur vs. professional sewing
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that an amateur sews normally, while a professional interlocks stitches. The Gemara defines an amateur as one who cannot remove a full needle at once (R. Yannai's school) or cannot align a seam in one pass (R. Yose bar Chanina). For professional interlocking, R. Yochanan says it means skipping stitches, and Rabbah bar Shmuel says it means dog-tooth stitching.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that an amateur sews in his usual manner during Chol HaMoed.
The Gemara asks: what defines an amateur for this purpose?
The school of Rabbi Yannai defines an amateur as one who cannot remove a full needleful of thread in one pull.
Rabbi Yose bar Chanina defines an amateur as one who cannot align a seam in a single pass of the garment.
The Mishnah states that a professional interlaces stitches.
The Gemara asks: what does 'מכליב' (interlacing) mean?
Rabbi Yochanan explains that 'מכליב' means skipping stitches.
Rabbah bar Shmuel explains that 'מכליב' means dog-tooth stitching.

items.text: Dispute over 'mesargin' and 'mematchin' for beds
items.text_en: Dispute over 'mesargin' and 'mematchin' for beds
items.desc_en: The Mishnah permits weaving bed ropes. Rav Dimi reports a dispute between R. Chiya bar Abba and R. Assi in the names of Chizkiya and R. Yochanan: one says mesargin means warp and weft, mematchin means warp without weft; the other says mesargin means warp without weft, mematchin means tightening if loose.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may weave bed ropes during חול המועד (the intermediate festival days).
The Gemara asks what the terms 'mesargin' and 'mematchin' mean.

Rav Dimi reports a dispute between Rabbi Chiya bar Abba and Rabbi Assi in the names of Chizkiya and Rabbi Yochanan: one says 'mesargin' means warp and weft, 'mematchin' means warp without weft; the other says 'mesargin' means warp without weft, 'mematchin' means tightening if loose.

items.text: Challenge from baraita of Rav Tachlifa bar Shaul
items.text_en: Challenge from baraita of Rav Tachlifa bar Shaul
items.desc_en: A baraita states that one may not initially twist ropes. The Gemara analyzes this: according to the view that mesargin is warp and weft, the baraita's prohibition on twisting ropes is consistent. But according to the view that mesargin is warp without weft, the baraita's prohibition is obvious, since even warp and weft are forbidden. This poses a difficulty.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the previous discussion by citing a baraita of Rav Tachlifa bar Shaul that rules one may not twist ropes לכתחילה (a-priori).

sub.text: First answer (consistent with mesargin = warp and weft)
sub.text_en: First answer (consistent with mesargin = warp and weft)
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to the view that mesargin means warp and weft, the baraita's prohibition on twisting ropes is consistent and not redundant.

sub.text: Objection (according to mesargin = warp without weft)
sub.text_en: Objection (according to mesargin = warp without weft)
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that according to the view that mesargin means warp without weft, the baraita's prohibition is obvious and redundant, posing a difficulty.

items.text: Resolution via Ravin's version of the dispute
items.text_en: Resolution via Ravin's version of the dispute
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak questions R. Chiya bar Avin about the view that mesargin is warp without weft, citing a Mishnah of R. Meir that a bed is considered woven only after three interwoven sections. Ravin then reports that all agree mesargin means warp and weft; the dispute is only about mematchin: one says warp without weft, the other says tightening if loose.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's question to Rabbi Chiya bar Avin
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's question to Rabbi Chiya bar Avin
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak challenges Rabbi Chiya bar Avin by asking who holds that mesargin means warp without weft, citing Rabbi Meir's Mishnah that a bed is considered woven only after three interwoven sections.
Ravin reports that all agree mesargin means warp and weft; the dispute is only about mematchin: one says warp without weft, the other says tightening if loose.

items.text: Support from baraita with R. Meir and R. Yose
items.text_en: Support from baraita with R. Meir and R. Yose
items.desc_en: A baraita states: R. Meir permits mesargin and certainly mematchin; R. Yose permits mematchin but not mesargin; Yesh Omrim forbid mematchin entirely. The Gemara analyzes: according to the view that mematchin is warp without weft, Yesh Omrim's prohibition makes sense. But according to the view that mematchin is tightening if loose, why would Yesh Omrim forbid that? The answer: since one can fill the bed with clothes, we do not trouble to tighten.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited presenting three positions: Rabbi Meir permits both mesargin and certainly mematchin, Rabbi Yose permits mematchin but not mesargin, and Yesh Omrim forbid mematchin entirely.

The Gemara questions: according to the view that mematchin is warp without weft, the Yesh Omrim's prohibition is understandable; but according to the view that mematchin is tightening if loose, why would Yesh Omrim forbid that?
The Gemara answers: yes, since one can fill the bed with clothes, we do not trouble to tighten the ropes.

items.text: Mishnah on mill repairs and Gemara's definitions
items.text_en: Mishnah on mill repairs and Gemara's definitions
items.desc_en: The Mishnah permits setting up an oven, stove, or mill during Chol HaMoed, but R. Yehuda forbids initially 'mechabshin' the mill. The Gemara asks what mechabshin means: Rav Yehuda says it means chiseling the millstone; Rav Yechiel says it means the eye socket.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah permits setting up an oven, stove, or mill during Chol HaMoed, but Rabbi Yehuda forbids initially 'mechabshin' the mill.
The Gemara asks what the term 'מכבשין' (mechabshin) means.
Rav Yehuda explains that 'מכבשין' means chiseling the millstone (ניקור ריחיא).
Rav Yechiel explains that 'מכבשין' means the eye socket (בת עינא) of the millstone.

items.text: Baraita on mill repairs and analysis
items.text_en: Baraita on mill repairs and analysis
items.desc_en: A baraita records a dispute: R. Eliezer permits setting up a mill provided one does not complete the work; Sages permit even completing; R. Yehuda in his name permits setting up a new mill and mechabshin an old one; Yesh Omrim forbid mechabshin entirely. The Gemara analyzes: according to Rav Yehuda (chiseling), the distinction between old and new makes sense. According to Rav Yechiel (eye socket), an old mill's eye socket is for widening slightly.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited recording a dispute about setting up ovens and millstones during חול המועד (the intermediate festival days): Rabbi Eliezer permits but forbids completing the work, the Sages permit even completing, Rabbi Yehuda in his name permits setting up a new mill and mechabshin an old one, and Yesh Omrim forbid mechabshin entirely.

The Gemara resolves the baraita: according to Rav Yehuda who interprets mechabshin as chiseling the millstone, the distinction between old and new is clear; according to Rav Yechiel who interprets it as the eye socket, an old mill's eye socket is for widening slightly.

items.text: Stories of Rav Huna and Rav Chama on mill chiseling
items.text_en: Stories of Rav Huna and Rav Chama on mill chiseling
items.desc_en: Rav Huna heard someone chiseling a mill during Chol HaMoed and cursed him, following Yesh Omrim. Rav Chama taught that one may chisel mills during Chol HaMoed, and in the name of R. Meir, even trimming the hooves of one's riding horse or donkey is permitted.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna hears a man chiseling a mill during Chol HaMoed and curses him, following the opinion of Yesh Omrim.
Rav Chama teaches that one may chisel mills during Chol HaMoed, and in the name of Rabbi Meir, even trimming the hooves of one's riding horse or donkey is permitted.

items.text: Permitted and prohibited mill-related work
items.text_en: Permitted and prohibited mill-related work
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins by stating that a mill donkey is prohibited (for work during Chol HaMoed). It then cites Rav Yehuda who permitted various mill-related tasks, and Rava who permitted grooming horses and building certain structures.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that a mill donkey is prohibited for work during Chol HaMoed.
Rav Yehuda permits various mill-related tasks: trimming the donkey's hooves, setting up the mill, building the mill, its water channel, and the trough.
Rava permits grooming horses and building a stable and a bench.

items.text: Bloodletting for animals on Chol HaMoed
items.text_en: Bloodletting for animals on Chol HaMoed
items.desc_en: Rava permitted bloodletting for animals during Chol HaMoed. Abaye cited a supporting baraita that one may let blood from an animal and not withhold healing.

sub.desc_en: Rava permits bloodletting for an animal during Chol HaMoed.
Abaye cites a baraita that one may let blood from an animal and not withhold healing during Chol HaMoed, supporting Rava's ruling.

items.text: Sifting worms and tying wells
items.text_en: Sifting worms and tying wells
items.desc_en: Rava permitted sifting worms because it is amateur work. Rav Yitzchak bar Ami quoting Rav Chisda prohibited tying wells because it is professional work.

sub.desc_en: Rava permits sifting worms from flour during חול המועד (the intermediate festival days) because it is considered amateur work (מעשה הדיוט).

sub.text: Rav Yitzchak bar Ami quoting Rav Chisda
sub.text_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Ami quoting Rav Chisda
sub.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Ami in the name of Rav Chisda rules that tying well ropes (קיטורי בירי) is forbidden during חול המועד because it is professional work (מעשה אומן).

items.text: Leveling ground for storage vs. for planting
items.text_en: Leveling ground for storage vs. for planting
items.desc_en: Rava ruled that leveling ground for a storage house is permitted, but for planting is prohibited. The Gemara explains the difference: removing high soil and placing it on low soil is for storage, while removing high soil and placing it on low soil is for planting.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that leveling ground for a storage house (בית דרי) is permitted, but for planting (ארעא) is forbidden.
The Gemara clarifies the distinction: moving high soil to high and low to low is for storage, while moving high to low is for planting.

items.text: Gathering wood for fuel vs. for land
items.text_en: Gathering wood for fuel vs. for land
items.desc_en: Rava ruled that gathering wood for fuel is permitted, but for the land is prohibited. The explanation: taking large branches and leaving small ones is for fuel, while taking both large and small is for the land.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that gathering wood (זיכי) is permitted if intended for fuel (ציבי) but prohibited if intended for the land (ארעא).
The Gemara clarifies the distinction: taking only large branches and leaving small ones indicates intent for fuel, while taking both large and small indicates intent for the land.

items.text: Opening water channels for fish vs. for land
items.text_en: Opening water channels for fish vs. for land
items.desc_en: Rava ruled that opening water channels for fish is permitted, but for the land is prohibited. The explanation: opening two openings, one above and one below, is for fish; opening one opening is for the land.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that opening water channels for fish is permitted, but for the land is prohibited.
The Gemara clarifies the distinction: opening two openings, one above and one below, indicates intent for fish; opening one opening indicates intent for the land.

items.text: Cutting a palm tree for animals vs. for the tree
items.text_en: Cutting a palm tree for animals vs. for the tree
items.desc_en: Rava ruled that cutting a palm tree for animals is permitted, but for the tree is prohibited. The explanation: cutting entirely from one side is for animals; cutting from both sides is for the tree and prohibited.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that cutting a palm tree for animal feed is permitted during חול המועד (the intermediate festival days).
Rava rules that cutting a palm tree for the tree's own benefit is prohibited during חול המועד.
The Gemara clarifies the distinction: cutting all branches from one side indicates intent for animal feed (permitted), while cutting from both sides indicates intent for the tree (prohibited).

items.text: Handling spoiled dates
items.text_en: Handling spoiled dates
items.desc_en: Rava ruled that cutting spoiled dates is permitted, but pressing them is prohibited. Rav Pappa added that once they begin to rot, they are like lost merchandise and permitted.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that cutting spoiled dates is permitted, but pressing them is prohibited.
Rav Pappa adds that once the dates begin to rot, they are considered lost merchandise and therefore permitted.

items.text: Lost merchandise and debt collection
items.text_en: Lost merchandise and debt collection
items.desc_en: Rava ruled that any merchandise is prohibited (to sell during Chol HaMoed), but Rabbi Yosei bar Avin permitted it if it is lost merchandise. The Gemara relates that Ravina sold his business at a higher price after the holiday, and that Rav Ashi permitted collecting a debt from borrowers who are only available now, as it is like lost merchandise.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that any merchandise (פרגמטיא) is forbidden to sell during Chol HaMoed.
Rabbi Yosei bar Avin qualifies that lost merchandise (דבר האבד) is permitted.
Ravina delayed selling his business until after the holiday and sold it for double the price, illustrating the lost-merchandise exception.

sub.text: Rav Ashi's ruling on debt collection
sub.text_en: Rav Ashi's ruling on debt collection
sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi permits Ravina to collect a debt during Chol HaMoed because the borrowers are only available now, treating it as lost merchandise.

items.text: Support from a baraita on idolatry
items.text_en: Support from a baraita on idolatry
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that similarly permits certain activities regarding idolatry, supporting the principle of lost merchandise.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that similarly permits certain activities regarding idolatry, supporting the principle of lost merchandise.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Permitted transactions at gentile fairs
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Permitted transactions at gentile fairs
items.desc_en: The Mishnah permits buying animals, slaves, houses, fields, and vineyards from a gentile fair during Chol HaMoed, and even writing and registering in their courts, because it is like rescuing from their hands.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah permits buying animals, slaves, houses, fields, and vineyards from a gentile fair during Chol HaMoed, and even writing and registering in their courts, because it is like rescuing from their hands.

items.text: Gemara: Rav permits building a tower for a guard, and Rav Yehuda permits building ovens and mills
items.text_en: Gemara: Rav permits building a tower for a guard, and Rav Yehuda permits building ovens and mills
items.desc_en: Rav permits building a watchtower for a guard because it is amateur work, but professional work is forbidden. Rav Yehuda permits building ovens and mills. A contradiction is raised from a baraita that forbids building an oven from scratch, resolved by distinguishing between summer and winter.

sub.desc_en: Rav permits building a watchtower for a guard during חול המועד (the intermediate festival days), distinguishing between amateur work (מַעֲשֵׂה הֶדְיוֹט) which is permitted and professional work (מַעֲשֵׂה אוּמָּן) which is forbidden.
Rav Yehuda permits building ovens and mills during חול המועד (the intermediate festival days), extending the leniency to other structures.
The gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita taught by Rabbah bar Shmuel that explicitly forbids building an oven from scratch during חול המועד (the intermediate festival days).

The gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between summer (ימוֹת הַחַמָּה) when ovens are not urgently needed and winter (ימוֹת הַגְּשָׁמִים) when they are, permitting construction only in the latter case.

items.text: Mishnah: Permitted repairs and pickling
items.text_en: Mishnah: Permitted repairs and pickling
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists permitted activities: making a parapet for a roof or balcony as amateur work, sealing cracks by hand or foot but not with tools, repairing broken door parts, and pickling foods that can be eaten during the festival.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing permitted activities: making a parapet for a roof or balcony as amateur work, but not as professional work.
The Mishnah continues: sealing cracks and smoothing them by hand or foot, but not with tools.
The Mishnah lists repairing broken door parts (hinge, socket, beam, lock, key) during the festival, provided one does not intend to do his work during the festival.
The Mishnah concludes: all pickled foods that one can eat during the festival may be pickled.

items.text: Gemara: Defining amateur work and clarifying the Mishnah's wording
items.text_en: Gemara: Defining amateur work and clarifying the Mishnah's wording
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef defines amateur work as using a reed and a board; a baraita says one ties with a pebble but does not plaster with mud. The Gemara then clarifies that the Mishnah's phrase 'smoothing cracks with a roller' means smoothing like a roller by hand and foot, not with a proper tool.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what constitutes amateur work (מעשה הדיוט) in the context of the Mishnah.
Rav Yosef defines amateur work as using a reed and a board (הוצא ודפנא).
A baraita supports the definition: one ties with a pebble but does not plaster with mud.
The Gemara questions the Mishnah's wording: if smoothing with a roller (מעגילה) is permitted, why mention hand and foot separately?
The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah means smoothing like a roller by hand and foot, not with a proper tool (מחלציים).

items.text: Gemara: Contradiction regarding repairing broken door parts and resolution
items.text_en: Gemara: Contradiction regarding repairing broken door parts and resolution
items.desc_en: A contradiction is raised: the Mishnah permits repairing broken door parts, but a baraita says that until the days of a certain person a hammer struck in Jerusalem, implying it was forbidden afterward. Rav Chisda resolves by distinguishing between scythes and axes; Rav Pappa says before and after the decree; Rav Ashi attributes the views to Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yossi.

sub.desc_en: The gemara raises a contradiction: the Mishnah permits repairing broken door parts during חול המועד (the intermediate festival days), but a baraita states that until a certain person's days a hammer struck in Jerusalem, implying that afterward it was forbidden.
The gemara initially resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between blacksmiths (נפחי) and carpenters (נגרי), implying different types of work.
Rav Chisda objects that this distinction is illogical, as people would say that a loud sound (blacksmith) is forbidden but a quiet sound (carpenter) is permitted.
Rav Chisda resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between scythes (מגלי) and axes (חציני), two types of tools with different noise levels.
Rav Pappa resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between before and after the decree that forbade certain work during חול המועד.

Rav Ashi resolves the contradiction by attributing the Mishnah to Rabbi Yehuda and the baraita to Rabbi Yossi, citing Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avdimi that the Tanna who permits changing something during חול המועד for a lost object is not Rabbi Yossi.

items.text: Gemara: Practical ruling in accordance with Rabbi Yossi
items.text_en: Gemara: Practical ruling in accordance with Rabbi Yossi
items.desc_en: Ravina states that the current practice of raising door sockets during Chol HaMoed follows Rabbi Yossi's lenient view.

sub.desc_en: Ravina states that the current practice of raising door sockets during Chol HaMoed follows Rabbi Yossi's lenient view.

items.text: Gemara: Permissibility of salting fish caught during Chol HaMoed
items.text_en: Gemara: Permissibility of salting fish caught during Chol HaMoed
items.desc_en: Rava permits salting fish caught in a pond, as they are considered lost property if left unsalted. Abaye objects based on the Mishnah that only pickling for immediate consumption is allowed. Rava responds that since they were brought for eating and would spoil, it is like lost merchandise. An alternative version has Rava permitting even catching and salting, with the fish being eaten with bread.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara describes a situation where everyone caught fish from a pond, and Rava permitted salting them.
Abaye objects, citing the Mishnah that only pickling for immediate consumption is permitted during Chol HaMoed.
Rava responds that since the fish were brought for eating and would spoil if left, they are considered lost merchandise and therefore permitted.
An alternative version states that Rava permitted even catching, bringing, and salting the fish.
Abaye again objects, citing the same Mishnah that only pickling for immediate consumption is taught.
Rava responds that these fish can also be eaten with bread, citing Shmuel's practice of eating sixty breads with fish.

items.text: Gemara: Anecdotes about fish preparation and health advice
items.text_en: Gemara: Anecdotes about fish preparation and health advice
items.desc_en: Rav recounts visiting Rav Shappir and being served a fish prepared in three ways. He then shares advice from Ada the fisherman: fish near spoiling is best, how to prepare and eat fish, and that fish, leeks, and milk are good for the body but not for the bed, and should be eaten with water, not beer or wine.

sub.desc_en: Rav visits Rav Shappir's house and is served a fish prepared in three ways: one-third cooked, one-third salted, and one-third roasted.
Rav reports Ada the fisherman's advice: a fish near spoiling is best; it should be roasted with its brother (salt), eaten with its father (water), and drunk after with its father (water).
Rav further quotes Ada the fisherman: fish, leeks, and milk strengthen the body but weaken the bed, and should be eaten with water, not beer or wine.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Tasks for a mourner during Chol HaMoed
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Tasks for a mourner during Chol HaMoed
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if someone overturned his olives and then became an avel or was forced by circumstances, or if workers misled him, he may load the first beam and leave it until after the festival. Rabbi Yosi says he may pour and finish, and seal it as usual.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if someone overturned his olives and then became an avel or was forced by circumstances, or if workers misled him, he may load the first beam and leave it until after the festival. Rabbi Yehuda says so; Rabbi Yosi says he may pour and finish, and seal it as usual.

items.text: Gemara's transition: Mourning vs. Chol HaMoed
items.text_en: Gemara's transition: Mourning vs. Chol HaMoed
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah opens with mourning and ends with Chol HaMoed. Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi says this teaches that things permitted in Chol HaMoed are forbidden during mourning. Rav Ashi clarifies that the real question is whether tasks that cause loss are permitted in Chol HaMoed, since mourning prohibitions are rabbinic and thus lenient.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with mourning and ends with the festival. Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi says: things permitted during the festival are forbidden during mourning.

sub.text: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi's inference
sub.text_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi's inference
sub.desc_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi infers that things permitted in Chol HaMoed are forbidden during mourning.

Rav Ashi rejects the inference, explaining that the Mishnah uses a 'not only' formulation: even in Chol HaMoed, where the Torah prohibition of work is more severe, the rabbis permitted work in a case of loss.

items.text: Tosefta supporting Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi
items.text_en: Tosefta supporting Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi
items.desc_en: A Tosefta is cited that lists tasks permitted for an avel during his mourning: overturning olives, loading a barrel, raising flax from the marsh, raising wool from the vat, and irrigating his field when the water season arrives. Rabbi Yehuda adds that he may also sow a fallow field or a field ready for flax, but the Sages restrict this to only if he would otherwise suffer loss.

sub.desc_en: A baraita like Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi: these are the things done for a mourner during his mourning: his overturned olives — they load for him, and his barrel and his flax — they bring up from the press, and his wool — they bring up from the dyeing vat, and they irrigate his field from when its water season arrives.
Rabbi Yehuda adds that one may also sow a fallow field or a field ready for flax for the avel.
The Sages object that if the field is not sown early, it can be sown later, or if not flax, another crop can be sown, implying no loss.

items.text: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's lenient ruling
items.text_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's lenient ruling
items.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel permits a mourner to perform tasks that would otherwise be forbidden if there is no other craftsman available, such as pressing inverted olives, sealing a barrel, raising flax or wool, if no other expert exists. He says the mourner may do these privately.

sub.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says: if his olives are overturned and there is no craftsman but him, his barrel to seal and there is no craftsman but him, his flax to bring up from the press and his wool to bring up from the dyeing vat and there is no craftsman but him — this one may do it discreetly.

sub.text: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's additional ruling
sub.text_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's additional ruling
sub.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds that a mourner who is a public craftsman, barber, or bath attendant may work when the festival arrives and no other craftsman is available.

items.text: Categories of workers: tenants, sharecroppers, contractors
items.text_en: Categories of workers: tenants, sharecroppers, contractors
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists categories: arisim (tenants), hakirim (sharecroppers), kablanim (contractors) — these may have others work for them. But chamarim (donkey drivers), gamalim (camel drivers), and sappanim (boatmen) may not work for others unless they are hired or contracted to others. A day worker may not work even in another city. If the work belongs to others but is in the mourner's hand, even if it is a contract, he may not do it.

sub.desc_en: The tenants, sharecroppers, and contractors — these may have others do for them. The donkey drivers, camel drivers, and sailors — these may not do; but if they were hired or contracted with others — these may do. A day worker even in another city — he may not do. If another's work was in his hand, even though it was a contract — he may not do.

The Gemara questions the Mishnah's phrasing: if even a contract is forbidden, is it not obvious that non-contract work is forbidden? On the contrary, a contract should be considered his own work and thus permitted.
The Gemara resolves the difficulty by emending the Mishnah to read: whether it is a contract or not, he may not do the work.

items.text: Work in the mourner's own house vs. another's house
items.text_en: Work in the mourner's own house vs. another's house
items.desc_en: If the work is in the mourner's own house and belongs to others, they may not do it. But if it is in another's house, they may do it.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma rules that if the mourner's work is in his own house, others may not do it, but if it is in another's house, they may do it.

items.text: Story of Mari bar Ravina and Mar bar Rav Acha's camel
items.text_en: Story of Mari bar Ravina and Mar bar Rav Acha's camel
items.desc_en: Mari bar Ravina and Mar bar Rav Acha had a shared camel. A mishap occurred to Mar bar Rav Acha's camel, and he broke it. Rav Ashi questioned why Mar bar Rav Acha, a great man, would not worry about loss to others, citing a Tosefta that says hired or contracted workers may do work for others. The Gemara concludes that a distinguished person is different.

sub.desc_en: Marion bar Ravin and Mar bar Rav Acha bar Rava had a camel of Torah together. An incident happened to Mar bar Rav Acha bar Rava and he broke his camel. Rav Ashi said: a great man like Mar bar Rav Acha does this? He does not worry about his own loss, but about others' loss?! And it is taught: if they were hired or contracted with others — these may do!
Rav Ashi questions how a great man like Mar bar Rav Acha could disregard loss to others, given that he would not worry about his own loss.
Cites a baraita that hired or contracted workers may do work for others, implying that even in mourning one should not cause loss to others.
The Gemara resolves that a distinguished person (אדם חשוב) is different and may act leniently in such cases.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling on accepting payment within and outside the techum
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on accepting payment within and outside the techum
items.desc_en: Shmuel rules that accepting payment (kabbalat kabbala) is forbidden within the techum but permitted outside. Rav Pappa adds that even outside the techum, it is forbidden if there is a nearby town. Rav Mesharshiya further limits the leniency to Shabbat and Yom Tov, but forbids it on Chol HaMoed due to frequent travelers.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that accepting payment (קיבול) is forbidden within the techum but permitted outside.
Rav Pappa qualifies that even outside the techum, it is forbidden if there is a nearby town.
Rav Mesharshiya further limits the leniency to Shabbat and Yom Tov, but forbids it on Chol HaMoed due to frequent travelers.

items.text: Mar Zutra's building project and the exception for an important person
items.text_en: Mar Zutra's building project and the exception for an important person
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra built a mansion with workers receiving payment outside the techum. Rav Safra and Rav Huna bar Chinana did not enter, and some say he also did not enter. The Gemara questions this based on Shmuel's leniency, and answers that an important person is different, or that they assisted with straw.

sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra built a mansion with workers receiving payment outside the techum; Rav Safra and Rav Huna bar Chinana did not enter, and some say he also did not enter.
The Gemara questions why Mar Zutra's workers were considered problematic, citing Shmuel's ruling that workers receiving payment outside the techum are permitted.
The Gemara answers that an important person (אדם חשוב) is different and subject to stricter standards.
An alternative answer states that Mar Zutra assisted the workers with straw, making the work his own and thus forbidden.

items.text: Rav Chama permits workers of the Exilarch to work for free
items.text_en: Rav Chama permits workers of the Exilarch to work for free
items.desc_en: Rav Chama permitted the workers of the Exilarch's house to work on Chol HaMoed because they do not receive wages, so it is considered merely a favor, and we have no concern.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chama permits the workers of the Exilarch's house to work on Chol HaMoed because they receive no wages, so it is merely a favor and not a concern.

items.text: Baraitot on accepting work for after the festival
items.text_en: Baraitot on accepting work for after the festival
items.desc_en: Two baraitot state that one may accept work on Chol HaMoed to be done after the festival, but not during the festival. The second adds that one may not measure, weigh, or count in the usual manner. A general rule is given: what one may do, one may tell a non-Jew to do; what one may not do, one may not tell a non-Jew.

sub.desc_en: The first baraita states that one may accept work (קבלת) on Chol HaMoed to be performed after the festival, but not during the festival.
The first baraita gives a general rule: what one may do oneself, one may tell a non-Jew to do; what one may not do, one may not tell a non-Jew to do.
The second baraita repeats the rule about accepting work on Chol HaMoed for after the festival.
The second baraita adds that one may not measure, weigh, or count in the usual weekday manner.

items.text: Baraitot on animal husbandry during Chol HaMoed
items.text_en: Baraitot on animal husbandry during Chol HaMoed
items.desc_en: A baraita forbids mating animals on Chol HaMoed, including firstborns and disqualified consecrated animals. Another baraita adds that Rabbi Yehuda permits mating a female donkey that is in heat to prevent her from cooling, and for other animals, one may bring them into a pen.

sub.desc_en: The first baraita forbids mating animals on Chol HaMoed, including firstborns (בכור) and disqualified consecrated animals (פסולי המוקדשין).
The second baraita adds that Rabbi Yehuda permits mating a female donkey in heat to prevent her from cooling, and for other animals one may bring them into a pen (לבקרות).

items.text: Baraita on corralling animals and the ruling of Rav Yosef
items.text_en: Baraita on corralling animals and the ruling of Rav Yosef
items.desc_en: A baraita forbids corralling animals on Shabbat, Yom Tov, and Chol HaMoed, but if they come on their own, it is permitted. One may not assist them or assign a guard. However, for a long-term hired worker, one may assist and assign a guard. Rabbi says on Shabbat it is with goodwill, on Yom Tov with meals, on Chol HaMoed with wages. Rav Yosef rules like Rabbi.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that one may not corral animals on Shabbat, Yom Tov, or Chol HaMoed, but if they come on their own, it is permitted.
The baraita adds that one may not assist the animals or assign a guard for them.
The baraita rules that for a long-term hired worker (by the week, month, or year), one may assist and assign a guard.
Rabbi distinguishes the payment method: on Shabbat it is with goodwill, on Yom Tov with meals, on Chol HaMoed with wages.
Rav Yosef rules that the halacha follows Rabbi's opinion.

items.text: Mishnah on wine in a pit and the Gemara's analysis
items.text_en: Mishnah on wine in a pit and the Gemara's analysis
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses one whose wine is in a pit and is interrupted by mourning or duress: Rabbi Yosei permits drawing and sealing in the usual way, while Rabbi Yehuda requires making a partition to prevent souring. The Gemara explains that both cases are necessary to show each rabbi's reasoning.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case of one whose wine is in a pit and is interrupted by mourning or duress: Rabbi Yosei permits drawing and sealing in the usual way, while Rabbi Yehuda requires making a partition to prevent souring.
The Gemara explains that both cases in the Mishnah are necessary to show each rabbi's reasoning, as each case might otherwise lead to a mistaken concession.

items.text: Rav Yitzchak bar Abba and Rav Yosef on the Mishnah's author
items.text_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Abba and Rav Yosef on the Mishnah's author
items.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Abba says the Tanna who permits change on Chol HaMoed for a lost item is not Rabbi Yosei. Rav Yosef rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Abba identifies the Tanna who permits change on Chol HaMoed for a lost item as not being Rabbi Yosei.
Rav Yosef rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei.

items.text: Question about a beer barrel and the application of Rabbi Yosei's ruling
items.text_en: Question about a beer barrel and the application of Rabbi Yosei's ruling
items.desc_en: They asked Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak whether one may open a beer barrel on Chol HaMoed. He said Sinai (Rav Yosef) ruled like Rabbi Yosei. They objected that Rabbi Yosei spoke of wine, not beer. The Gemara explains that the reason for wine is great loss, and beer also has loss, as Abaye's mother taught about the proper age for beer.

sub.text: Questioners' question to Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak
sub.text_en: Questioners' question to Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak
sub.desc_en: They asked Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak whether one may open a beer barrel on Chol HaMoed.
He answered them that Sinai (Rav Yosef) ruled like Rabbi Yosei.
They objected that Rabbi Yosei's ruling was about wine, not beer.
The Gemara explains that the reason for wine is great loss, and beer also has loss.
Abaye's mother taught that beer at six se'ah is drinkable, but at eight it is not, showing loss if not opened in time.

items.text: Rav's statement on the laws of Moed and the dispute about sealing vessels
items.text_en: Rav's statement on the laws of Moed and the dispute about sealing vessels
items.desc_en: Rav Chama bar Gurya said in Rav's name that the laws of Moed are like the laws of Kutim (Samaritans) in halakha, meaning they are disjointed and cannot be derived from one another. Shmuel says one may seal a kuzta but not a barrel; Rav Dimi from Nehardea says the opposite. Mar is concerned about loss, the other about effort. Abaye concludes that the laws of Moed are like the laws of Shabbat.

sub.text: Rav Chama bar Gurya citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chama bar Gurya citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Chama bar Gurya reports in Rav's name that the laws of Moed are like the laws of Kutim — disjointed and not derivable from one another.
Shmuel permits sealing a kuzta but not a barrel; Rav Dimi says the opposite, one concerned about loss and the other about effort, illustrating the disjointed nature of Moed laws.
Abaye concludes that the laws of Moed are like the laws of Shabbat, providing a unifying principle.

items.text: Opening Mishnah excerpt
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah excerpt
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that some labors are exempt but forbidden, while others are permitted ab initio during Chol HaMoed.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah introduces the principle that some labors during Chol HaMoed are exempt from a sin-offering but forbidden, while others are permitted לכתחילה (the ideal standard).

items.text: Rav Huna's harvesting and the dispute about attached produce
items.text_en: Rav Huna's harvesting and the dispute about attached produce
items.desc_en: Rav Huna harvested during Chol HaMoed. Rabbah bar Rav Huna challenged him with a baraita that distinguishes between detached and attached produce. Rav Huna responded that the baraita is an individual opinion (Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel citing Rabbi Yosi), and the Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yosi would permit threshing with cows, concluding that the baraita about change in mourning does not follow Rabbi Yosi.

sub.desc_en: The gemara reports that Rav Huna had his grain harvested during Chol HaMoed.

Rabbah bar Rav Huna challenges Rav Huna by citing a baraita that permits only detached produce for loss prevention, but prohibits attached produce entirely unless one has nothing to eat, and even then forbids threshing with cows.
Rav Huna responds that the baraita is an individual opinion (Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel citing Rabbi Yosi) and not accepted as binding law.
The gemara questions whether Rabbi Yosi would permit threshing with cows, citing Rav Yitzchak bar Abba that the baraita about change in mourning practice does not follow Rabbi Yosi.
The gemara resolves that since people do not normally thresh with cows, doing so on Chol HaMoed is not considered a change (שינוי) and thus is permitted even according to Rabbi Yosi.

items.text: Baraita on grinding, cutting wood, and making beer
items.text_en: Baraita on grinding, cutting wood, and making beer
items.desc_en: A baraita permits grinding, cutting wood, and making beer for the festival, but forbids it otherwise; leftover is permitted. A contradiction is raised about making beer with an allowance for deception, resolved as a dispute between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yosi bar Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: A baraita permits grinding and cutting wood during the festival for festival needs, and allows leftover produce.
The baraita permits making beer during the festival for festival needs, but forbids deception (הערמה).
The gemara raises a contradiction: another baraita permits deception (הערמה) in making beer, contrary to the first baraita.
The gemara resolves the contradiction as a dispute between Tanna Kamma, who forbids deception, and Rabbi Yosi bar Yehuda, who permits it.

items.text: Rav's harvesting and Samuel's reaction
items.text_en: Rav's harvesting and Samuel's reaction
items.desc_en: Rav harvested wheat during Chol HaMoed; Samuel was upset. The Gemara explains that Rav did so because he had nothing to eat, and Samuel was not informed of that, or because Rav was an important person.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that Rav harvested wheat during Chol HaMoed, and Samuel was upset when he heard about it.
The Gemara asks whether Samuel's upset implies he follows the minority opinion that prohibits all detached harvesting.
The Gemara answers that Samuel was upset because Rav harvested wheat, which does not spoil and thus was not a case of loss (דבר האבד).
The Gemara asks why Rav harvested if it was not a case of loss.
The Gemara answers that Rav had nothing to eat, and Samuel was not informed of that circumstance.
The Gemara offers an alternative resolution: an important person (אדם חשוב) is different and may be held to a stricter standard.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia's actions and Rabbi Ami's reaction
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia's actions and Rabbi Ami's reaction
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia went out with a donkey's pack-saddle and drank water heated by a gentile. Rabbi Ami was upset, but Rav Yosef explains that both actions were permitted, and the reason for the upset is that an important person should be more stringent.

sub.desc_en: The gemara reports that Rabbi Yehuda Nesia went out with a donkey's pack-saddle and drank water heated by a gentile, and Rabbi Ami was upset.
Rav Yosef asks why Rabbi Ami was upset.
Rav Yosef suggests that if the upset was due to the pack-saddle, it is permitted because a baraita classifies such items as movable in a courtyard.

Rav Yosef suggests that if the upset was due to drinking water heated by a gentile, it is permitted because Rav's ruling exempts anything edible raw from the prohibition of בישולי גוים (food cooked by a gentile).
Rav Yosef concludes that the reason for Rabbi Ami's upset is that an important person (אדם חשוב) is different and should be more stringent.

items.text: Cutting a palm tree for its sawdust and Rav Ashi's incident
items.text_en: Cutting a palm tree for its sawdust and Rav Ashi's incident
items.desc_en: Rav Chananel citing Rav permits cutting a palm tree even for its sawdust, but Abaye curses this ruling. Rav Ashi went to cut his tree during Chol HaMoed; Rav Sheila challenged him, and Rav Ashi admitted he did not accept the ruling. His axe slipped, nearly cutting his leg, and he desisted.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chananel in the name of Rav permits cutting a palm tree during Chol HaMoed even if one only needs its sawdust.
Abaye curses this ruling, indicating strong disapproval.
Rav Ashi goes to cut his tree during Chol HaMoed; Rav Sheila challenges him, and Rav Ashi admits he does not accept the ruling.
Rav Ashi's axe slips, nearly cutting his leg, and he desists from the work.

items.text: Permitted agricultural activities and Rabbi Yannai's orchard
items.text_en: Permitted agricultural activities and Rabbi Yannai's orchard
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda permitted uprooting flax, cutting keshuta, and uprooting sesame for their uses. Rabbi Yannai harvested his orchard when its time came during Chol HaMoed, and the next year everyone delayed their harvest; Rabbi Yannai declared his orchard ownerless.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda permits uprooting flax, cutting keshuta, and uprooting sesame during Chol HaMoed.
Abaye questions Rav Yosef about the purpose of uprooting sesame, since flax is for washing and keshuta is for beer.
Rav Yosef answers that sesame is useful for the oil that is in them.
Rabbi Yannai harvested his orchard when its time came during Chol HaMoed.
The next year everyone delayed their harvest to Chol HaMoed, so Rabbi Yannai declared his orchard ownerless to discourage the practice.

items.text: Mishnah on bringing in produce and the Gemara's discussion
items.text_en: Mishnah on bringing in produce and the Gemara's discussion
items.desc_en: The Mishnah permits bringing in produce due to thieves and removing flax from the steeping pit to prevent loss, provided one does not intend to do work on the festival. The Gemara adds that it must be done discreetly, and discusses whether the penalty applies to the heirs if the person dies.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may bring in produce due to thieves and remove flax from the steeping pit to prevent loss, provided one does not intend to do work on the festival, and if one did intend, the items are lost.
A baraita adds that the produce must be brought in discreetly (בצנעא) into one's house.
Rav Yosef had bundles of flax and brought them in during the daytime.
Abaye objects to Rav Yosef, citing the baraita that requires discreet (בצנעא) entry.
Rav Yosef answers that for these bundles, daytime is discreet (צנעא) because at night many men and torches would be needed, which would be conspicuous.

sub.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's question to Rabbi Zeira
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's question to Rabbi Zeira
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira: if one intended to do work on the festival and then died, do his heirs inherit the penalty (קנס) of losing the items?
The Gemara introduces the conditional inquiry (אם תימצי לומר) to frame the discussion about whether the penalty applies to the heirs.

items.text: Fines that pass to the son after the father's death
items.text_en: Fines that pass to the son after the father's death
items.desc_en: The Gemara explores whether a rabbinic fine imposed on a father is inherited by his son. It compares cases of blemishing a firstborn, selling a slave to a gentile, and improving a field in the Sabbatical year, concluding that the fine applies only to the father, not the son.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by asking whether a rabbinic fine (קנס) imposed on a father for blemishing a firstborn animal is inherited by his son, noting that the prohibition is biblical.
The Gemara extends the question to the case of selling a slave to a gentile, where the father is fined because he constantly removes the slave from commandments.
The Gemara poses the dilemma: is the fine imposed on the person (גברא) and thus lapses with his death, or on the property (ממונא) and thus passes to the son?
Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina cites a baraita about a field improved during the Sabbatical year, concluding that the fine applies only to the father, not the son, and analogizes to the current case.

items.text: Mishnah: Purchasing only for the needs of the festival or for the seller's sustenance
items.text_en: Mishnah: Purchasing only for the needs of the festival or for the seller's sustenance
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that during Chol HaMoed one may only purchase houses, slaves, and animals if needed for the festival or if the seller has nothing to eat.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that during Chol HaMoed one may only purchase houses, slaves, and animals if needed for the festival or if the seller has nothing to eat.

items.text: Gemara: Hiring a worker who has nothing to eat
items.text_en: Gemara: Hiring a worker who has nothing to eat
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman whether one may hire a worker who has nothing to eat during Chol HaMoed. Rav Nachman initially suggests that the Mishnah's phrase 'or for the seller who has nothing to eat' includes hiring a worker, but then retracts. Abaye brings a supporting baraita about writing loan documents.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman whether one may hire a worker who has nothing to eat during Chol HaMoed.
Rav Nachman initially suggests that the Mishnah's phrase 'or for the seller who has nothing to eat' includes hiring a worker.
Rav Nachman retracts and explains that the Mishnah is merely specifying the seller, not adding a new category.
Abaye brings a supporting baraita about writing loan documents for someone who has nothing to eat, implying that hiring a worker is permitted.

items.text: Objection from the baraita of three craftsmen on Erev Pesach
items.text_en: Objection from the baraita of three craftsmen on Erev Pesach
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet objects that if hiring a worker with nothing to eat were permitted, all labor would be permitted on Chol HaMoed. Rav Pappa and Ravina counter with examples of building and writing that are permitted for other reasons. Rav Ashi resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between Chol HaMoed (where only loss is permitted) and the fourteenth of Nisan (where only festival needs are permitted).

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet cites a baraita listing three craftsmen who work on Erev Pesach until noon, implying that if hiring a worker with nothing to eat were permitted on Chol HaMoed, all labor would be permitted.
Rav Sheshet argues that if hiring a worker with nothing to eat were permitted, then all forms of labor would be permitted on Chol HaMoed, which is not the case.
Rav Pappa objects that building should also be permitted because a collapsing wall in the public domain may be rebuilt due to danger.
Ravina objects that a scribe should also be permitted because writing marriage documents, divorces, and receipts is allowed on Chol HaMoed.
Rav Ashi resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between Chol HaMoed, where only loss permits labor, and the fourteenth of Nisan, where only festival needs permit labor.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara: Moving items and bringing vessels from the craftsman
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara: Moving items and bringing vessels from the craftsman
items.desc_en: The Mishnah forbids moving from house to house but permits moving within the courtyard, and forbids bringing vessels from the craftsman unless one fears for them. The Gemara resolves contradictions between this Mishnah and a baraita by distinguishing between the fourteenth of Nisan and Chol HaMoed, or between trusting and not trusting the craftsman.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rules for moving items and bringing vessels from the craftsman during Chol HaMoed.
The Gemara questions the contradiction between the Mishnah's initial blanket prohibition and its later permission to move within the courtyard.
Abaye resolves the contradiction by explaining that the Mishnah's lenient clause refers to a house within the same courtyard.
Rav Pappa reports that Rava challenged them with a contradiction between the Mishnah's prohibition on bringing vessels from the craftsman and a baraita that permits it.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between the fourteenth of Nisan and Chol HaMoed, or alternatively between a case where the craftsman is trusted and one where he is not.

items.text: Resolving the contradiction about bringing vessels
items.text_en: Resolving the contradiction about bringing vessels
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction between the Mishnah's ruling that one may not bring vessels from a craftsman and a baraita that permits bringing certain vessels. It resolves that the baraita refers to bringing, while the Mishnah prohibits taking them, and the contradiction is resolved by the earlier explanation.
