sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that permits bringing certain vessels from a craftsman during חול המועד (the intermediate festival days), which contradicts the Mishnah's prohibition.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that the baraita discusses bringing vessels, while the Mishnah prohibits taking them away, consistent with the earlier explanation.

items.text: Mishnah: Covering dried figs and selling produce
items.text_en: Mishnah: Covering dried figs and selling produce
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may cover dried figs with straw, and Rabbi Yehuda adds that one may also pile them. Sellers of produce, garments, and vessels may sell discreetly for the needs of the festival. Hunters, threshers, and grinders may work discreetly. Rabbi Yossi says they imposed a stringency on themselves.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that one may cover dried figs with straw and that sellers of produce, garments, and vessels may sell discreetly for the needs of the festival.
Rabbi Yehuda adds that one may also pile the dried figs.
Rabbi Yossi states that the hunters, threshers, and grinders imposed a stringency on themselves.

items.text: Dispute on the meaning of me'abbin
items.text_en: Dispute on the meaning of me'abbin
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba and Rabbi Assi dispute in the name of Chizkiya and Rabbi Yochanan: one says mechappin means lightly covering and me'abbin means piling; the other says mechappin means both lightly covering and piling, while me'abbin means making a heap. A baraita supports the latter view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute between Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba and Rabbi Assi, both citing Chizkiya and Rabbi Yochanan.
One opinion holds that 'מחפין' means lightly covering and 'מעבין' means piling.
The other opinion holds that 'מחפין' includes both lightly covering and piling, while 'מעבין' means making a heap.
A baraita supports the second opinion, stating that 'מעבין' means making a heap, in the words of Rabbi Yehuda.

items.text: Clarifying Rabbi Yossi's statement
items.text_en: Clarifying Rabbi Yossi's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yossi's statement 'they imposed a stringency on themselves' means they did not work at all or that they worked discreetly. It brings a baraita specifying that the merchants of Tiberias, hunters of Akko, and threshers of Tzippori imposed a stringency on themselves not to work at all.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question about Rabbi Yosei's statement: whether the merchants of Tiberias completely refrained from selling, or whether they sold discreetly.

The Gemara resolves the question by citing a baraita where Rabbi Yosei explicitly states that the merchants of Tiberias, the fishers of Akko, and the threshers of Tzippori completely refrained from their work.

items.text: Defining chiltah, targis, and tisni
items.text_en: Defining chiltah, targis, and tisni
items.desc_en: Abaye defines these terms as grains that are one part to two, one to three, and one to four. Rav Dimi says they are kunta (a type of grain). The Gemara questions this from a baraita about impurity, and answers that they are peeled grains, hence susceptible to impurity.

sub.desc_en: Abaye defines chiltah, targis, and tisni as grains that are one part to two, one to three, and one to four, respectively.
Rav Dimi says these terms refer to kunta (a type of grain).
The Gemara objects from a baraita that these grains are susceptible to impurity everywhere, which fits Abaye's definition (they are prepared for impurity) but not Rav Dimi's (kunta is not prepared).
The Gemara answers that the grains are peeled (soaked in water to remove the husk), which makes them susceptible to impurity, and explains the name chiltah as 'taking their parts' (peeling).

items.text: Further challenge from a vow
items.text_en: Further challenge from a vow
items.desc_en: A baraita states that one who vows from grain is permitted to eat rice, chiltah, targis, and tisni. This supports Abaye's view that these are not considered grain, but challenges Rav Dimi's view that they are a type of grain. The question remains unresolved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises another objection from a baraita about a vow from grain, which permits these grains, but according to Rav Dimi's opinion they should be considered actual grain and thus forbidden.
The Gemara explains that according to Abaye's view (that these are not grain) the baraita is fine, but according to Rav Dimi's view (that they are a type of grain) it is problematic.
The Gemara concludes that the challenge remains unresolved (קשיא).

items.text: Rav Huna's leniency for merchants and the distinction
items.text_en: Rav Huna's leniency for merchants and the distinction
items.desc_en: Rav Huna permitted certain merchants to sell in the market as usual. Rav Kahana challenged from a baraita about opening a shop on Chol HaMoed. The Gemara resolves that the baraita refers to fruit, while Rav Huna's case involves spices, which are permitted.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna permitted certain merchants to sell openly in the market, and Rav Kahana objected by citing a baraita that restricts such sales to the last day of the festival.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between fruit, which is permitted, and spices, which are not.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between fruit (פֵירֵי), which is restricted, and spices (תַבְלִין), which are permitted.

items.text: Conclusion of the chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of the chapter
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the chapter with the standard formula 'Hadran alach Mi Shehafach'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the chapter with the standard closing formula 'הדרן עלך' (we return to you).

items.text: Beginning of the next Mishnah: Who may shave and launder
items.text_en: Beginning of the next Mishnah: Who may shave and launder
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists those who may shave on Chol HaMoed: one coming from overseas, from captivity, from prison, a released excommunicate, one who was permitted by a sage, a nazir, and a metzora. Similarly, those who may launder are listed.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists those who may shave during חול המועד (the intermediate festival days), including travelers, prisoners, and those released from impurity.
The Mishnah lists those who may shave on Chol HaMoed: one coming from overseas, from captivity, from prison, a released excommunicate, one permitted by a sage, a nazir, and a metzora.
The Mishnah lists those who may launder during חול המועד (the intermediate festival days), including travelers and prisoners.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Permitted and forbidden persons
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Permitted and forbidden persons
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists those who are permitted to shave and launder during Chol HaMoed: a released nidduy, one who was released by a sage, and various types of cloths and people emerging from impurity. All other people are forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists those permitted to shave and launder during Chol HaMoed, including a released nidduy and those emerging from impurity, while forbidding all others.

items.text: Gemara's question and answer: Why are others forbidden?
items.text_en: Gemara's question and answer: Why are others forbidden?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why all other people are forbidden. It cites a baraita about the mishmar and ma'amad who are forbidden to shave and launder, and Rabba bar bar Chana quoting Rabbi Elazar that the reason is so they do not enter their watch disheveled. Similarly, the Gemara explains that the prohibition for others is so they do not enter the festival disheveled.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why all other people are forbidden to shave and launder during the festival.
The Gemara cites a baraita that the mishmar and ma'amad are forbidden to shave and launder, with permission on Thursday for Shabbat honor.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana quoting Rabbi Elazar
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana quoting Rabbi Elazar
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Elazar explains that the baraita's reason is to prevent entering the watch disheveled, and the Gemara applies the same logic to the festival.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's dilemma: Lost item on erev regel
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's dilemma: Lost item on erev regel
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks whether one who lost an item on the eve of the festival is permitted to shave, since he was prevented (anus). Abaye objects that people would say all serikin are forbidden but serikei Baytos are permitted. The Gemara resolves by citing Mar bar Rav Ashi that his belt proves his situation. A variant version asks about a craftsman who lost an item, and the dilemma remains unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks whether one who lost an item on the eve of the festival is considered an anus (forced) and thus permitted to shave, or whether the lack of public evidence prohibits it.
Abaye objects that people would say all serikin (those who shave) are forbidden, but the serikei Baytos (those who lost items) are permitted, creating a false impression.

The Gemara rejects Abaye's objection by citing Rabbi Asi quoting Rabbi Yochanan that one with only one garment may launder it during חול המועד (the intermediate festival days), yet there too people might say all serikin are forbidden but serikei Baytos are permitted.
Mar bar Rav Ashi resolves that in the case of the single garment, his belt (which he also launders) proves his situation, so the objection does not apply.

sub.text: Rav Ashi's variant version of Rabbi Zeira's dilemma
sub.text_en: Rav Ashi's variant version of Rabbi Zeira's dilemma
sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi presents a variant version of Rabbi Zeira's dilemma: a craftsman who lost an item on the eve of the festival — is his profession sufficient public evidence, or not? The dilemma remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Dispute about one coming from overseas: Rabbi Yehuda vs. Sages
items.text_en: Dispute about one coming from overseas: Rabbi Yehuda vs. Sages
items.desc_en: The Mishnah's ruling about one coming from overseas is not in accord with Rabbi Yehuda, who forbids shaving because he left without permission. Rava distinguishes between traveling for pleasure (lashut), which all agree is forbidden, and for sustenance (limezonot), which all agree is permitted; the dispute is only for profit (lehervicha). A baraisa is reconciled to show that Rabbi Yehuda's view applies when he left without permission (for pleasure), and the Sages' view when he left with permission (for sustenance).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's ruling about one coming from overseas does not follow Rabbi Yehuda, who forbids shaving because he left without permission.
Rava distinguishes three cases: traveling for pleasure (lashut) is universally forbidden, for sustenance (limezonot) is universally permitted, and the dispute is only for profit (lehervicha).

The Gemara objects by citing a baraisa where Rabbi says Rabbi Yehuda's view applies when he left without permission, and the Sages' view when he left with permission, and analyzes that the only consistent interpretation is that the dispute is about profit (lehervicha).
The Gemara objects further from the continuation of the baraisa, questioning how the Sages' view can apply to profit if Rabbi Yehuda's view already applies to that case.

The Gemara resolves the objection by reinterpreting the baraisa: Rabbi Yehuda's view applies to the Sages when he left without permission (for pleasure), and the Sages' view applies to Rabbi Yehuda when he left with permission (for sustenance).

items.text: Shmuel's ruling: A child born on Chol HaMoed
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling: A child born on Chol HaMoed
items.desc_en: Shmuel rules that a child born during Chol HaMoed is permitted to be shaved during the festival, as there is no greater prison than this. However, this applies only during the festival, not before. Rav Pinchas challenges this from a baraisa that equates those permitted to shave during the festival with those permitted during their mourning period, implying that if one is forbidden during the festival, they are also forbidden during mourning.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that a child born during Chol HaMoed may be shaved during the festival because there is no greater prison than this, but only during the festival, not before.

Rav Pinchas challenges Shmuel from a baraita that equates those permitted to shave during the festival with those permitted during their mourning period, implying that if one is forbidden during the festival, they are also forbidden during mourning.

items.text: Question about minor's mourning during the festival
items.text_en: Question about minor's mourning during the festival
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a minor is forbidden to shave during the festival, which would imply that mourning practices apply to a minor. It cites a baraita that one tears garments for a minor due to distress. Rav Ashi deflects by suggesting the baraita does not say 'these are forbidden' but rather some are forbidden and some permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a minor is forbidden to shave during the festival, which would imply that mourning practices apply to a minor.
The Gemara cites a baraita that one tears garments for a minor due to distress, implying mourning practices apply to a minor.
Rav Ashi deflects by suggesting the baraita does not say 'these are forbidden' but rather some are forbidden and some permitted.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling on a minor
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on a minor
items.desc_en: Ammemar or Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi teaches that Shmuel ruled: a minor is permitted to shave during the festival, whether born during the festival or before.

sub.text: Ammemar or Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi citing Shmuel
sub.text_en: Ammemar or Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi citing Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Ammemar or Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi teaches that Shmuel ruled: a minor is permitted to shave during the festival, whether born during the festival or before.

items.text: Support and counter-argument from a baraita
items.text_en: Support and counter-argument from a baraita
items.desc_en: Rav Pinchas cites a baraita that those permitted to shave during the festival are permitted during their mourning, implying those forbidden are forbidden. The Gemara argues that if a minor is forbidden, mourning applies to a minor, contradicting the earlier baraita about tearing garments. Rav Ashi again deflects.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pinchas cites a baraita that those permitted to shave during the festival are also permitted during their mourning, implying the inverse for those forbidden.
The Gemara argues that if a minor is forbidden to shave, then mourning applies to a minor, contradicting the baraita that only tearing garments is done for a minor due to emotional distress.
Rav Ashi deflects by questioning whether the baraita explicitly states 'forbidden' or merely implies some are forbidden and some permitted.

items.text: Principle: Mourning not observed during the festival
items.text_en: Principle: Mourning not observed during the festival
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that a mourner does not observe mourning during the festival, citing the verse 'And you shall rejoice in your festival.' It explains that if the mourning began before the festival, a public positive commandment overrides a private one; if it began during the festival, a private commandment does not override a public one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that a mourner does not observe mourning during the festival, citing the verse 'And you shall rejoice in your festival.'

The Gemara explains that if mourning began before the festival, a public positive commandment overrides a private one; if it began during the festival, a private commandment does not override a public one.

items.text: Question about a banned person (menuddeh) during the festival
items.text_en: Question about a banned person (menuddeh) during the festival
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef raises the question whether a banned person observes his ban during the festival. He cites a baraita that courts judge capital, lashes, and monetary cases, and if one does not obey, they ban him. Abaye objects that this might only be to examine his case, not to enforce the ban. The Gemara discusses the concern of delaying judgment.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef asks whether a banned person (מנודה) observes his ban during the festival, and cites a baraita that courts judge cases and ban those who disobey.
The Gemara objects: if the ban does not apply during the festival, how could the court impose a ban now that would be overridden by the festival?
Abaye answers that the court's action is only to examine his case, not to enforce the ban, analogous to capital cases where the court does not execute on a festival.
The Gemara cites a baraita that a Sanhedrin that executed someone does not eat that day, showing that court proceedings interfere with festival joy.
The Gemara resolves that just as in capital cases the court examines the case without executing, here too the ban is only for examination, but Rav Yosef objects that this would delay judgment.

items.text: Procedure for capital cases on a festival
items.text_en: Procedure for capital cases on a festival
items.desc_en: The Gemara describes the procedure: they examine the case in the morning, then eat and drink all day, and at sunset they complete the judgment and execute.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the objection by describing the procedure for capital cases on a festival: they examine the case in the morning, eat and drink all day, and at sunset complete the judgment and execute.

items.text: Abaye's and Rava's discussion on a banned person who was released
items.text_en: Abaye's and Rava's discussion on a banned person who was released
items.desc_en: Abaye cites a baraita about a banned person whom the Sages permitted. Rava clarifies that it means the Sages permitted him after he appeased his adversary and they released him, not that the ban was automatically lifted by the festival.

sub.desc_en: Abaye cites a baraita about a banned person (מנודה) whom the Sages permitted, implying that the ban is not automatically lifted by the festival.
Rava clarifies that the baraita means the Sages permitted him after he appeased his adversary and they released him, not that the ban was lifted by the festival itself.

items.text: Question about a leper during the festival
items.text_en: Question about a leper during the festival
items.desc_en: Abaye raises the question whether a leper observes his leprosy practices during the festival. He cites a baraita about a nazirite and a leper from their impurity to their purification, implying that during impurity he does observe. The Gemara deflects that this is a 'not necessary' statement. Rava then cites a verse to include a High Priest, showing that a leper observes his leprosy during the festival.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks whether a leper observes his leprosy practices during the festival, and cites a baraita about a nazirite and a leper from their impurity to their purification, implying that during impurity he does observe.
The Gemara deflects that the baraita is a 'not necessary' statement, teaching that even during purification one might delay offerings, so it does not prove the case.
Rava cites a verse to include a High Priest, showing that a leper observes his leprosy during the festival, and concludes that this proves the point.

items.text: Mourner forbidden in haircutting
items.text_en: Mourner forbidden in haircutting
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that a mourner is forbidden in haircutting, deriving from the verse to the sons of Aaron 'Do not shave your heads' implying that everyone else is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that a mourner is forbidden in haircutting, deriving from the verse to the sons of Aaron 'Do not shave your heads' implying that everyone else is forbidden.

items.text: Opening question: Are those under a ban and lepers permitted to cut hair?
items.text_en: Opening question: Are those under a ban and lepers permitted to cut hair?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a person under a ban (מְנוּדֶּה) and a leper (מְצוֹרָע) are permitted to cut their hair. It brings a baraita that states they are forbidden to cut hair and launder clothes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether those under a ban (מְנוּדִּין) and lepers (מְצוֹרָעִין) are permitted to cut their hair.
The Gemara brings a baraita that states both are forbidden to cut hair and launder clothes.

items.text: Law of a person who died while under a ban
items.text_en: Law of a person who died while under a ban
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the treatment of a person who died while under a ban. The court stones his coffin, and Rabbi Yehuda explains that they place a large stone on his coffin to teach that one who dies under a ban is treated this way.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the basic law: for one who died under a ban, the court stones his coffin.
Rabbi Yehuda clarifies that the court does not build a pile of stones like that of Achan, but rather places a large stone on the coffin, teaching that one who dies under a ban is stoned.

items.text: Head covering for a mourner, one under a ban, and a leper
items.text_en: Head covering for a mourner, one under a ban, and a leper
items.desc_en: The Gemara establishes that a mourner is obligated in head covering (עֲטִיפַת הָרֹאשׁ) from the verse to Ezekiel. It then questions whether one under a ban is obligated, and Rav Yosef brings a proof from a baraita that they sit wrapped like those under a ban and mourners, but Abaye distinguishes between a ban from heaven and a human ban. For a leper, the Gemara proves from the verse 'וְעַל שָׂפָם יַעְטֶה' that he is obligated in head covering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara establishes that a mourner is obligated in head covering (עֲטִיפַת הָרֹאשׁ) by inferring from God's command to Ezekiel not to cover his head, implying that everyone else is obligated.
The Gemara asks whether one under a ban (מְנוּדֶּה) is obligated in head covering.
Rav Yosef brings a supporting baraita that those under a ban sit wrapped like mourners, implying they are obligated in head covering.
Abaye objects that the baraita may refer to a ban from heaven (מְנוּדֶּה לַשָּׁמַיִם), which is more severe, and does not prove the case for a human ban.
The Gemara asks whether a leper (מְצוֹרָע) is obligated in head covering.
The Gemara proves from the verse 'וְעַל שָׂפָם יַעְטֶה' (and he shall cover his upper lip) that a leper is obligated in head covering, and concludes the matter.

items.text: Tefillin for a mourner, one under a ban, and a leper
items.text_en: Tefillin for a mourner, one under a ban, and a leper
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that a mourner is forbidden to wear tefillin, derived from the verse to Ezekiel. It then asks about one under a ban and leaves it unresolved (תֵּיקוּ). For a leper, it brings a verse and a dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva: Rabbi Eliezer says 'וְרֹאשׁוֹ יִהְיֶה פָרוּעַ' means growing hair, while Rabbi Akiva argues it refers to something external to the body, possibly tefillin. Rav Pappa clarifies it refers to a hat or scarf.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara deduces that a mourner is forbidden to wear tefillin, based on the verse to Ezekiel 'bind your turban (פְּאֵרְךָ) upon you', implying others are forbidden.
The Gemara asks about one under a ban (מנודה) regarding tefillin and leaves it unresolved (תֵּיקוּ).
The Gemara asks about a leper (מצורע) regarding tefillin and cites a verse: 'וְרֹאשׁוֹ יִהְיֶה פָרוּעַ' — Rabbi Eliezer interprets this as growing hair.
Rabbi Akiva argues that just as 'הֲוָיָיה' (being) in the garment refers to something external to the body, so too 'הֲוָיָיה' in the head refers to something external — presumably tefillin.
Rav Pappa resolves that the external head covering refers not to tefillin but to a hat (כומתא) or scarf (סודרא).

items.text: Greeting for a mourner, one under a ban, and a leper
items.text_en: Greeting for a mourner, one under a ban, and a leper
items.desc_en: The Gemara establishes that a mourner is forbidden to greet others, from the verse 'הֵאָנֵק דּוֹם'. It then asks about one under a ban; Rav Yosef brings a proof from a baraita comparing them to people rebuked by God, but Abaye distinguishes a ban from heaven. For a leper, the Gemara proves from 'וְעַל שָׂפָם יַעְטֶה' that he is forbidden to greet. It then questions whether this also applies to one under a ban, and Rav Acha bar Pinchas in the name of Rav Yosef explains that the baraita lists other matters and also forbids greeting.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that a mourner is forbidden to greet others, deriving this from the verse 'הֵאָנֵק דּוֹם' (be silent) said to Ezekiel.
The Gemara asks what the law is regarding one under a ban (מנודה) and greeting others.
Rav Yosef brings a proof from a baraita that compares one under a ban to people rebuked by God, implying they are forbidden to greet.
Abaye objects that the baraita refers to a ban from heaven (מנודה לשמים), which is more severe, and thus cannot prove the law for a human-imposed ban.
The Gemara asks what the law is regarding a leper (מצורע) and greeting others.
The Gemara brings a proof from the verse 'וְעַל שָׂפָם יַעְטֶה' (and he shall cover his upper lip), which is interpreted to mean that a leper is forbidden to greet others.
The Gemara concludes that a leper is indeed forbidden to greet others.
The Gemara asks whether we can also derive the law for one under a ban from this same baraita about the leper.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Pinchas in the name of Rav Yosef
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Pinchas in the name of Rav Yosef
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Pinchas in the name of Rav Yosef explains that the baraita lists other matters in which the leper is like one under a ban and a mourner, but regarding greeting, it states separately that he is forbidden, so the comparison does not extend to the ban.

items.text: Torah study for a mourner, one under a ban, and a leper
items.text_en: Torah study for a mourner, one under a ban, and a leper
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that a mourner is forbidden to engage in Torah study, from the verse 'דֹּם'. It then asks about one under a ban; Rav Yosef brings a baraita that a person under a ban may study and others may study with him, and he may be hired and others hired for him, but one under a severe ban (מוּחְרָם) has restrictions. Rav adds that he may sell water in the willow market. For a leper, the Gemara brings a baraita that zavim, lepers, and those who engage with niddot are permitted to read Torah, Prophets, and Writings, and to study midrash, Talmud, halakhot, and aggadot, but those with seminal emissions are forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that a mourner is forbidden to engage in Torah study, deriving this from the verse 'דֹּם' (be silent) said to Ezekiel.
The Gemara asks what the law is regarding one under a ban (מנודה) with respect to Torah study.
Rav Yosef brings a baraita that a person under a ban (מנודה) may study and others may study with him, and he may be hired and others hired for him.
The baraita adds that one under a severe ban (מוחרם) may not study or be taught, but may study alone to avoid interruption and may run a small shop for sustenance.
Rav adds that a person under a ban may sell water in the willow market, and the Gemara concludes that this proves the point.
The Gemara asks what the law is regarding a leper (מצורע) with respect to Torah study.

The Gemara brings a baraita that zavim, lepers, and those who engage with niddot are permitted to read Torah, Prophets, and Writings, and to study midrash, Talmud, halakhot, and aggadot, but those with seminal emissions are forbidden, concluding that a leper is permitted to study.

items.text: Laundering for a mourner, one under a ban, and a leper
items.text_en: Laundering for a mourner, one under a ban, and a leper
items.desc_en: The Gemara establishes that a mourner is forbidden to launder clothes, from the story of the wise woman of Tekoa. It then asks about those under a ban and lepers, and brings a baraita that they are forbidden to cut hair and launder clothes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara establishes that a mourner is forbidden to launder clothes, citing the biblical story of the wise woman of Tekoa.
The Gemara asks what the law is regarding those under a ban and lepers with respect to laundering.
The Gemara brings a baraita that those under a ban and lepers are forbidden to cut hair and launder clothes, concluding the matter.

items.text: Tearing garments for a mourner, one under a ban, and a leper
items.text_en: Tearing garments for a mourner, one under a ban, and a leper
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that a mourner is obligated in tearing garments (קְרִיעָה), from the verse to the sons of Aaron. It then asks about one under a ban and leaves it unresolved (תֵּיקוּ). For a leper, it proves from the verse 'בְּגָדָיו יִהְיוּ פְרוּמִים' that he is obligated in tearing. The daf ends with a baraita from bar Kappara about the mourner's obligation to overturn the bed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara deduces that a mourner is obligated in tearing garments (קְרִיעָה) from the verse to the sons of Aaron, implying all others are obligated.
The Gemara asks about one under a ban (מְנוּדֶּה) regarding tearing garments, and leaves it unresolved (תֵּיקוּ).
The Gemara proves from the verse 'בְּגָדָיו יִהְיוּ פְרוּמִים' that a leper is obligated in tearing garments.
The daf ends with a baraita from Bar Kappara stating that a mourner is obligated in overturning the bed.

items.text: Opening: Overturning beds for mourner and leper
items.text_en: Opening: Overturning beds for mourner and leper
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the practice of overturning beds for a mourner and a leper, citing a verse about God's image. It ends with a question about the mourner and leper regarding bed overturning, left unresolved (תֵּיקוּ).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by citing a verse about God's image and the practice of overturning beds for a mourner and a leper.
The Gemara asks whether a מנודה (excommunicated person) and a מצורע (leper) are also required to overturn their beds, and leaves the question unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Prohibition of work for mourner, banned person, and leper
items.text_en: Prohibition of work for mourner, banned person, and leper
items.desc_en: The mourner is prohibited from work based on a verse. Rav Yosef brings a baraita to infer that a banned person is also prohibited during the day but permitted at night, though the Gemara limits this to other restrictions. A second baraita shows a banned person may study and be hired, confirming the prohibition. The leper's status is left unresolved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that a mourner is prohibited from work, deriving this from a verbal analogy with the festival (חג).

The Gemara asks whether a banned person (מנודה) is also prohibited from work, and Rav Yosef brings a baraita that distinguishes between day (prohibited) and night (permitted) for both the banned person and the mourner.
The Gemara rejects the inference, clarifying that the baraita's comparison applies only to other restrictions, not to the prohibition of work.
A second baraita is cited, stating that a banned person may study and be hired, which confirms that he is prohibited from work.
The Gemara asks about the leper's status regarding work, but leaves the question unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Prohibition of bathing for mourner, banned person, and leper
items.text_en: Prohibition of bathing for mourner, banned person, and leper
items.desc_en: The mourner is prohibited from bathing, derived from a verse about anointing. Rav Yosef brings a baraita indicating that a banned person is only prohibited from bathing his whole body, but not his face, hands, and feet. The leper's status is left unresolved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that a mourner is prohibited from bathing, deriving this from the verse 'וְאַל תָּסוּכִי שֶׁמֶן' (and do not anoint with oil), since bathing is included in anointing.
The Gemara asks what the status of a banned person (מנודה) is regarding bathing.

Rav Yosef brings a supporting baraita (תא שמע) that when they said a mourner is prohibited from bathing, they only meant bathing the whole body, but face, hands, and feet are permitted, and the same applies to a banned person and a mourner.
The Gemara infers that the baraita applies to all three categories (mourner, banned person, and leper), but this is rejected.
The Gemara rejects the inference, clarifying that the baraita only applies to the remaining categories (mourner and banned person), not the leper.
The Gemara asks what the status of a leper (מצורע) is regarding bathing, and leaves it unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Prohibition of wearing sandals for mourner, banned person, and leper
items.text_en: Prohibition of wearing sandals for mourner, banned person, and leper
items.desc_en: The mourner is prohibited from wearing sandals, inferred from God's command to Ezekiel. Rav Yosef brings a baraita that a banned person is only prohibited in the city but permitted on the road. The leper's status is left unresolved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that a mourner is prohibited from wearing sandals, inferred from God's command to Ezekiel to put on his sandals, implying others are forbidden.
The Gemara asks what the rule is for a banned person (מנודה) regarding wearing sandals.
Rav Yosef brings a supporting baraita that a banned person is prohibited from wearing sandals only in the city but permitted on the road, and the same applies to a mourner.
The Gemara rejects the inference, clarifying that the baraita refers only to the other prohibitions (שארא) and not to sandals.
The Gemara asks what the rule is for a leper (מצורע) regarding wearing sandals, and leaves it unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Prohibition of marital relations for mourner, banned person, and leper
items.text_en: Prohibition of marital relations for mourner, banned person, and leper
items.desc_en: The mourner is prohibited from marital relations, inferred from David's comfort of Bathsheba. Rav Yosef brings a proof that Israelites in the desert, who were banned, engaged in marital relations. Abaye objects that a heavenly ban is lighter. The Gemara debates the severity, and a baraita shows a leper is prohibited, but this does not extend to a banned person.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that a mourner is prohibited from marital relations, deriving this from the verse about David comforting Bathsheba after the child's death.
Rav Yosef asks about a banned person's marital relations and brings a supporting evidence that the Israelites in the desert, who were banned, engaged in marital relations.
Abaye objects that a heavenly ban is lighter, so the case of the Israelites in the desert may not apply to a human-imposed ban.
The Gemara questions Abaye's characterization, noting that he previously said a heavenly ban is more severe, and concludes that Abaye is uncertain and rejects both possibilities.
The Gemara cites a baraita that a leper is prohibited from marital relations, based on the verse 'וְיָשַׁב מִחוּץ לְאׇהֳלוֹ' (he shall dwell outside his tent), interpreting 'tent' as his wife.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Rav Pinchas in the name of Rav Yosef
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Pinchas in the name of Rav Yosef
sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether this also applies to a banned person, and Rav Huna bar Rav Pinchas in the name of Rav Yosef resolves that the baraita only equates the leper to a mourner and banned person in other matters, not in the prohibition of marital relations.

items.text: Sending offerings for mourner, banned person, and leper
items.text_en: Sending offerings for mourner, banned person, and leper
items.desc_en: A mourner does not send his offerings, based on Rabbi Shimon's teaching. Rav Yosef brings a proof that Israelites in the desert, who were banned, sent offerings. Abaye objects that a heavenly ban is different. The Gemara concludes with uncertainty. A baraita shows a leper may send offerings after his purification.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that a mourner does not send his offerings, citing a baraita of Rabbi Shimon who derives from the word 'שלמים' (peace-offerings) that the offerer must be 'שלם' (whole), not an אונן (acute mourner).
The Gemara asks whether a banned person (מנודה) may send his offerings, and Rav Yosef brings a proof that the Israelites in the desert, who were banned, sent their offerings.
Abaye objects that a heavenly ban (מנודה לשמים) is different because it is lighter (קיל), so the proof from the desert is not applicable to a human-imposed ban.
The Gemara rejects Abaye's objection by noting that Abaye himself elsewhere called the heavenly ban severe (חמיר), so he is uncertain and pushes the question aside.
The Gemara brings a baraita to resolve the question about a leper (מצורע), showing that after his purification he may send his sin-offering, implying that a leper is permitted to send offerings.

items.text: Opening Mishnah dispute
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah dispute
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon regarding the tenth of an ephah offering, with Rabbi Yehuda stating it is his tenth and Rabbi Shimon linking the offering to the priest's ability to enter the sanctuary.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states Rabbi Yehuda's position that the tenth of an ephah offering is his own.
Rabbi Shimon argues that the offering depends on the priest's ability to enter the sanctuary, linking the tenth of an ephah to the priest's fitness for entry.

items.text: Derivation of court procedures from Torah verses
items.text_en: Derivation of court procedures from Torah verses
items.desc_en: Rava derives various court procedures—summoning, setting a date, excommunication, confiscation of property, and publicizing the sin—from biblical verses, primarily from the stories of Korach and the judges of Israel.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks: from where do we derive that a court sends an agent to summon a person to court, and cites the verse where Moses sent for Datan and Aviram.

Rava derives the procedures of summoning to court, appearing before a great authority, naming the litigants, setting a date, and postponing the date, all from verses in the Korach narrative and the book of Isaiah.
Rava derives that if a person insults the court agent and the agent reports it, it is not considered לשון הרע (evil speech), from the verse 'Will you gouge out the eyes of those men?'
Rava derives the practice of excommunication (שמתא) and the ban of property (חרם) from the verses 'Curse Meroz' and 'Curse, curse'.

Rava derives that one who eats or drinks with an excommunicated person or stands within four cubits of him is also subject to the ban, and that the sin must be publicized, from the verse 'For they did not come to the aid of the Lord'.

items.text: Ulla's statement about Barak's excommunication of Meroz
items.text_en: Ulla's statement about Barak's excommunication of Meroz
items.desc_en: Ulla states that Barak excommunicated Meroz with four hundred shofar blasts, and there is a dispute whether Meroz was a great man or a star, as per the verse 'From heaven they fought, the stars.'

sub.desc_en: Ulla states that Barak excommunicated Meroz with four hundred shofar blasts.
Some say Meroz was a great man.
Others say Meroz was a star.
The verse 'From heaven they fought, the stars' is cited to support the interpretation that Meroz was a star.

items.text: Further derivations and definition of hardafa
items.text_en: Further derivations and definition of hardafa
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives additional court actions—confiscation of property, beating, cursing, hair-plucking, swearing, binding, and pursuing (hardafa)—from verses, and defines hardafa as a sequence: immediate niddui, repetition after thirty days, and excommunication after sixty days.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of confiscating property and cites the verse from Ezra about one who does not come to the assembly.
The Gemara asks for the source of beating, cursing, hair-plucking, and swearing, citing Nehemiah's actions.
The Gemara asks for the source of binding, tying, and pursuing (hardafa), citing the verse from Ezra.
The Gemara asks the meaning of the term 'lishroshi' in the verse.

sub.text: Ada Mari quoting Nechemya bar Baruch quoting Rav Chiyya bar Avin quoting Rav Yehuda
sub.text_en: Ada Mari quoting Nechemya bar Baruch quoting Rav Chiyya bar Avin quoting Rav Yehuda
sub.desc_en: Ada Mari explains that 'lishroshi' means hardafa (pursuit/excommunication).
The Gemara asks for the definition of hardafa.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda brei d'Rav Shmuel bar Shilat quoting Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda brei d'Rav Shmuel bar Shilat quoting Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda brei d'Rav Shmuel bar Shilat in the name of Rav defines hardafa as a sequence: immediate niddui, repetition after thirty days, and excommunication after sixty days.

items.text: Rav Chisda's ruling on warning for monetary cases
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's ruling on warning for monetary cases
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda rules that for monetary cases, one warns the person on Monday, Thursday, and Monday, but for contempt of court, the ban is immediate.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Chinana citing Rav Chisda
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Chinana citing Rav Chisda
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Chinana reports Rav Chisda's ruling that for monetary cases one warns the person on Monday, Thursday, and Monday, but for contempt of court (אפקירותא) the ban is immediate.

items.text: Case of the butcher and Abaye's dilemma
items.text_en: Case of the butcher and Abaye's dilemma
items.desc_en: A butcher who insulted Rav Tovi bar Matna was excommunicated by Abaye and Rava. When the butcher later appeased his opponent, Abaye was uncertain whether to lift the ban before thirty days, and concluded that for contempt, the ban must last thirty days, and that the original three judges cannot be replaced by another three to lift it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts a case where a butcher insulted Rav Tovi bar Matna, and Abaye and Rava excommunicated him.
After the butcher appeased his opponent, Abaye was uncertain whether to lift the ban before thirty days or leave it in place since the rabbis wanted to enter.

sub.text: Rav Idi bar Avin's answer in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Idi bar Avin's answer in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Abaye asked Rav Idi bar Avin, who cited Rav Tachlifa bar Avimi in the name of Shmuel: 'A judge who bans can also lift the ban.'
Abaye distinguished that the lenient rule applies to monetary cases, but for contempt (אפקירותא), the ban must last thirty days.
The Gemara infers that Abaye held that the original three judges who excommunicated cannot be replaced by another three to lift the ban.

items.text: Inquiry about lifting a ban by different judges
items.text_en: Inquiry about lifting a ban by different judges
items.desc_en: The Gemara inquires whether three other judges can lift a ban imposed by the original three, and proves from a baraita about niddui hierarchy that a student's ban is valid for his honor, each judge can annul his part, and the original three cannot be replaced.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether three other judges can lift a ban imposed by the original three.
The Gemara cites a baraita detailing the hierarchy of niddui (ban) from a student to the nasi (patriarch), showing that a ban imposed by a higher authority cannot be annulled by a lower one.

The Gemara derives three conclusions from the baraita: a student's ban for his own honor is valid, each judge can annul his part, and the original three judges cannot be replaced by others to lift the ban.

items.text: Amemar's ruling that other judges can lift the ban
items.text_en: Amemar's ruling that other judges can lift the ban
items.desc_en: Amemar rules that three other judges can lift the ban, and explains that the baraita about Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel means the deceased judge's part is not annulled until three others come and lift it.

sub.desc_en: Amemar rules that three other judges can lift the ban imposed by the original three.
Rav Ashi objects by citing the baraita where Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says the deceased judge's part is not annulled.
Amemar explains that the baraita does not mean the ban is never annulled, but rather that it is not annulled until three other judges come and lift it.

items.text: Duration of niddui and nezifa, and a story of Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi
items.text_en: Duration of niddui and nezifa, and a story of Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi
items.desc_en: The Tannaim teach that niddui lasts at least thirty days and nezifa seven days, with a verse as a reminder. Rav Chisda says their niddui is like their nezifa. A story illustrates that Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi's father (Rabbi) was offended, and Bar Kappara imposed nezifa on himself for thirty days.

sub.desc_en: The Tannaim teach that niddui lasts at least thirty days and nezifa at least seven days, with a verse as a reminder.
Rav Chisda explains that their niddui is like their nezifa, and their nezifa is seven days and no more.
A story is introduced: Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi and Bar Kappara were studying, and Rabbi Shimon said a matter needs Rabbi, prompting Bar Kappara to ask what Rabbi says.
Rabbi Shimon told his father Rabbi, who became offended; Bar Kappara came to appease him but was rebuffed, and imposed nezifa on himself for thirty days.

items.text: Rabbi's decree against teaching in the market
items.text_en: Rabbi's decree against teaching in the market
items.desc_en: Rabbi decreed that students should not study in the market, and he expounded a verse about the thigh being like jewels, implying modesty.

sub.desc_en: The gemara reports that Rabbi decreed students should not teach in the market, and he expounded the verse 'חַמּוּקֵי יְרֵכַיִךְ' (the curves of your thighs) to teach that just as the thigh is hidden, so too Torah study should be modest.

items.text: Opening principle: Torah study in private
items.text_en: Opening principle: Torah study in private
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the principle that words of Torah should be studied in private, citing a verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the principle that words of Torah should be studied in private, citing a verse.

items.text: Story of Rabbi Chiyya's nezifah
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Chiyya's nezifah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya taught Torah publicly to his nephews, angering Rabbi. Rabbi Chiyya was placed in nezifah for thirty days. On the thirtieth day, Rabbi sent conflicting messages, and Rabbi Chiyya came based on the first message. Rabbi applied a verse about divine favor.

sub.desc_en: The story opens: Rabbi Chiyya taught Torah publicly to his nephews, angering Rabbi, who placed him in nezifah for thirty days.
On the thirtieth day, Rabbi sent a message to come, then sent a second message not to come.
The gemara asks what Rabbi initially thought and what he later thought, explaining the principle of מקצת היום ככולו (a part of the day is like the whole).
Rabbi Chiyya came based on the first message, and Rabbi applied the verse 'ברצות ה' דרכי איש גם אויביו ישלים אתו' (When God favors a man's ways, even his enemies make peace with him).

items.text: Justification for public Torah study
items.text_en: Justification for public Torah study
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya justifies his public teaching with the verse 'Wisdom cries aloud in the streets'. Rabbi responds that he misunderstood the verse, which Rava explains means that one who studies Torah in private will have his Torah publicized. The Gemara resolves a contradiction with another verse, and notes Rabbi Chiyya's interpretation of a different verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks Rabbi Chiyya why he taught Torah publicly in the marketplace.
Rabbi Chiyya answers that he acted based on the verse 'Wisdom cries aloud in the streets' (Proverbs 1:20).
Rabbi objects that Rabbi Chiyya has not properly studied or been taught the correct interpretation of the verse.
Rava explains that the verse means one who studies Torah in private will have his Torah publicized, not that one should teach in public.
The Gemara objects with the verse 'I have not spoken in secret from the beginning' (Isaiah 48:16), which seems to contradict the idea of private study.
The Gemara resolves that the verse refers specifically to the days of the public assembly (כלה), when Torah is taught openly.
The Gemara asks how Rabbi Chiyya interprets the verse 'The curves of your thighs' (Song of Songs 7:2).
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Chiyya interprets the verse as referring to charity and acts of loving-kindness.

items.text: Duration of nezifah for a nasi vs. an ordinary person
items.text_en: Duration of nezifah for a nasi vs. an ordinary person
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers that nezifah for a nasi is thirty days, but for an ordinary person it is only one day, as illustrated by the story of Shmuel and Mar Ukva. Mar Ukva inadvertently caused Shmuel to walk behind him, and Shmuel imposed a one-day nezifah on himself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the story of Rabbi Chiyya that nezifah for a nasi is thirty days, but immediately notes that the case of a nasi is different.
The Gemara answers that nezifah for an ordinary person is only one day, and supports this with the story of Shmuel and Mar Ukva.

items.text: Additional cases of one-day nezifah
items.text_en: Additional cases of one-day nezifah
items.desc_en: Two more stories illustrate one-day nezifah: a woman who did not defer to a Torah scholar was told by Rav Nachman to observe nezifah for one day; and Zutra bar Toviyah, who questioned Rav Yehuda about a verse, was placed in nezifah for one day.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara tells a story of a woman who did not defer to a Torah scholar, and Rav Nachman instructed her to observe nezifah for one day.
The Gemara tells a story of Zutra bar Toviyah who questioned Rav Yehuda about a verse, and Rav Yehuda placed him in nezifah for one day.

items.text: Aggadic discussion of David's last words and humility
items.text_en: Aggadic discussion of David's last words and humility
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the verse 'These are the last words of David', identifying the 'first words' as the song he sang after being saved from Saul. God rebukes David for singing over Saul's downfall. The Gemara then expounds on David's humility, his sitting on the ground to teach, and God's praise that David could annul divine decrees. A bat kol limits this to the matter of Uriah.

sub.text: Zutra bar Toviyah's question to Rav Yehuda
sub.text_en: Zutra bar Toviyah's question to Rav Yehuda
sub.desc_en: Zutra bar Toviyah asks Rav Yehuda what the 'first words' of David are, implied by the verse 'These are the last words of David'.

sub.text: Narrative: Rav Yehuda's silence and Zutra's persistence
sub.text_en: Narrative: Rav Yehuda's silence and Zutra's persistence
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda remains silent, then Zutra repeats the question, and Rav Yehuda rebukes him, imposing a one-day rebuke on himself.
The Gemara identifies the 'first words' as the song David sang when God saved him from Saul.
God rebukes David for singing a song over Saul's downfall, noting that had David been Saul, he would have destroyed many Davids.
The Gemara explains that the term 'Cushite' in the psalm refers to Saul, highlighting his unusual deeds.
The Gemara provides two more analogies where 'Cushite' indicates unusualness: Zipporah and Zedekiah.
The Gemara adds a fourth analogy: Israel is called 'Cushites' to indicate their distinctiveness among the nations.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani explains that David 'raised the yoke of repentance'.
Rabbi Avahu explains that God says: 'I rule over man, but the righteous rule over Me, for they annul My decrees.'
Rabbi Avahu interprets the verse 'These are the names of the mighty men' as referring to David's heroic deeds.
The Gemara describes David's humility: he sat on the ground to teach Torah after his teacher Ira died, refusing cushions.
Rav explains that because David humbled himself, God said he would be like Him, able to annul divine decrees.
The Gemara explains that David was head of the three patriarchs, and that he was soft as a worm in Torah study but hard as wood in war.

sub.text: Gemara's exposition of David's military prowess
sub.text_en: Gemara's exposition of David's military prowess
sub.desc_en: The Gemara describes David killing eight hundred with one arrow, but lamenting that he could not kill a thousand.
A bat kol (heavenly voice) declares that David's ability to annul decrees applies only regarding the matter of Uriah the Hittite.

items.text: Introduction of a new teaching chain
items.text_en: Introduction of a new teaching chain
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a new statement with multiple transmission chains, setting up the next discussion.

sub.text: Rabbi Tanchum bar Rabbi Chiyya / Rabbi Yaakov bar Acha / Rabbi Simlai / Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Rabbi Tanchum bar Rabbi Chiyya / Rabbi Yaakov bar Acha / Rabbi Simlai / Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a new statement with multiple transmission chains, attributing it to Rabbi Tanchum bar Rabbi Chiyya via Rabbi Yaakov bar Acha and Rabbi Simlai, with alternative versions citing Rabbi Tanchum in the name of Rav Huna, or Rav Huna alone.

items.text: A student excommunicated for the honor of his teacher
items.text_en: A student excommunicated for the honor of his teacher
items.desc_en: The Gemara establishes that a student excommunicated for the honor of his teacher is truly excommunicated, citing a baraita that distinguishes between excommunication by a teacher and by a student. It then questions whether this applies to matters of Heaven, concluding it must be for the teacher's own honor.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that a student who excommunicated someone for his teacher's honor, his excommunication is valid, and cites a baraita that distinguishes between excommunication by a teacher and by a student.
The Gemara questions whether the excommunication is for matters of Heaven or for the teacher's own honor, concluding it must be for the teacher's own honor.

items.text: A scholar who judges himself and the case of the unpopular scholar
items.text_en: A scholar who judges himself and the case of the unpopular scholar
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef states that a Torah scholar may judge himself in a clear matter. The Gemara then recounts a case of a scholar whose rulings were unpopular, and Rav Yehuda seeks advice on whether to excommunicate him. Rabbi Yochanan's teaching is cited: a teacher must be like an angel of God for students to seek Torah from him.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef states that a Torah scholar may judge himself in a clear matter.
The Gemara recounts a case of a scholar whose rulings were unpopular, and Rav Yehuda deliberates whether to excommunicate him.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan via Rabba bar bar Chana
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan via Rabba bar bar Chana
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana cites Rabbi Yochanan's teaching that a teacher must be like an angel of God for students to seek Torah from him.

items.text: Rav Yehuda excommunicates the scholar and later smiles at him
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda excommunicates the scholar and later smiles at him
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda excommunicates the scholar. When Rav Yehuda later falls ill and the scholar visits with the Sages, Rav Yehuda smiles. The scholar questions this, and Rav Yehuda explains he was not mocking him but rejoicing that he did not flatter even a great man like him.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda excommunicates the scholar; later, when Rav Yehuda falls ill and the scholar visits with the Sages, Rav Yehuda smiles at him.
The scholar questions Rav Yehuda, asking whether excommunication was not enough, that he also mocks him by smiling.
Rav Yehuda explains that he was not mocking the scholar, but rejoicing that he did not flatter even a great man like him.

items.text: The scholar seeks release from the ban and dies
items.text_en: The scholar seeks release from the ban and dies
items.desc_en: After Rav Yehuda's death, the scholar asks the Sages to release him, but they say only Rabbi Yehuda Nasi can do so. Rabbi Ammi examines his case but hesitates due to Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani's objection citing the maidservant's ban. Rabbi Zeira infers from the elder's arrival that he should not be released. The scholar leaves weeping, is stung by a hornet, and dies. He is buried in the judges' cave but not the pious ones' cave.

sub.desc_en: After Rav Yehuda's death, the banned scholar comes to the study hall and asks the Sages to release him from the ban.
The Sages tell him that no one as important as Rav Yehuda is present to release him, and direct him to go to Rabbi Yehuda Nasi.
The scholar goes to Rabbi Yehuda Nasi, who instructs Rabbi Ammi to examine his case and release him if appropriate.
Rabbi Ammi examines the case and is inclined to release him.

Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani objects by citing the precedent of the maidservant of Rabbi's house, whose ban was not treated lightly for three years, arguing that the scholar's ban should be treated even more seriously.
Rabbi Zeira infers from the elder's unusual arrival at the study hall that the scholar should not be released.
The scholar is not released; he leaves weeping.
A hornet stings the scholar on his penis and he dies; he is buried in the judges' cave but not the pious ones' cave.

items.text: Reason for burial in judges' cave: acting like Rabbi Ila'i
items.text_en: Reason for burial in judges' cave: acting like Rabbi Ila'i
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the scholar was buried in the judges' cave because he acted like Rabbi Ila'i, who taught that if one's evil inclination overcomes him, he should go to a place where he is unknown and do as he pleases in private to avoid desecrating God's name publicly.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the scholar was buried in the judges' cave, and answers that he acted like Rabbi Ila'i.

The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Ila'i teaches that if one's evil inclination overcomes him, he should go to a place where he is unknown and do as he pleases in private to avoid desecrating God's name publicly.

items.text: The maidservant's excommunication and Reish Lakish's case
items.text_en: The maidservant's excommunication and Reish Lakish's case
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts the story of the maidservant of Rabbi's house who excommunicated a man for hitting his adult son, citing the prohibition against placing a stumbling block before the blind. Then Reish Lakish excommunicated a man for eating figs from his orchard, but the man countered that he owed money but not excommunication. The Sages ruled that Reish Lakish's ban is valid but the other's is not, and advised the man to go to the Nasi for release.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the maidservant of Rabbi's house and recounts how she excommunicated a man for hitting his adult son, citing the prohibition of placing a stumbling block before the blind.
A baraita is cited to support that the verse about placing a stumbling block before the blind refers to hitting an adult son.
The Gemara recounts how Reish Lakish excommunicated a man for eating figs from his orchard, and the man objected that he owed money but not excommunication.
The Sages ruled that Reish Lakish's ban is valid but the other's is not, and advised the man to go to the Nasi for release.

items.text: Excommunication of a court president and a Torah scholar
items.text_en: Excommunication of a court president and a Torah scholar
items.desc_en: Rav Huna reports a decree in Usha: a court president who sins is not excommunicated but told to stay home; if he repeats, he is excommunicated due to desecration of God's name. This disagrees with Reish Lakish, who says a Torah scholar who sins is not excommunicated publicly, as per the verse about covering him like night.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna reports a decree from Usha: a court president who sins is not excommunicated but told to stay home; if he repeats, he is excommunicated due to desecration of God's name.
Reish Lakish disagrees, stating that a Torah scholar who sins is not excommunicated publicly, as per the verse about covering him like night.

items.text: A scholar excommunicating himself and the meaning of shamta
items.text_en: A scholar excommunicating himself and the meaning of shamta
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra the Pious would excommunicate himself first before excommunicating another scholar, and would release himself upon entering his lodging. Rav Giddel says a scholar may excommunicate and release himself. Rav Pappa boasts he never excommunicated a scholar; instead, in the West they appoint a lash for a scholar but not for excommunication. The meaning of shamta is debated: Rav says 'death there,' Shmuel says 'desolation,' and it is effective like a plaster on an oven.

sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra the Pious would excommunicate himself first before excommunicating another scholar, and would release himself upon entering his lodging.
Rav Giddel says in the name of Rav that a scholar may excommunicate and release himself.
Rav Pappa boasts he never excommunicated a scholar; instead, in the West they appoint a lash for a scholar but not for excommunication.
The Gemara asks the meaning of the term 'שמתא' (shamta).
Rav says 'שמתא' means 'death there' (שם מיתה).
Shmuel says 'שמתא' means 'desolation' (שממה), and it is effective like a plaster on an oven.

items.text: The entry and exit of the ban through 248 limbs
items.text_en: The entry and exit of the ban through 248 limbs
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish states that just as the ban enters through 248 limbs, so it exits through 248 limbs. He supports this with gematria: 'cherem' equals 248 for entry, and 'racheim' equals 248 for exit, from the verse 'In wrath remember mercy.'

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish states that the ban enters and exits through 248 limbs.
The gemara supports entry with the gematria of 'חרם' (cherem) equaling 248.
The gemara supports exit with the gematria of 'רחם' (racheim) equaling 248.

items.text: Stories of excommunication: a dog and a strongman
items.text_en: Stories of excommunication: a dog and a strongman
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef tells of a dog that ate scholars' shoes; they excommunicated it, and fire consumed its ear. Then a strongman was harassing a scholar; Rav Yosef advised excommunicating him, but the scholar feared him. Rav Yosef then told him to take a potsherd and place it in a jug, implying a symbolic act.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef declares that he cast excommunication (שמתא) on a dog's ear, and the ear itself acted (i.e., was consumed by fire).
The story is told of a dog that ate the shoes of the rabbis; they excommunicated it, and fire fell on its ear and consumed it.
A strongman was harassing a certain scholar; the scholar came before Rav Yosef, who told him to excommunicate the strongman, but the scholar said he was afraid of him.
Rav Yosef tells the scholar to take a potsherd and place it in a jug, implying a symbolic act to overcome fear.

items.text: Explanation of 'Shifurei' and 'Tevara'
items.text_en: Explanation of 'Shifurei' and 'Tevara'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the terms 'Shifurei' (retribution) and 'Tevara' (breaking), citing a baraita that wherever the Sages set their eyes, there is either death or poverty.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'Shifurei' means and explains it as retribution taken from the person.
The Gemara asks what 'Tevara' means and Rav Yitzchak bar Rav Yehuda answers that it breaks tall houses.
A baraita is cited where Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel states that wherever the Sages set their eyes, there is either death or poverty.

items.text: Nazirite and leper: whether they had leisure
items.text_en: Nazirite and leper: whether they had leisure
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira whether the leniency for a nazirite and leper to shave during the festival applies only when they had no leisure before the festival, or even when they had leisure. Rabbi Zeira answers from a baraita that they are permitted even if they had leisure, so as not to delay their offerings.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira whether the permission for a nazirite and leper to shave during the festival applies only when they had no leisure before the festival, or even when they had leisure.
Rabbi Zeira answers by citing a baraita that distinguishes between those who had no leisure (permitted) and those who had leisure (forbidden).
The baraita adds that a nazirite and leper are permitted even if they had leisure, so as not to delay their offerings.

items.text: The mourner whose eighth day falls on Shabbat Erev Regel
items.text_en: The mourner whose eighth day falls on Shabbat Erev Regel
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes a baraita that permits a priest and a mourner to shave during the festival. It clarifies that the mourner's case is when his seventh day falls on Shabbat Erev Regel, so he could not shave before the festival. The Tanna of our Mishnah holds like the Rabbis that partial day is not considered as the whole day, while the baraita holds like Abba Shaul that it is.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that a priest and a mourner are permitted to shave during the festival.
The Gemara asks: In what circumstances does this mourner case apply?
The Gemara objects: If his eighth day fell on Erev Regel, he should have shaved before the festival.
The Gemara answers: Rather, his eighth day fell on Shabbat Erev Regel, so he could not shave on Shabbat.
The Gemara objects: He could have shaved on Erev Shabbat before Shabbat.

sub.text: Rav Chisda citing Ravina bar Sheila
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda citing Ravina bar Sheila
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda cites Ravina bar Sheila that the halacha follows Abba Shaul, and the Sages agree with Abba Shaul that when the eighth day falls on Shabbat Erev Regel, one may shave on Erev Shabbat.
The Gemara resolves: The case is when his seventh day fell on Shabbat Erev Regel, so he could not shave before the festival.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the baraita's Tanna
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the baraita's Tanna
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Tanna of the baraita holds like Abba Shaul that partial day is considered as the whole day, and since Shabbat prevented shaving, he is considered forced.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of our Mishnah's Tanna
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of our Mishnah's Tanna
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Tanna of our Mishnah holds like the Sages that partial day is not considered as the whole day, so the seven-day mourning period is not yet complete.

items.text: The priest whose watch ended during the festival
items.text_en: The priest whose watch ended during the festival
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the case of the priest: his watch ended during the festival itself. The Tanna of our Mishnah considers him as one whose watch did not end because all watches share the offerings, while the baraita considers his personal watch as ended.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: In what circumstances does this priest's case arise? If his watch ended on the eve of the festival, he should have shaved then.

The Gemara answers: No, it is necessary where his watch ended during the festival itself; the Tanna of our Mishnah considers him as one whose watch did not end because all watches share the offerings, while the baraita considers his personal watch as ended.

items.text: Shaving during mourning when bereavements follow one another
items.text_en: Shaving during mourning when bereavements follow one another
items.desc_en: A baraita states that those permitted to shave during the festival are also permitted during their mourning period, but another baraita forbids it. Rav Chisda resolves the contradiction: the leniency applies when bereavements followed one another, and even then only with a razor and water, not scissors or fuller's earth. Rav Chisda deduces that a mourner is forbidden in laundering.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that those permitted to shave during the festival are also permitted to shave during their mourning period.
The Gemara objects that another baraita forbids shaving during mourning.
Rav Chisda in the name of Rav Sheila resolves the contradiction: the lenient baraita applies when bereavements followed one another (תְּכָפוּהוּ אֲבָלָיו).
The Gemara objects: if the leniency is for one whose bereavements followed one another, why specify 'all these' — even anyone else would be permitted.
A baraita is cited: one whose bereavements followed one another and whose hair became heavy may lighten it with a razor and wash his garment with water.
Rav Chisda qualifies the baraita: the leniency applies only with a razor and water, not with scissors or fuller's earth.
Rav Chisda deduces from the baraita's restriction to water that a mourner is forbidden in laundering (תִּכְבּוֹסֶת).

items.text: Nail-cutting during the festival and mourning: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yossi
items.text_en: Nail-cutting during the festival and mourning: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yossi
items.desc_en: A baraita records a dispute: Rabbi Yehuda forbids nail-cutting during the festival and during mourning, while Rabbi Yossi permits both. Ulla rules: the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda for mourning and Rabbi Yossi for the festival. Shmuel's opinion is introduced but cut off.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with a ruling: just as haircutting is forbidden during the festival, so too nail-cutting is forbidden during the festival according to Rabbi Yehuda, while Rabbi Yossi permits it.
The baraita extends the same dispute to mourning: just as a mourner is forbidden to cut hair, so too he is forbidden to cut nails according to Rabbi Yehuda, while Rabbi Yossi permits it.
Ulla rules that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Yehuda for mourning and Rabbi Yossi for the festival; Shmuel's opinion is introduced but cut off.

items.text: Opening ruling: Halacha follows Rabbi Yosei in mourning
items.text_en: Opening ruling: Halacha follows Rabbi Yosei in mourning
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the halacha follows Rabbi Yosei both regarding the festival and mourning, as Samuel said the halacha follows the one who is lenient in mourning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that the halacha follows Rabbi Yosei regarding both the festival and mourning, citing Samuel's principle that the halacha follows the lenient position in mourning.

items.text: Story of Samuel and Pinchas: The covenant of the lips
items.text_en: Story of Samuel and Pinchas: The covenant of the lips
items.desc_en: A story is told about Samuel's brother Pinchas who had an incident, and Samuel came to ask him about it. Samuel noticed his long nails and asked why he didn't cut them. Pinchas responded that if Samuel were in his situation, he wouldn't treat it lightly. Later, Pinchas had an incident and Samuel came to ask him, and Pinchas threw his nail clippings at Samuel, asking if there is no covenant of the lips. Rabbi Yochanan derives from Abraham that there is a covenant of the lips.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara tells a story about Pinchas, Shmuel's brother, who had an incident; Shmuel came to ask about it, noticed Pinchas's long nails, and questioned why he didn't cut them, to which Pinchas responded that if Shmuel were in his situation, he wouldn't treat it lightly.
The story continues: later Shmuel had an incident, and Pinchas came to ask him; Pinchas threw his nail clippings at Shmuel, asking if there is no covenant of the lips.
Rabbi Yochanan derives from Abraham that there is a covenant of the lips, citing the verse where Abraham said he and the lad would return, and indeed both returned.

items.text: Clarification: Nail cutting includes both hands and feet
items.text_en: Clarification: Nail cutting includes both hands and feet
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially thought that cutting nails of the hand is permitted but not of the foot. Rav Anan bar Tachlifa says that Samuel clarified that there is no difference between hand and foot nails.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara initially assumes that cutting hand nails is permitted during חול המועד (the intermediate festival days) but foot nails are not.

sub.text: Rav Anan bar Tachlifa citing Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Anan bar Tachlifa citing Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Anan bar Tachlifa clarifies that Shmuel explicitly stated there is no distinction between hand and foot nails — both are permitted.

items.text: Rav Chiya bar Ashi and Rav Shemen bar Abba: Nail cutting in a barber's manner is prohibited
items.text_en: Rav Chiya bar Ashi and Rav Shemen bar Abba: Nail cutting in a barber's manner is prohibited
items.desc_en: Rav Chiya bar Ashi says in the name of Rav that cutting nails in a barber's manner (with instruments) is prohibited. Rav Shemen bar Abba recounts that he was standing before Rabbi Yochanan in the study hall during Chol HaMoed, and Rabbi Yochanan cut his nails with his teeth and threw them away. From this, three things are derived: it is permitted to cut nails during Chol HaMoed, there is no concern for disgust, and it is permitted to throw them away.

sub.text: Rav Chiya bar Ashi citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chiya bar Ashi citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiya bar Ashi reports in the name of Rav that cutting nails in a barber's manner (בגנוסטרא) is prohibited during Chol HaMoed.
Rav Shemen bar Abba testifies that he saw Rabbi Yochanan in the study hall during Chol HaMoed cut his nails with his teeth and throw them away.
The Gemara derives three halachic conclusions from Rabbi Yochanan's action: it is permitted to cut nails during Chol HaMoed, there is no concern for disgust, and it is permitted to throw them away.

items.text: Objection and resolution: The three laws of nails
items.text_en: Objection and resolution: The three laws of nails
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects with a baraita that states three things about nails: one who buries them is righteous, one who burns them is pious, and one who throws them away is wicked, because a pregnant woman might step on them and miscarry. The Gemara resolves that in a study hall, women are not commonly present, and even if they are swept outside, since the location has changed, the concern is different.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that states three rules about nails: one who buries them is righteous, one who burns them is pious, and one who throws them away is wicked, because a pregnant woman might step on them and miscarry.
The Gemara resolves that in a study hall women are not commonly present, and even if nails are swept outside, since the location has changed, the concern is different.

items.text: Rav Yehuda and others: Permitting nails and mustache for a groom
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda and others: Permitting nails and mustache for a groom
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says in the name of Rav that a couple came from Chamtan before Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and asked for nails, and he permitted them. If they asked for a mustache, he permitted them. Shmuel says they even asked for a mustache and he permitted. Avitul the scribe says in the name of Rav Pappa that the mustache is from corner to corner. Rabbi Ami says it is a mustache that interferes with eating. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says it seems to him like a mustache that interferes.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in the name of Rav that a couple came from Chamtan before Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and asked about nails, and he permitted them.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav (continued)
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav (continued)
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda adds that if they asked about a mustache, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi also permitted it.
Shmuel adds that they even asked about a mustache and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi permitted it.

sub.text: Avitul Sefra in the name of Rav Pappa
sub.text_en: Avitul Sefra in the name of Rav Pappa
sub.desc_en: Avitul the scribe defines in the name of Rav Pappa that the permitted mustache is from corner to corner of the mouth.
Rabbi Ami specifies that the mustache which interferes with eating is the one permitted.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak concludes that in his own case, his mustache seems like one that interferes with eating, thus permitting him to trim it.

items.text: Avitul Sefra: Pharaoh's measurements and sorcery
items.text_en: Avitul Sefra: Pharaoh's measurements and sorcery
items.desc_en: Avitul Sefra says in the name of Rav Pappa that Pharaoh who lived in Moses' time was one cubit tall, his beard was one cubit, and his penis was one cubit and a handbreadth, to fulfill the verse that low men are raised up. He also says that Pharaoh was a sorcerer, as the verse says he went out to the water.

sub.desc_en: Avitul Sefra reports in the name of Rav Pappa that Pharaoh of Moses' time was one cubit tall, with a one-cubit beard and a one-cubit-plus-handbreadth penis, fulfilling the verse that low men are raised up.
Avitul Sefra further reports in the name of Rav Pappa that Pharaoh was a sorcerer, as the verse says he went out to the water.

items.text: Laundering during Chol HaMoed: One who has only one shirt
items.text_en: Laundering during Chol HaMoed: One who has only one shirt
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists those who may launder during the festival, including one coming from a sea voyage. Rav Asi says in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that one who has only one shirt may launder it during Chol HaMoed. Rabbi Yirmeya objects from the Mishnah that only those listed may launder, implying one with one shirt may not. Rabbi Yaakov explains that the Mishnah refers to one who has two shirts but they are dirty. Rav Yitzchak bar Yaakov bar Giyorei sends in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that linen garments may be laundered during Chol HaMoed. Rava objects with a baraita about hand towels.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists those who may launder during Chol HaMoed, including one coming from a sea voyage.

sub.text: Rav Asi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rav Asi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rav Asi reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that one who has only one shirt may launder it during Chol HaMoed.
Rabbi Yirmeya objects from the Mishnah that only those listed may launder, implying one with one shirt may not.
Rabbi Yaakov explains to Rabbi Yirmeya that the Mishnah refers to one who has two shirts but they are dirty.

sub.text: Rav Yitzchak bar Yaakov bar Giyorei in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Yaakov bar Giyorei in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Yaakov bar Giyorei sends in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that linen garments may be laundered during Chol HaMoed.
Rava objects with a baraita about hand towels, challenging the leniency for linen garments.

items.text: Opening discussion on barbers and flax garments
items.text_en: Opening discussion on barbers and flax garments
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's allowance for barbers, and Abaye challenges Bar Hidya's report that flax garments were laundered in Tiberias during the festival, suggesting it may not have been with rabbinic approval.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's allowance for barbers but not for flax garments.
