Abaye explains that the Mishnah permits even other types, and Bar Hidya reports seeing flax garments laundered in Tiberias during the festival.
Abaye challenges Bar Hidya's report, suggesting the laundering may not have been with rabbinic approval.

items.text: Mishnah: Documents permitted to be written during the festival
items.text_en: Mishnah: Documents permitted to be written during the festival
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists documents that may be written during Chol HaMoed, including betrothal documents, bills of divorce, receipts, wills, gifts, prosbuls, valuation documents, sustenance documents, halitzah and refusal documents, court rulings, and letters of permission.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the types of documents that may be written during Chol HaMoed, including betrothal documents, bills of divorce, receipts, wills, gifts, prosbuls, valuation documents, sustenance documents, halitzah and refusal documents, court rulings, and letters of permission.

items.text: Gemara: Betrothal documents and the permissibility of betrothal
items.text_en: Gemara: Betrothal documents and the permissibility of betrothal
items.desc_en: Shmuel permits betrothal during Chol HaMoed lest another precede him. The Gemara attempts to support this from the Mishnah's allowance of writing betrothal documents, but concludes they refer to engagement terms (שטרי פסיקתא) as per Rav Giddel's teaching about verbal commitments.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel permits betrothal during Chol HaMoed lest another precede him.
The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah's allowance of writing betrothal documents supports Shmuel's ruling.
The Gemara rejects the support, explaining that the Mishnah refers to engagement terms (שטרי פסיקתא), not actual betrothal documents.
Rav Giddel cites Rav's teaching that verbal commitments regarding dowry are binding, clarifying that the Mishnah's documents record such promises, not betrothals.

items.text: Further support for betrothal permissibility
items.text_en: Further support for betrothal permissibility
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita stating that one may not marry during the festival but may betroth, and the school of Shmuel explicitly permits betrothal but not marriage or betrothal feasts. This confirms Shmuel's ruling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to support Shmuel's ruling by citing a baraita that prohibits marriage during the festival but implies betrothal is permitted.
The Gemara rejects the proof, explaining that the baraita uses a 'not only' formulation: not only betrothal (which involves no מצוה) is forbidden, but even marriage (which is a מצוה) is forbidden.

sub.text: Supporting baraita from the school of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita from the school of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita from the school of Shmuel that explicitly permits betrothal but prohibits marriage and betrothal feasts, confirming Shmuel's ruling.

items.text: Contradiction and resolution regarding Shmuel's concern
items.text_en: Contradiction and resolution regarding Shmuel's concern
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: Shmuel said a heavenly voice announces each person's match, so why fear another? The resolution is that the concern is about another's prayers. A story about Rava illustrates the danger of praying for a specific match.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Shmuel's concern about another man betrothing a woman first, citing Shmuel's own statement that a heavenly voice announces each person's match daily.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: the concern is that another man's prayers might cause him to be matched with the woman first.

A story about Rava illustrates the danger of praying for a specific match, as Rava rebukes a man who prayed for a particular woman, warning that if she is not destined for him, he will cause her to die or be lost.

items.text: Teaching on divine matchmaking and suspicion
items.text_en: Teaching on divine matchmaking and suspicion
items.desc_en: Rav in the name of Rabbi Reuven ben Istrobili teaches from Torah, Prophets, and Writings that a wife is from God. A second teaching states that a person is not suspected of something unless they have done it, or at least part of it, or at least thought about it, or at least rejoiced when others did it.

sub.text: Rav citing Rabbi Reuven ben Istrobili
sub.text_en: Rav citing Rabbi Reuven ben Istrobili
sub.desc_en: Rav teaches in the name of Rabbi Reuven ben Istrobili that a wife is from God, citing verses from Torah, Prophets, and Writings.

sub.text: Rav citing Rabbi Reuven ben Istrobili (second teaching)
sub.text_en: Rav citing Rabbi Reuven ben Istrobili (second teaching)
sub.desc_en: Rav further teaches in the name of Rabbi Reuven ben Istrobili that a person is not suspected of something unless they have done it, or part of it, or thought about it, or rejoiced when others did it.

items.text: Challenges and refinements to the suspicion principle
items.text_en: Challenges and refinements to the suspicion principle
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov challenges the principle from the spies who spoke against God without having done so; the Gemara answers they acted to anger. Another challenge from those who suspected Moses of adultery is answered as due to hatred. Rabbi Yosei and Rav Pappa affirm the principle. The Gemara distinguishes between a persistent rumor (קלא דפסיק) and a non-persistent one, with further qualifications about intervals, fear, recurrence, and enemies.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov challenges the principle that a person is only suspected of something they have done, citing the spies who spoke falsely against God without having done so.
The Gemara answers that the spies acted to anger God, not out of genuine suspicion, so the principle remains intact.

sub.text: Gemara's objection from the incident of Moses
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection from the incident of Moses
sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises another challenge from those who suspected Moses of adultery, citing Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak's interpretation.
The Gemara answers that those suspicions were driven by hatred, not by actual wrongdoing, so the principle is not refuted.
Rabbi Yosei affirms the principle by expressing his desire to be among those suspected without cause.
Rav Pappa testifies that he himself was suspected of something but was innocent, supporting the principle.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a persistent rumor (קלא דפסיק) and a non-persistent one.
The Gemara asks how long a non-persistent rumor must last to be considered significant.
Abaye reports that his mother said the rumor lasts a day and a half.
The Gemara qualifies that the rule applies only if the rumor did not pause intermittently; if it paused, it is disregarded.
The Gemara further qualifies that if the pause was due to fear, the rumor is still considered persistent.
The Gemara adds that the rule applies only if the rumor does not recur, and only if the suspected person has no enemies; otherwise, enemies may have spread the rumor.

items.text: Mishnah: Prohibited and permitted writings during the festival
items.text_en: Mishnah: Prohibited and permitted writings during the festival
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that promissory notes may not be written during the festival unless the lender does not trust the borrower or the borrower has nothing to eat. Additionally, Torah scrolls, tefillin, and mezuzot may not be written or corrected, though Rabbi Yehuda permits one to write tefillin and mezuzot for oneself.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that promissory notes may not be written during the festival, unless the lender does not trust the borrower or the borrower has nothing to eat.
The Mishnah adds that Torah scrolls, tefillin, and mezuzot may not be written or corrected during the festival, not even a single letter in the Torah of Ezra.
Rabbi Yehuda permits a person to write tefillin and mezuzot for himself during the festival.

items.text: Opening Mishnah excerpt
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah excerpt
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may spin tekhelet on his thigh for his tzitzit during Chol HaMoed.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may spin tekhelet on his thigh for his tzitzit during Chol HaMoed.

items.text: Baraita on writing tefillin and spinning tekhelet
items.text_en: Baraita on writing tefillin and spinning tekhelet
items.desc_en: A baraita presents a dispute: Rabbi Meir permits writing for oneself and spinning for others only as a favor; Rabbi Yehuda allows deception by selling and rewriting; Rabbi Yosei permits writing and selling for one's livelihood. Rav rules in accordance with Rabbi Yosei.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites three Tannaic positions: Rabbi Meir permits writing tefillin and mezuzot for oneself and spinning tekhelet for others only as a favor; Rabbi Yehuda allows a ruse of selling his own and then writing anew; Rabbi Yosei permits writing and selling normally for his livelihood.
Rabbi Yehuda permits deception: one may sell his existing tefillin and then write new ones for himself.
Rabbi Yosei permits writing and selling in the usual manner for one's livelihood.

items.text: Baraita on spinning with a stone or spindle
items.text_en: Baraita on spinning with a stone or spindle
items.desc_en: Another baraita discusses the method of spinning: Rabbi Eliezer forbids using a stone, while the Sages permit it; Rabbi Yehuda in his name permits a stone but not a spindle, and the Sages permit both. Rav Yehuda and Rabbi Yochanan rule in accordance with the Sages, and the halakha is established accordingly.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited presenting three positions on spinning with a stone or spindle during חול המועד (the intermediate festival days): Rabbi Eliezer forbids a stone, the Sages permit it; Rabbi Yehuda in his name permits a stone but not a spindle, and the Sages permit both.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda and Rabbi Yochanan's ruling
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda and Rabbi Yochanan's ruling
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel, and Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan, rule that the הלכה (binding law) permits both a stone and a spindle, and the halakha is established that one may write and sell as needed for his livelihood.

items.text: Mishnah on mourning periods before a festival
items.text_en: Mishnah on mourning periods before a festival
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states: If one buries his dead three days before a festival, the seven-day mourning period is canceled; eight days before, the thirty-day period is canceled. Shabbat counts but does not interrupt; festivals interrupt but do not count. Rabbi Eliezer says that since the Temple's destruction, Shavuot is like Shabbat; Rabban Gamliel says Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur are like festivals; the Sages rule that Shavuot is like festivals, while Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur are like Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule: one who buries his dead three days before a festival cancels the seven-day mourning period; eight days before cancels the thirty-day period.
The Mishnah explains the principle: Shabbat counts toward mourning but does not interrupt; festivals interrupt but do not count.
Rabbi Eliezer states that since the Temple's destruction, Shavuot (עֲצֶרֶת) is treated like Shabbat.
Rabban Gamliel rules that Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur are like festivals (רְגָלִים).
The Sages reject both positions and rule: Shavuot is like festivals, while Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur are like Shabbat.

items.text: Gemara on decrees and days
items.text_en: Gemara on decrees and days
items.desc_en: Rav and Rabbi Huna distinguish between 'decrees' (gezeirot) which are canceled, and 'days' (yamim) which are not; Rav Sheshet argues that even days are canceled. The Gemara explains that days are not canceled because if one did not shave before the festival, he is forbidden to shave after it.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that decrees (גזירות) are canceled but days (ימים) are not canceled.
Rabbi Huna agrees with Rav's distinction between decrees and days.
Rav Sheshet objects and argues that even days are canceled.
The Gemara explains why days are not canceled: if one did not shave before the festival, he is forbidden to shave after it.

items.text: Opening baraita and Abba Shaul's leniency
items.text_en: Opening baraita and Abba Shaul's leniency
items.desc_en: A baraita states that one who buries his dead three days before a festival has the seven-day decree canceled, and eight days before cancels the thirty-day decree, allowing haircutting before the festival; if not done, it is forbidden afterward. Abba Shaul permits haircutting after the festival, arguing that just as the three-day observance cancels the seven-day decree, so too the seven-day observance cancels the thirty-day decree.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states the rule that burying three days before a festival cancels the seven-day decree, and eight days before cancels the thirty-day decree, allowing haircutting before the festival; if not done, it is forbidden afterward.

Abba Shaul permits haircutting after the festival, arguing by analogy that just as the three-day observance cancels the seven-day decree, so too the seven-day observance cancels the thirty-day decree.

items.text: Gemara's question and resolution on Abba Shaul's view
items.text_en: Gemara's question and resolution on Abba Shaul's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Abba Shaul's mention of 'seven' when the baraita says 'eight', and explains that Abba Shaul holds that a partial day counts as a full day, and the seventh day counts for both the seven and thirty. Rav Chisda citing Ravina bar Sheila rules the halakha follows Abba Shaul.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Abba Shaul's mention of 'seven' when the baraita explicitly says 'eight'.
The Gemara explains that Abba Shaul holds that a partial day counts as a full day (מקצת היום ככולו), and the seventh day counts for both the seven and thirty.

sub.text: Rav Chisda citing Ravina bar Sheila
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda citing Ravina bar Sheila
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda citing Ravina bar Sheila rules that the halakha follows Abba Shaul.

items.text: Sages' agreement with Abba Shaul in a specific case
items.text_en: Sages' agreement with Abba Shaul in a specific case
items.desc_en: The Sages agree with Abba Shaul that when the eighth day of mourning falls on Shabbat eve before the festival, one may shave on Friday (Shabbat eve).

sub.desc_en: The Sages agree with Abba Shaul that when the eighth day of mourning falls on Shabbat eve before the festival, one may shave on Friday (Shabbat eve).

items.text: Rav Amram's ruling aligned with Abba Shaul
items.text_en: Rav Amram's ruling aligned with Abba Shaul
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whose opinion Rav Amram's ruling (that a mourner may bathe once the comforters have left) follows, and concludes it follows Abba Shaul.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whose opinion Rav Amram's ruling (that a mourner may bathe once the comforters have left) follows.
The Gemara answers that Rav Amram's ruling follows Abba Shaul.

items.text: Dispute between Abaye, Rava, and Nehardeans on halakha
items.text_en: Dispute between Abaye, Rava, and Nehardeans on halakha
items.desc_en: Abaye rules halakha like Abba Shaul regarding day seven, and the Sages agree regarding day thirty. Rava rules halakha like Abba Shaul only for day thirty, not day seven. The Nehardeans rule halakha like Abba Shaul in both cases, citing Shmuel's principle that halakha follows the lenient in mourning.

sub.desc_en: Abaye rules that the halakha follows Abba Shaul regarding day seven, and the Sages agree regarding day thirty because of the principle that part of the day is like the whole.
Rava rules that the halakha follows Abba Shaul only for day thirty, not for day seven.
The Nehardeans rule that the halakha follows Abba Shaul in both cases, citing Shmuel's principle that halakha follows the lenient in mourning.

items.text: Derivation of thirty days from the Torah
items.text_en: Derivation of thirty days from the Torah
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives the thirty-day mourning period from a gezerah shavah between 'pera' (untrimmed hair) here and in the nazirite context, where naziriteship is thirty days, as derived from the gematria of 'kadosh yihyeh' (thirty).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks the source for the thirty-day mourning period and answers with a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) between 'פֶּרַע' (untrimmed hair) here and in the nazirite context, where the period is thirty days.
The Gemara asks the source for the thirty-day nazirite period, and Rav Mattana answers that the gematria of 'יִהְיֶה' (will be) in the verse 'קָדוֹשׁ יִהְיֶה' (he shall be holy) equals thirty.

items.text: Rav Huna's ruling on third day before festival
items.text_en: Rav Huna's ruling on third day before festival
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua states that all agree when the third day of mourning falls on the eve of the festival, the mourner is forbidden to bathe until evening. Rav Nechemya bar Yehoshua reports that Rav Papi and Rav Papa (and Rav Huna) concur with this ruling.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua rules that when the third day of mourning falls on the eve of the festival, all agree the mourner is forbidden to bathe until evening.
Rav Nechemya bar Yehoshua reports that Rav Papi and Rav Papa (and in one version also Rav Huna bar Yehoshua) concur with the ruling that the mourner is forbidden to bathe until evening.

items.text: Abaye's inquiry to Rava: does the festival count toward thirty?
items.text_en: Abaye's inquiry to Rava: does the festival count toward thirty?
items.desc_en: Abaye asks Rava whether one who buries his dead during the festival counts the festival toward the thirty-day count. He clarifies that the question is only about the thirty-day count, since the seven-day count is not observed during the festival. Rava answers that it does not count. The Gemara brings a supporting baraita about one who buries two days before the festival.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks Rava whether one who buries his dead during the festival counts the festival toward the thirty-day count, clarifying that the question is only about the thirty-day count since the seven-day count is not observed during the festival.
Rava answers that the festival does not count toward the thirty-day count.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita about one who buries two days before the festival, implying that the festival counts toward the thirty-day count.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Regel interrupts avelut but not public mourning
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Regel interrupts avelut but not public mourning
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a festival interrupts mourning that is due to avelut, but does not interrupt public mourning. It then gives a case: if one buried his dead three days before the end of the festival, he counts seven days after the festival; the first four days the public is involved, the last three they are not, because they were already involved during the festival, and the festival counts for him.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general rule: a festival (רגל) interrupts private mourning (אבל) but does not interrupt public mourning (עסקי רבים).

The Mishnah gives a case: if one buried his dead three days before the end of the festival, he counts seven days after the festival; the public is involved for the first four days but not the last three, because they were already involved during the festival, and the festival counts for him.

items.text: Gemara's question and objection
items.text_en: Gemara's question and objection
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's statement refers to the latter part (seifa) or the first part (reisha). It then brings an objection from a baraita that states that if one buried his dead at the beginning of the festival, the festival counts for him for the thirty-day period, and the public is not involved because they were already involved during the festival. This is a refutation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's statement refers to the latter part (seifa) or the first part (reisha).

The Gemara brings an objection from a baraita that states that if one buried his dead at the beginning of the festival, the festival counts for him for the thirty-day period, and the public is not involved because they were already involved during the festival, concluding that this is a refutation.

items.text: Ravin's report: Even if buried during the festival
items.text_en: Ravin's report: Even if buried during the festival
items.desc_en: When Ravin came, he said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that even if one buried his dead during the festival, the festival counts. Rabbi Elazar also taught this to his son Rabbi Pedat.

sub.text: Ravin's report in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Ravin's report in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Ravin reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that even if one buried his dead during the festival, the festival counts toward the mourning period.

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar's teaching to his son Rabbi Pedat
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's teaching to his son Rabbi Pedat
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar also taught his son Rabbi Pedat the same ruling: even if one buried his dead during the festival, the festival counts.

items.text: Debate on kefiyat hamita before the festival
items.text_en: Debate on kefiyat hamita before the festival
items.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma states that if one overturned his bed three days before the festival, he does not need to overturn it after the festival. Rabbi Eliezer says even one day or even one hour suffices. Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon identifies this with Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel. Rav Huna in the name of Rabbi Yochanan rules like the lenient opinion, while Rava rules like the Tanna who says three days. Ravina is asked and rules like the lenient opinion.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents a dispute: the Tanna Kamma requires three days of bed overturning before the festival to exempt after it, while Rabbi Eliezer says even one day or one hour suffices.
Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon identifies the Tanna Kamma's position with Beit Shammai (three days) and Rabbi Eliezer's with Beit Hillel (even one day).
Rav Huna reports Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that even one day or one hour suffices (lenient), while Rava rules like the Tanna Kamma who requires three days (stringent).
Rav Chaviva asks Ravina for the halachic ruling, and Ravina rules leniently: even one day or even one hour suffices.

items.text: Derivation of seven days of mourning from the festival
items.text_en: Derivation of seven days of mourning from the festival
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba, Rabbi Ami, and Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha derive that mourning is seven days from the verse 'I will turn your festivals into mourning' — just as a festival is seven days, so mourning is seven days. The Gemara questions this, suggesting it could be derived from Shavuot which is one day, but that verse is needed for Reish Lakish's derivation about shema rechoka.

sub.desc_en: The narrative sets the scene: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba, Rabbi Ami, and Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha were sitting together, and a halachic ruling emerged from their discussion.

The rabbis derive that mourning lasts seven days from the verse 'וְהָפַכְתִּי חַגֵּיכֶם לְאֵבֶל' (I will turn your festivals into mourning), applying a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy): just as a festival (חג) is seven days, so too mourning is seven days.
The Gemara objects: why not derive mourning from Shavuot (עצרת), which is only one day, implying mourning is one day?

The Gemara rejects the objection: that verse is needed for Reish Lakish's derivation that a distant report of death (שמועה רחוקה) applies only one day, since Shavuot is called a 'חג' (festival) and is only one day.

items.text: Shema rechoka and shema kerova: dispute and ruling
items.text_en: Shema rechoka and shema kerova: dispute and ruling
items.desc_en: A baraita defines shema kerova as within thirty days (observed seven and thirty), shema rechoka as after thirty days (observed only one day) according to Rabbi Akiva, while the Sages say both are observed seven and thirty. Rabbi Yochanan rules that generally the law follows the majority, but here it follows Rabbi Akiva because Shmuel said the law follows the lenient opinion in mourning.

sub.desc_en: The baraita defines shema kerova (within thirty days) as observed seven and thirty, and shema rechoka (after thirty days) as observed only one day, according to Rabbi Akiva.
The Sages disagree with Rabbi Akiva, ruling that both shema kerova and shema rechoka are observed seven and thirty days.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that although the general principle is to follow the majority, here the law follows Rabbi Akiva's lenient position because Shmuel stated that the law follows the lenient opinion in mourning.

items.text: Practical cases and objection regarding shema rechoka for parents
items.text_en: Practical cases and objection regarding shema rechoka for parents
items.desc_en: Rav Chanina and Rav Natan bar Ami receive news of a parent's death from a distant place and are told shema rechoka is only one day. An objection is raised that this rule applies only to the five מתי מצוה, but for parents it is seven and thirty. The Gemara answers that this is an individual opinion, and brings a precedent of Rabbi Tzadok and Rabbi Achiya who observed seven and thirty for a distant report. The Gemara then questions this with a story about Rav.

sub.text: Narrative: Rav Chanina and Rav Natan bar Ami
sub.text_en: Narrative: Rav Chanina and Rav Natan bar Ami
sub.desc_en: Two cases are presented: Rav Chanina and Rav Natan bar Ami each receive distant news of a parent's death and are told that a distant report (שמועה רחוקה) is observed only one day.

An objection is raised: the rule that a distant report is observed only one day applies only to the five מתי מצוה (those who die without anyone to tend to them), but for parents it is seven and thirty days.
Rava answers that the objection is an individual opinion (יחידאה) and not accepted, citing precedents: Rabbi Tzadok and Rabbi Achiya observed seven and thirty days for a distant report.
The Gemara questions the precedent with a story about Rav, who, upon ascending to the land of Israel, asked about his father's status, implying a different practice.

items.text: Inference from the story of Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Achiya
items.text_en: Inference from the story of Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Achiya
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers three halakhot from the story of Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Achiya: that a mourner is forbidden to wear sandals, that a distant report of a death is observed only for one day, and that part of the day is considered as the whole day.

sub.text: Story of Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Achiya
sub.text_en: Story of Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Achiya
sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts the story where Rabbi Chiyya asks about his mother's status, then instructs his attendant to remove his sandals and follow him to the bathhouse.
The Gemara infers three halakhot from the story: a mourner is forbidden to wear sandals, a distant report of a death is observed only for one day, and part of the day is considered as the whole day.

items.text: Clarification of the story's participants
items.text_en: Clarification of the story's participants
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Achiya are two distinct individuals, not the same person.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Achiya are two distinct individuals, not the same person.

items.text: Distant report heard on a festival or Shabbat
items.text_en: Distant report heard on a festival or Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Avin and Rabbi Adda of Caesarea teach that if one hears a close report on a festival or Shabbat, and after the festival or Shabbat it becomes a distant report, he observes only one day of mourning.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Avin rules that if one hears a close report on a festival and it becomes distant after the festival, the festival counts toward the mourning period, and he observes only one day of mourning.

sub.text: Rabbi Adda of Caesarea before Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Adda of Caesarea before Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Adda of Caesarea cites a baraita before Rabbi Yochanan that the same rule applies if one hears a close report on Shabbat and it becomes distant after Shabbat.

items.text: Debate about tearing garments for a distant report
items.text_en: Debate about tearing garments for a distant report
items.desc_en: Rabbi Mani and Rabbi Chanina debate whether one must tear garments for a distant report. Rabbi Mani argues no, since there is no seven-day mourning; Rabbi Chanina argues yes. The Gemara brings a baraita about tearing for a deceased relative when one has no garment, and Rabbi Zeira limits it to the five specified relatives, but for parents one always tears.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether one must tear garments for a distant report (שמועה רחוקה).
Rabbi Mani rules that one does not tear for a distant report.
Rabbi Chanina rules that one does tear for a distant report.

sub.text: Rabbi Mani's objection to Rabbi Chanina
sub.text_en: Rabbi Mani's objection to Rabbi Chanina
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Mani objects to Rabbi Chanina: if there is no seven-day mourning, can there be tearing without it?

sub.text: Supporting baraita (Isi, father of Rabbi Zeira)
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita (Isi, father of Rabbi Zeira)
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that one who has no garment to tear during the seven days tears later, but after seven days does not tear.
Rabbi Zeira limits the baraita to the five specified relatives, but for parents one always tears.
The Gemara explains that the baraita about tearing after seven days applies only to honor of one's father and mother.

items.text: Relatives for whom one mourns
items.text_en: Relatives for whom one mourns
items.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma lists the relatives for whom one mourns, based on the priestly impurity list. Rabbi Akiva adds secondary relatives, Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar limits it to grandson and grandfather, and the Sages say one mourns with anyone he mourns for. The Gemara clarifies the difference between the Sages and the Tanna Kamma is about mourning with the relative in the same house.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by listing the primary relatives for whom one mourns, based on the priestly impurity list: wife, father, mother, brother, sister, son, and daughter.
The baraita adds secondary relatives: a brother and virgin sister from the same mother, and a married sister from either parent.
Rabbi Akiva rules that one mourns for the secondary relatives of those primary relatives (e.g., one's son's son or father's father).
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar limits mourning for secondary relatives to only a grandson and a grandfather.
The Sages rule that one mourns with anyone for whom he mourns (i.e., the same list as the Tanna Kamma).
The Gemara asks: the Sages' ruling seems identical to the Tanna Kamma's list — what is the difference between them?
The Gemara answers: the difference is that the Sages require mourning with the relative when living in the same house, as illustrated by the following story.
Rav and Rav Huna each instructed their sons: in the presence of the relative (i.e., in the same house), observe mourning; not in their presence, do not observe mourning.

items.text: Mourning for in-laws
items.text_en: Mourning for in-laws
items.desc_en: Mar Ukva considered sitting shiva for his father-in-law, but Rav Huna told him that the Sages only required mourning for a father-in-law or mother-in-law out of respect for one's spouse. The Gemara brings baraitot detailing the obligations of a spouse whose in-law dies, and resolves a contradiction by distinguishing between a father-in-law/mother-in-law and other relatives.

sub.desc_en: Mar Ukva's father-in-law died, and he considered sitting shiva for seven and thirty days, but Rav Huna rebuked him, stating that the Sages only required mourning for a father-in-law or mother-in-law out of respect for one's spouse.
A baraita is cited detailing that when a spouse's parent dies, the surviving spouse must observe mourning practices together with their partner.
Another baraita is brought that appears to contradict the first, allowing the spouse to perform certain personal services for the mourner.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a father-in-law/mother-in-law, where full mourning is required, and other relatives, where only limited practices apply, and a supporting baraita confirms this distinction.

items.text: Tearing while standing
items.text_en: Tearing while standing
items.desc_en: Ameimar tore his garment for his grandson while sitting, but when his son arrived, he tore again while standing. Rav Ashi asks the source for tearing while standing, and Ameimar cites Job who stood up and tore his garment.

sub.desc_en: Ameimar tore his garment for his grandson while sitting, and when his son arrived he tore again in his presence, then remembered he had torn while sitting and stood up and tore while standing.
Rav Ashi asks Ameimar for the source of the requirement to tear while standing.
Ameimar answers by citing the verse that Job stood up and tore his garment, establishing the practice of tearing while standing.

items.text: Standing requirement for keri'ah
items.text_en: Standing requirement for keri'ah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether tearing must be done standing, citing verses about Iyov and David. It distinguishes between cases where standing is explicit and where it is not, and concludes that the requirement is derived from the verse about the king. The discussion also addresses the mourner's obligation to overturn the bed, with Rabbi Yochanan emphasizing that sitting on a bed without overturning it does not fulfill the obligation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether standing is required for tearing, citing a verse about the yevama (levirate widow) and a baraita that allows sitting, standing, or reclining.
An anonymous answer distinguishes the yevama case, where standing is not explicit, from the mourner's case, where the verse says 'he arose and tore'.
Rami bar Chama cites Iyov's standing and tearing as proof for the standing requirement, but the Gemara objects that Iyov may have done an extra act, just as he shaved his head.
The Gemara resolves by citing the king's standing and tearing, but again objects that the king may have done an extra act, just as he lay on the ground.
A baraita is cited stating that sitting on a bed without overturning it does not fulfill the obligation, and Rabbi Yochanan explains that the mourner failed to overturn the bed.
An anonymous answer explains that sitting on a bed is like sitting on the ground, which does not fulfill the obligation of overturning the bed.

items.text: Prohibitions for a mourner and teaching in public
items.text_en: Prohibitions for a mourner and teaching in public
items.desc_en: The baraita lists prohibitions for a mourner, including work, bathing, and Torah study, but allows teaching if the public needs it. Stories about Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai illustrate how a mourner may teach through an intermediary without directly addressing the public.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists prohibitions for a mourner, including work, bathing, and Torah study, but allows teaching if the public needs it, and recounts that Rabbi Yosei taught all day after his son's death.

sub.text: Story about Rabbah bar bar Chanah
sub.text_en: Story about Rabbah bar bar Chanah
sub.desc_en: When Rabbah bar bar Chanah suffered a loss and hesitated to teach, Rabbi Chanina cited the baraita that a mourner may teach if needed, but Rav added that he may not appoint a translator (תורגמן).

The gemara resolves the issue by citing a baraita: when Rabbi Yehuda bar Ilai was in mourning, he whispered to Rabbi Chananya ben Akavya, who relayed to a translator (תורגמן), who then taught the public.

items.text: Dispute on tefillin during mourning
items.text_en: Dispute on tefillin during mourning
items.desc_en: A baraita presents the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua: Rabbi Eliezer says a mourner is forbidden to don tefillin for the first three days, while Rabbi Yehoshua says only the first two days. Each cites a verse to support his position, and the Gemara reconciles the verses by noting that Moshe's mourning was uniquely intense and that the essence of bitterness is only one day.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents the dispute: Rabbi Eliezer forbids tefillin for the first three days, Rabbi Yehoshua for only the first two, with different rules for removing them if new faces arrive.
Rav Matna and Rav Eina each cite a verse to support Rabbi Eliezer's three-day period (from Moshe's mourning) and Rabbi Yehoshua's two-day period (from 'its end is like a bitter day').

The Gemara reconciles the verses: Moshe's mourning was uniquely intense, so his three days do not set the norm, and 'its end is like a bitter day' indicates that the essence of bitterness is only one day, supporting Rabbi Yehoshua's two-day limit.

items.text: Ruling on tefillin and removing them
items.text_en: Ruling on tefillin and removing them
items.desc_en: Ulla rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Eliezer regarding removing tefillin when new faces arrive, and Rabbi Yehoshua regarding donning them. A dilemma arises about the second day according to Ulla, and a baraita supports that one may remove and don tefillin even a hundred times. Rava disagrees, stating that once donned, one does not remove them, and he holds that the halakha follows the tanna who says three days.

sub.desc_en: Ulla rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Eliezer regarding removing tefillin and Rabbi Yehoshua regarding donning them.
A dilemma is raised: according to Ulla, on the second day does one remove tefillin or not?
A baraita is cited: Ulla says one may remove and don tefillin even a hundred times, and Yehuda ben Teima supports this.
Rava objects, stating that once one has donned tefillin, one does not remove them, and he holds that the halakha follows the tanna who says three days.

items.text: Distinction for a mitzvah
items.text_en: Distinction for a mitzvah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the earlier ruling about a mourner being prohibited from work applies only to a mitzvah, not to other cases.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the earlier contradiction by stating that the case of a mitzvah is different.

items.text: Baraitot on mourning restrictions
items.text_en: Baraitot on mourning restrictions
items.desc_en: Three baraitot are cited: a mourner is prohibited from work for three days, from going to the house of mourning, and from greeting others, with graduated leniencies after three days.

sub.desc_en: The first baraita states that a mourner is prohibited from work for the first three days, even if poor, and thereafter may work discreetly at home.
The second baraita adds that a mourner does not visit the house of mourning for three days, and thereafter sits among the comforted, not the comforters.
The third baraita rules that a mourner is prohibited from greeting for three days, from three to seven may respond but not initiate, and thereafter may greet normally.

items.text: Challenge from Rabbi Akiva's practice
items.text_en: Challenge from Rabbi Akiva's practice
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the prohibition of greeting from a story where Rabbi Akiva greeted the public at his sons' funeral. It resolves that the honor of the many is different.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the prohibition of greeting within three days by citing a baraita about Rabbi Akiva's conduct at his sons' funeral.
The baraita recounts that Rabbi Akiva stood on a large bench and publicly greeted the mourners, saying 'go to your homes in peace.'
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by stating that the honor of the many (כבוד רבים) is different, permitting greeting in such a case.

items.text: Contradiction with greeting a mourner within thirty days
items.text_en: Contradiction with greeting a mourner within thirty days
items.desc_en: A baraita states that one who meets a mourner within thirty days offers condolences but does not greet him, while after thirty days he greets but does not offer condolences. Rav Idi bar Avin explains that the mourner may greet others because they are at peace, but others do not greet him because he is not at peace. The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction with the earlier baraita by distinguishing between the mourner's greeting and others' greeting.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: a baraita states that within thirty days one offers condolences but does not greet a mourner, while the earlier baraita (segments 3-7) says that after three days the mourner returns greetings.
The baraita continues with additional details: if a man remarried after his wife's death, one may not enter his home to console him, but may speak to him in the market with subdued speech.
Rav Idi bar Avin resolves the contradiction: the mourner may greet others because they are at peace, but others do not greet him because he is not at peace.
The Gemara objects: the earlier baraita says the mourner 'returns' greetings, implying that others do greet him, but Rav Idi bar Avin said others do not greet him.

The Gemara resolves the objection: in the earlier baraita, the mourner is known to be a mourner and others greet him, but in the later baraita the mourner is not known and must inform them, so he does not return greetings.

items.text: Contradiction with greeting within twelve months
items.text_en: Contradiction with greeting within twelve months
items.desc_en: Another baraita states that for a mourner within twelve months, one offers condolences but does not greet; after twelve months, one greets but does not offer condolences, except indirectly. Rabbi Meir compares offering condolences after twelve months to a doctor breaking a healed leg. The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between mourning for a parent (twelve months) and other relatives (thirty days), and explains that 'does not offer condolences' means not in the usual manner, but indirectly.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction by citing a baraita that distinguishes between greeting and offering condolences within and after twelve months for a mourner.
Rabbi Meir compares offering condolences after twelve months to a doctor who breaks a healed leg to demonstrate his medicine.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between mourning for a parent (twelve months) and other relatives (thirty days).
The Gemara explains that 'does not offer condolences' in the baraita means not in the usual manner, but indirectly (מן הצד).

items.text: Counting mourning days for one who arrives late
items.text_en: Counting mourning days for one who arrives late
items.desc_en: A baraita rules that if a mourner arrives from a close place within three days, he counts with the others; from a distant place, he counts for himself. After three days, even from a close place he counts for himself. Rabbi Shimon says even on the seventh day from a close place he counts with them. Rabbi Yochanan adds that this applies only if there is a 'great one of the house' present. The Gemara then raises an inquiry about this condition.

sub.desc_en: A baraita rules that a mourner arriving from a close place within three days counts mourning with the community, from a distant place counts alone, and after three days even from a close place counts alone; Rabbi Shimon adds that even on the seventh day from a close place he counts with them.
Rabbi Yochanan qualifies the baraita, stating that the leniency of counting with the community applies only when there is a 'great one of the house' (גדול הבית) present in the home.
The Gemara raises an inquiry about the precise meaning or scope of Rabbi Yochanan's condition regarding the 'great one of the house'.

items.text: Opening question: head of household who went to the cemetery
items.text_en: Opening question: head of household who went to the cemetery
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: If the head of the household went to the cemetery (but did not attend the burial), what is the law? Does he count the mourning period with the others?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: If the head of the household went to the cemetery (but did not attend the burial), does he count the mourning period with the others?

items.text: Resolution: distinction based on arrival within three days
items.text_en: Resolution: distinction based on arrival within three days
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan rules that even if the head of the household went to the cemetery, he counts with them. The Gemara notes a contradiction with a baraita that says he counts for himself, and resolves it by distinguishing between one who came within three days (counts with them) and one who came after three days (counts for himself), citing Rav's instruction to the people of Tzalbon.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan rules that even if the head of the household went to the cemetery, he counts the mourning period with them.
The Gemara objects: how can he count with them, when a baraita explicitly says he counts for himself?

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between one who arrived within three days (counts with them) and one who arrived after three days (counts for himself), citing Rav's instruction to the people of Tzalbon.

items.text: Rava's ruling for the people of Mechoza
items.text_en: Rava's ruling for the people of Mechoza
items.desc_en: Rava instructs the people of Mechoza that since they do not accompany the bier, they should begin counting from the time they turn away from the gate of the alley.

sub.desc_en: Rava instructs the people of Mechoza that since they do not accompany the bier, they should begin counting mourning from the time they turn away from the gate of the alley.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's opinion and its condition
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's opinion and its condition
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon says that even if one comes on the seventh day from a nearby place, he counts with them. Rabbi Chiyya bar Gammada in the name of Rabbi Yosei ben Shaul in the name of Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi) adds the condition that this applies only if he came and found comforters with him.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon states that even if a mourner arrives on the seventh day from a nearby place, he counts the mourning period together with the household.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Gammada in the name of Rabbi Yosei ben Shaul in the name of Rabbi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Gammada in the name of Rabbi Yosei ben Shaul in the name of Rabbi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Gammada transmits a tradition in the name of Rabbi Yosei ben Shaul citing Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi) that adds a condition: Rabbi Shimon's ruling applies only if the mourner came and found comforters with him.

items.text: Rav Anan's unresolved query
items.text_en: Rav Anan's unresolved query
items.desc_en: Rav Anan asks: If the comforters stirred to stand but did not stand, what is the law? The Gemara concludes with 'teiku' (let it stand unresolved).

sub.desc_en: Rav Anan asks: If the comforters stirred to stand but did not actually stand, what is the law regarding the mourner's counting of shiva?
The Gemara concludes with 'תיקו' (let it stand unresolved), indicating the question remains undecided.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's dual halakhic ruling
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's dual halakhic ruling
items.desc_en: A tradition from Rabbi Yochanan states: The halakha follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel in matters of tereifot (animals with fatal defects) and follows Rabbi Shimon in matters of mourning. The Gemara explains the latter (already discussed) and cites the Mishnah for the former: if intestines are perforated but pus seals them, the animal is kosher according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a tradition transmitted via colleagues of Rabbi Abba bar Chiyya, citing Rabbi Yochanan's dual ruling: the halakha follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel in matters of tereifot (animals with fatal defects) and follows Rabbi Shimon in matters of mourning.

The Gemara explains that the ruling regarding Rabbi Shimon on mourning was already discussed, and cites the Mishnah for Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling on tereifot: if intestines are perforated but pus seals them, the animal is kosher.

items.text: Clarification and dispute over the halakha
items.text_en: Clarification and dispute over the halakha
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana explains 'pus' as intestinal fluid that comes out under pressure. A certain Sage seeks to clarify the ruling from Rabbi Abba bar Chiyya bar Abba, who reveals that he actually said 'there is no halakha' regarding Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's view. Regarding Rabbi Shimon's view on mourning, there is a dispute: Rav Chisda and Rabbi Yochanan say halakha, Rav Nachman says no halakha. The Gemara concludes that the halakha does not follow Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel in tereifot, but does follow Rabbi Shimon in mourning, based on Shmuel's principle that the halakha follows the lenient view in mourning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'pus' (לֵיחָה) means, and Rav Kahana answers that it is intestinal fluid that comes out under pressure.
A certain Sage expresses his desire to ascend and hear the halakhic ruling directly from the master's mouth.

sub.text: The Sage's question to Rabbi Abba bar Chiyya bar Abba
sub.text_en: The Sage's question to Rabbi Abba bar Chiyya bar Abba
sub.desc_en: Upon ascending, the Sage finds Rabbi Abba bar Chiyya bar Abba and asks him whether the master said the halakha follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel regarding tereifot.

sub.text: Rabbi Abba bar Chiyya bar Abba's correction
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abba bar Chiyya bar Abba's correction
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Chiyya bar Abba clarifies that he actually said 'there is no halakha' regarding Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's view on tereifot.
The Sage asks what the ruling is regarding Rabbi Shimon's view on mourning.

sub.text: Rabbi Abba bar Chiyya bar Abba's report of the dispute
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abba bar Chiyya bar Abba's report of the dispute
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Chiyya bar Abba reports a dispute: Rav Chisda and Rabbi Yochanan say the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon, while Rav Nachman says there is no halakha.

The Gemara concludes that the halakha does not follow Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel in tereifot, but does follow Rabbi Shimon in mourning, based on Shmuel's principle that the halakha follows the lenient view in mourning.

items.text: Mishnah: on delaying the bier and reducing business
items.text_en: Mishnah: on delaying the bier and reducing business
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states: For all deceased, one who delays his bier (to eulogize) is praiseworthy; for his father and mother, it is disgraceful unless it is erev Shabbat or erev Yom Tov, when it is praiseworthy because he acts only for his parents' honor. For all deceased, if one wishes, he may reduce his business involvement, and if he wishes, he need not.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that delaying the bier for eulogies is praiseworthy for all deceased except one's parents, where it is disgraceful unless it is ערב שבת (Friday) or ערב יום טוב (eve of a festival), when it is praiseworthy because it is solely for the parents' honor.
The Mishnah adds that for all deceased, one may choose to reduce or not reduce his business involvement.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Distinction between parent and other deceased
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Distinction between parent and other deceased
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that for all other deceased, one may choose whether to remove the shoe or not, but for one's father and mother, one must remove it. This establishes the basic halakhic distinction.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that for all other deceased one may choose whether to remove the shoe or not, but for one's father and mother one must remove it.

items.text: Story of the great sage and Abaye's analysis
items.text_en: Story of the great sage and Abaye's analysis
items.desc_en: A story is told about a great sage who wanted to remove his shoe for his father but refrained. Abaye identifies the sages involved, and a difficulty is raised: if the great sage was Rabbi Yaakov bar Acha, why did he refrain when Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel was the Nasi and everyone is obligated to remove?

sub.desc_en: A story is told about a great sage whose father died; he and another great sage wanted to remove their shoes but refrained.
Abaye identifies the two great sages: one is Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi), the other is Rabbi Yaakov bar Acha, with an alternative version reversing the roles.
The Gemara explains that according to the version where the accompanying sage is Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi), it is understandable why he refrained from removing his shoe.

The Gemara raises a difficulty: according to the version where the great sage was Rabbi Yaakov bar Acha, why did he refrain from removing his shoe, since Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel was the Nasi and everyone is obligated to remove their shoe for him?

items.text: Mishnah: Haircut and entering houses of joy
items.text_en: Mishnah: Haircut and entering houses of joy
items.desc_en: The Mishnah continues: for all other deceased, one may cut hair after thirty days; for a parent, only when friends rebuke. For entering a house of joy, it is after thirty days for others, but after twelve months for a parent.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general rule: for all other deceased, one may cut hair after thirty days and enter a house of joy after thirty days; for a parent, one may cut hair only when friends rebuke and enter a house of joy only after twelve months.

items.text: Gemara: Distinction between joy of friendship and other joy
items.text_en: Gemara: Distinction between joy of friendship and other joy
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah says the leniency for entering a house of joy applies only to a joy of friendship. A contradiction is raised from a baraita, and Amemar resolves it by distinguishing between a partnership (אריסותא) and a payment (פורענותא).

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah states that the leniency of entering a house of joy after thirty days applies only to a joy of friendship (שמחת מרעות).
The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita that states both joy and friendship require a thirty-day waiting period.
The Gemara declares the contradiction difficult (קשיא).
Amemar presents an alternative version of Rabbah bar bar Chanah's statement: for a joy of friendship, one may enter immediately (לאלתר).
The Gemara again objects: the baraita still says both joy and friendship require thirty days.
Amemar resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a partnership (אריסותא) and a payment (פורענותא).

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara: Tearing garments
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara: Tearing garments
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that for all other deceased one tears a handbreadth, but for a parent until the heart is exposed. Rabbi Avahu cites a verse. Further, for a parent one tears all garments, and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar discusses a woman's procedure. Rabbi Yehuda requires separation of the tear, with a proof from David.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general rule: for all other deceased one tears a handbreadth, but for a parent one tears until the heart is exposed.
Rabbi Avahu cites a verse from David's tearing to prove that a handbreadth is the minimum for a valid tear.
The Mishnah rules that for other deceased one tears only the outermost garment, but for a parent one tears all garments, and the outer garment's hem does not impede.
The Mishnah states the rule applies equally to men and women, and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar adds that a woman tears the lower garment first, turns it behind her, then tears the upper one.
The Mishnah rules that for other deceased one may optionally separate the tear at the hem, but for a parent one must separate it.
Rabbi Yehuda states that any tear not separated at the hem is merely a worthless tear.
Rabbi Avahu explains Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning from the verse about David, which implies the tear must appear as two separate pieces.

items.text: Mishnah: Sewing and mending the tear
items.text_en: Mishnah: Sewing and mending the tear
items.desc_en: The Mishnah concludes: for all other deceased, one may baste after seven days and mend after thirty; for a parent, baste after thirty and never mend. A woman may baste immediately for her dignity.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that for all other deceased one may baste after seven days and mend after thirty, for a parent baste after thirty and never mend, and a woman may baste immediately for her dignity.

items.text: Gemara: Tearing by hand and outside, and the Nasi
items.text_en: Gemara: Tearing by hand and outside, and the Nasi
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that for a parent one tears by hand and from outside. Rav Chisda adds that the same applies to the Nasi. A baraita is cited that only for a parent is there no mending, excluding the Nasi. A story is told of Rav Chisda instructing Rav Chanan bar Rava to demonstrate tearing for the Nasi.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that for all deceased one may tear either by hand or with a tool, but for a parent one must tear by hand.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan via Rabbi Chiya bar Abba
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan via Rabbi Chiya bar Abba
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan adds that for all deceased one tears from inside the garment, but for a parent one tears from outside.
Rav Chisda extends the rule of tearing from outside to the Nasi (patriarch).
The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that only for mending (איחוי) are other relatives equated to parents, implying no other stringency applies.
The Gemara asks whether the baraita means that even the Nasi is not equated to parents for tearing from outside.
The Gemara answers that the baraita excludes the Nasi, so the Nasi is indeed equated to parents for tearing from outside.

sub.text: Narrative: Rav Chisda and Rav Chanan bar Rava
sub.text_en: Narrative: Rav Chisda and Rav Chanan bar Rava
sub.desc_en: A story is told: when a Nasi died, Rav Chisda instructed Rav Chanan bar Rava to bend over and demonstrate the tearing from outside, showing the practice.

items.text: Baraita: Mourning for a Sage, Av Beit Din, and Nasi
items.text_en: Baraita: Mourning for a Sage, Av Beit Din, and Nasi
items.desc_en: A baraita details the mourning practices for a Sage (tearing on the right), Av Beit Din (left), and Nasi (both sides). It also describes the cessation of study houses and changing seats in the synagogue upon their deaths.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating the mourning practice of tearing (חליצה) for a Sage on the right, for an Av Beit Din on the left, and for a Nasi on both sides.
A second baraita (תנו רבנן) details the cessation of study houses and the changing of seats in the synagogue upon the death of a Sage, Av Beit Din, and Nasi.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Mourners' conduct and storytelling
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Mourners' conduct and storytelling
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that mourners may go out after seven days, but Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha says they should sit and mourn, not stroll. It also notes that one does not recite halachic traditions or aggadah in the house of mourning, except for Rabbi Chananya ben Gamliel who did so.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that mourners may go out after seven days, but Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korcha restricts them to sitting and mourning rather than strolling in the market.
The Mishnah adds that one does not recite halachic traditions or aggadah in the house of mourning, except for Rabbi Chananya ben Gamliel who did so.

items.text: Baraita: Stages of mourning over weeks
items.text_en: Baraita: Stages of mourning over weeks
items.desc_en: A baraita outlines the progression of mourning restrictions: first week, the mourner does not leave his house; second week, he goes out but does not sit in his usual place; third week, he sits in his place but does not speak; fourth week, he is like everyone else. Rabbi Yehuda offers a different schedule, starting with the second week as the first restriction.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents the Tanna Kamma's view: a mourner's restrictions progress weekly — first week no leaving home, second week no sitting in usual place, third week no speaking, fourth week fully normal.

Rabbi Yehuda offers an alternative schedule: the first week's restriction is unnecessary because visitors come to comfort, so the first restriction begins in the second week, and the full progression shifts by one week.

items.text: Baraita: Remarriage after spouse's death
items.text_en: Baraita: Remarriage after spouse's death
items.desc_en: A baraita states that a man whose wife died may not remarry until after three festivals, with Rabbi Yehuda allowing after two. If he has no children, he may remarry immediately due to the mitzvah of procreation; if he has young children, he may remarry immediately for their sustenance. A story about Yosef HaKohen illustrates that he married his wife's sister only after thirty days.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with the general rule that a man whose wife died may not remarry until three festivals have passed.
Rabbi Yehuda offers a lenient position: the man is forbidden only after the first two festivals, and permitted after the third.
The baraita adds an exception: if the man has no children, he may remarry immediately due to the מצוה (commandment) of procreation (פריה ורביה).
Another exception: if the man has young children, he may remarry immediately for their sustenance (פרנסתן).
A story about Yosef HaKohen illustrates that even when remarrying for the sake of the children, he did not consummate the marriage until a later time.
Rav Pappa clarifies that the 'long time' mentioned in the story was after thirty days.

items.text: Baraita: Ironing restrictions during mourning
items.text_en: Baraita: Ironing restrictions during mourning
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses the prohibition on ironed garments for thirty days: all new or pressed garments are forbidden. Rabbi limits it to new garments only, and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon limits it to new white garments. Abaye and Rava each follow one of these opinions in practice.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that for thirty days, all garments — new or old that come from a press — are forbidden for ironing during mourning.
Rabbi limits the prohibition to new garments only, excluding old pressed ones.

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's opinion
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's opinion
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon further restricts the prohibition to only new white garments.
Abaye goes out in a worn-out cloak, following Rabbi's lenient opinion that only new garments are forbidden.
Rava goes out in a new red Roman garment, following Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's opinion that only new white garments are forbidden.

items.text: Fragment: Shabbat counting in mourning
items.text_en: Fragment: Shabbat counting in mourning
items.desc_en: A brief statement that Shabbat counts toward the mourning period but does not interrupt it, followed by a reference to the people of Yehuda and Galil.

sub.desc_en: The gemara states that Shabbat counts toward the mourning period but does not interrupt it, and then references the differing practices of the people of Yehuda and Galil.

items.text: Gemara's opening dispute on mourning on Shabbat
items.text_en: Gemara's opening dispute on mourning on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute: some say there is mourning on Shabbat (based on the mishna's term 'עולה'), others say there is no mourning on Shabbat (based on the term 'אינה מפסקת'). The Gemara questions the logic of the latter view and resolves both terms as stylistic choices.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the two opposing positions: some say there is mourning on Shabbat, others say there is no mourning on Shabbat.
The Gemara explains that the first position is based on the mishna's term 'עולה' (it rises), and the second on the term 'אינה מפסקת' (it does not interrupt).
The Gemara objects: if there is mourning on Shabbat, why does the mishna say 'אינה מפסקת' (it does not interrupt)? It should say it does interrupt.
The Gemara resolves that the term 'עולה' is used because the mishna's latter clause uses 'אינן עולים' (they do not rise), so the first clause uses 'עולה' for stylistic consistency.
The Gemara resolves the second position's term 'אינה מפסקת' as stylistic, because the latter clause uses 'מפסיקין' (they interrupt), so the first clause uses 'אינה מפסקת' for consistency.

items.text: Baraita on the onen's restrictions and Shabbat leniencies
items.text_en: Baraita on the onen's restrictions and Shabbat leniencies
items.desc_en: A baraita details the restrictions of an onen (whose deceased relative lies before him) and the leniencies on Shabbat: he may eat meat, drink wine, recite blessings, and is obligated in all commandments. Rabban Gamliel adds that being obligated in some obligates him in all.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with the rule that an onen (whose deceased relative lies before him) must eat in a different room, a friend's house, or behind a partition, but cannot eat normally.
The baraita lists the onen's weekday prohibitions: no reclining, no meat, no wine, no blessings, and exemption from all positive commandments.
The baraita states that on Shabbat the onen may recline, eat meat, drink wine, recite blessings, and is obligated in all commandments.
Rabban Gamliel adds that because the onen is obligated in some commandments on Shabbat, he is obligated in all of them.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's comment on the dispute
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's comment on the dispute
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that the only difference between the Tanna Kamma and Rabban Gamliel in the baraita is regarding marital relations (תַּשְׁמִישׁ הַמִּטָּה).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan resolves the dispute in the baraita by stating that the only practical difference between the Tanna Kamma and Rabban Gamliel is regarding marital relations (תַּשְׁמִישׁ הַמִּטָּה).

items.text: Gemara's attempted proof and rejection
items.text_en: Gemara's attempted proof and rejection
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute in the baraita is about whether mourning applies on Shabbat, but rejects this: the Tanna Kamma's leniencies are only because the deceased lies before him, and Rabban Gamliel's stringency is only because mourning has not yet taken effect. In the case of an onen whose relative is buried, both would agree.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute in the baraita is about whether mourning applies on Shabbat (יש אבלות בשבת) or not (אין אבלות בשבת).
The Gemara rejects the proof: the Tanna Kamma's leniencies apply only because the deceased lies before him (מתו מוטל לפניו), not because of a general rule about Shabbat.

The Gemara further rejects: Rabban Gamliel's stringency applies only where mourning has not yet taken effect (אכתי לא חל אבלות עליה), but in the case of an אונן (onen) whose relative is buried, both would agree.

items.text: Opening question: Is there mourning on Shabbat?
items.text_en: Opening question: Is there mourning on Shabbat?
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan asks Shmuel whether mourning practices apply on Shabbat. Shmuel answers that there is no mourning on Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan asks Shmuel whether mourning practices apply on Shabbat.
Shmuel answers that there is no mourning on Shabbat.

items.text: The mourner who engages in marital relations
items.text_en: The mourner who engages in marital relations
items.desc_en: The rabbis report in Shmuel's name that a mourner who engages in marital relations is liable to death. Rav Pappa corrects them, saying the statement was about prohibition, not liability, and was said in Rabbi Yochanan's name. He then reports a different statement from Shmuel: a mourner who did not perform keri'ah or periah is liable to death.

sub.desc_en: The rabbis sitting before Rav Pappa report in Shmuel's name that a mourner who engaged in marital relations is liable to death.
Rav Pappa corrects them, saying the statement was about prohibition (אָסוּר), not liability, and was said in Rabbi Yochanan's name.

Rav Pappa reports a different statement from Shmuel via Rav Tachlifa bar Avimi: a mourner who did not perform keri'ah (קְרִיעָה) or periah (פְּרִיעָה) is liable to death, citing the verse 'רָאשֵׁיכֶם אַל תִּפְרָעוּ וּבִגְדֵיכֶם לֹא תִפְרוֹמוּ וְלֹא תָמוּתוּ'.

items.text: A story about a mourner who engaged in marital relations
items.text_en: A story about a mourner who engaged in marital relations
items.desc_en: Rafram bar Pappa teaches in Eivel Rabbati that a mourner is forbidden to engage in marital relations, and relates a story of one who did and whose body was dragged by pigs.

sub.desc_en: Rafram bar Pappa cites a baraita from Eivel Rabbati that a mourner is forbidden to engage in marital relations during his mourning period.
Rafram bar Pappa relates a story of a mourner who violated this prohibition and whose corpse was subsequently dragged by pigs as a punishment.

items.text: Shmuel's list: obligations and permissions for a mourner
items.text_en: Shmuel's list: obligations and permissions for a mourner
items.desc_en: Shmuel lists practices that are obligatory (chovah) and those that are permitted (reshut) for a mourner. Rav disagrees regarding periat harosh. The Gemara explains Shmuel's reasoning and connects it to his other statements about keri'ah and atifah. Rav Nachman demonstrates the proper way to perform keri'ah.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel introduces a mnemonic list: practices that are obligatory (חובה) and those that are permitted (רשות) for a mourner.

The Gemara details Shmuel's list: periat harosh, returning the tear to the back, and overturning the bed are obligatory; wearing sandals, marital relations, and washing hands and feet in hot water in the evening are permitted. Rav adds that periat harosh is also permitted.
The Gemara questions Shmuel's distinction: if wearing sandals is permitted because not everyone wears them, why is periat harosh obligatory when not everyone goes bareheaded?

The Gemara resolves that Shmuel is consistent with his own views: he requires keri'ah to be done at the time of emotional heat (חימום) and atifah to be like Ishmaelites, and Rav Nachman demonstrates the proper keri'ah down to the beard.

items.text: Exception for wearing shoes on Shabbat
items.text_en: Exception for wearing shoes on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov quoting Rabbi Yochanan says that the permission to wear shoes on Shabbat applies only when one has no shoes on his feet; if he does, the shoes themselves testify that he is a mourner.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov in the name of Rabbi Yochanan resolves that the leniency of wearing shoes on Shabbat applies only when the mourner has no shoes on his feet; if he does, the shoes themselves testify that he is a mourner.

items.text: Keri'ah at the time of anger and the exception for Torah scholars
items.text_en: Keri'ah at the time of anger and the exception for Torah scholars
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Shmuel's rule that keri'ah must be at the time of anger, citing stories where Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan tore garments upon hearing of the death of their teachers. The Gemara answers that Torah scholars are different because they constantly recall their teachings, which is like the time of anger.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Shmuel's rule that a tear (קֶרַע) not made at the time of anger (שְׁעַת חִימּוּם) is invalid, citing that Shmuel himself tore twelve garments upon hearing of Rav's death, and Rabbi Yochanan tore thirteen cloaks upon hearing of Rabbi Chanina's death.
The Gemara answers that Torah scholars are different, because they are constantly recalling their teachings, which is akin to the time of anger.

items.text: Keri'ah for a mourner: front vs. back, and the exception for parents
items.text_en: Keri'ah for a mourner: front vs. back, and the exception for parents
items.desc_en: Ravin bar Adda reports to Rava a baraita: a mourner tears from the front all seven days, and if he changes garments, he tears again. On Shabbat, he tears from the back, and if he changes, he does not tear. The Gemara limits this to honoring one's father and mother.

sub.desc_en: Ravin bar Adda reports to Rava a baraita about a mourner's keri'ah (tearing): all seven days he tears from the front, and if he changes garments he tears again; on Shabbat he tears from the back, and if he changes he does not tear.
The Gemara limits the baraita's ruling to the case of honoring one's father and mother, implying that for other relatives the rule differs.

items.text: Dispute: Are these tears allowed to be sewn up?
items.text_en: Dispute: Are these tears allowed to be sewn up?
items.desc_en: The Gemara records a dispute between the father of Rav Oshaya and bar Kappara: one says these tears may not be sewn up, the other says they may. The Gemara attempts to resolve the dispute but concludes that Rav Oshaya heard the lenient opinion from bar Kappara, his teacher.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the tears made during mourning may be sewn up or not.

sub.text: Father of Rav Oshaya and Bar Kappara
sub.text_en: Father of Rav Oshaya and Bar Kappara
sub.desc_en: The Gemara records a dispute: one says they may not be sewn up, the other says they may.
The Gemara attempts to resolve the dispute by inferring Rav Oshaya's source, but concludes that he heard the lenient opinion from his teacher Bar Kappara, not from his father.

items.text: Private mourning practices on Shabbat
items.text_en: Private mourning practices on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rava says a mourner may walk with a cloak within his house. Abaye found Rav Yosef walking with a cloth on his head and questioned him, citing the rule that there is no mourning on Shabbat. Rav Yosef replied that Rabbi Yochanan said private matters are observed.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that a mourner may walk with a cloak within his house on Shabbat.
Abaye finds Rav Yosef walking with a cloth on his head and questions him, citing the rule that there is no mourning on Shabbat.
Rav Yosef replies that Rabbi Yochanan said private mourning practices are observed on Shabbat.

items.text: Halakha like Rabban Gamliel and a related teaching
items.text_en: Halakha like Rabban Gamliel and a related teaching
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a statement by Rav Giddel bar Menashya quoting Shmuel that the halakha follows Rabban Gamliel regarding Shavuot. An alternative version connects this to a teaching about a child within thirty days being buried with one woman and two men, but not with one man and two women.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah where Rabbi Eliezer rules that after the Temple's destruction, Shavuot is like Shabbat regarding mourning practices.

sub.text: Rav Giddel bar Menashya citing Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Giddel bar Menashya citing Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Giddel bar Menashya reports in Shmuel's name that the halakha follows Rabban Gamliel's position on Shavuot.
An alternative version applies Rav Giddel bar Menashya's statement to a different teaching.
The baraita rules that a child within thirty days is buried with one woman and two men, but not with one man and two women.

items.text: Mishnah: Laws of mourning for a child
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of mourning for a child
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the opinions of Abba Shaul, Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Akiva, Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, and Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya regarding the age at which a child is mourned publicly, including the use of a bier and the recitation of blessings. It also discusses the number of days of eulogy for poor and rich children.

sub.desc_en: Abba Shaul states that for a child under 30 days, there is no public mourning: no standing in a row, no blessing of mourners, and no consolation of mourners.
Rabbi Yehuda rules that a 30-day-old child is carried out on a bier (דלוסקמא) carried on the arm, and public mourning rites are performed.
Rabbi Akiva says a one-year-old child is carried out on a bed, and if the child's limbs appear older or younger, the bed is used accordingly.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar and Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya debate whether public eulogy depends on the child being carried on a bed or being known to the public.

sub.text: Rabbi Meir in the name of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Rabbi Meir in the name of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Meir in the name of Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Yishmael give different ages for eulogizing poor and rich children, with Rabbi Yehuda adding that children of the elderly are treated like poor children.

items.text: Rav Giddel bar Menashya rules like Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Rav Giddel bar Menashya rules like Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: Rav Giddel bar Menashya quotes Rav that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda's statement in the name of Rabbi Yishmael regarding the number of days of eulogy.

sub.text: Rav Giddel bar Menashya quoting Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Giddel bar Menashya quoting Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Giddel bar Menashya reports in the name of Rav that the binding law (הלכה) follows Rabbi Yehuda's statement in the name of Rabbi Yishmael regarding the number of days of eulogy.

items.text: The source for make-up days for Shavuot
items.text_en: The source for make-up days for Shavuot
items.desc_en: Rabbi Anani bar Sason and Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha each taught that the day before Shavuot and Shavuot itself count as fourteen days of mourning, but Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Sheshet objected, noting that this teaching actually originates from Rabbi Elazar quoting Rabbi Oshaya. The Gemara then cites Rabbi Elazar's derivation from the verse comparing Shavuot to Passover.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Anani bar Sason taught at the entrance of the Nasi's house that the day before Shavuot and Shavuot itself together count as fourteen days of mourning.
Rabbi Ammi heard the teaching and was offended, objecting that it was not Rabbi Anani's own but rather a tradition from Rabbi Elazar quoting Rabbi Oshaya.
Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha taught the same ruling at the synagogue of the Exilarch, that the day before Shavuot and Shavuot itself count as fourteen days.
Rabbi Sheshet heard the teaching and was offended, objecting that it was not Rabbi Yitzchak's own but rather a tradition from Rabbi Elazar quoting Rabbi Oshaya.

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar quoting Rabbi Oshaya's derivation
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar quoting Rabbi Oshaya's derivation
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Elazar quoting Rabbi Oshaya who derives from the verse comparing Shavuot to Passover that Shavuot has make-up days for the entire seven days of the festival.

items.text: Rav Pappa and Ravina extend the principle to other festivals
items.text_en: Rav Pappa and Ravina extend the principle to other festivals
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa instructed Rav Avya Sava to teach that the day before Rosh Hashanah and Rosh Hashanah count as fourteen days.
