Ravina then adds that the day before Sukkot, Sukkot, and Shemini Atzeret count as twenty-one days. When questioned by Rav Chaviva, Ravina explains that he follows Rabban Gamliel's opinion.

sub.text: Rav Pappa instructing Rav Avya Sava
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa instructing Rav Avya Sava
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa directs Rav Avya Sava to teach that the day before Rosh Hashanah and Rosh Hashanah together count as fourteen days of mourning restrictions.
Ravina adds that the day before Sukkot, Sukkot, and Shemini Atzeret together count as twenty-one days.
Rav Chaviva questions Ravina, asking whether Ravina indeed holds that the day before Rosh Hashanah and Rosh Hashanah count as fourteen days.
Ravina explains that his ruling follows the opinion of Rabban Gamliel.

items.text: Mishnah: Laws of rending, removing shoes, and the meal of comfort
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of rending, removing shoes, and the meal of comfort
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that only the relatives of the deceased perform the acts of rending garments, removing shoes, and the meal of comfort, and the meal of comfort is only held on an upright bier.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that only the relatives of the deceased perform the acts of rending garments, removing shoes, and the meal of comfort, and the meal of comfort is only held on an upright bier.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's exemption for a scholar
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's exemption for a scholar
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's statement that one is not obligated to tear for a scholar, citing a baraita that says 'a scholar who died — everyone is like his relatives.' It clarifies that this means everyone tears, bares, and holds a meal in the broad place for him. The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah refers to a non-scholar.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's exemption for a scholar by citing a baraita that says 'a scholar who died — everyone is his relatives.'

The Gemara clarifies that the baraita means 'everyone is like his relatives' — everyone tears, bares, and holds a meal in the broad place for him — and resolves that the Mishnah refers to a non-scholar.

items.text: Obligation for an upright person
items.text_en: Obligation for an upright person
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers that if the deceased is an upright person, one is obligated to tear. It cites a baraita that children die young so that one would weep and mourn for an upright person. The Gemara corrects this: it is because one did not weep and mourn for an upright person, and whoever does so has all his sins forgiven.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that if the deceased is an upright person (אדם כשר), one is obligated to tear.
A baraita is cited: children die young so that one would weep and mourn for an upright person.
The Gemara objects: would God take a 'deposit' (ערבון) from the parent by causing the child's death as a guarantee for future mourning?
The Gemara corrects: the baraita means that children die because the parent did not weep and mourn for an upright person, and whoever does so has all sins forgiven.

items.text: Obligation for one present at the moment of death
items.text_en: Obligation for one present at the moment of death
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that if one was present at the moment of death, he is obligated to tear, citing Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar who compares it to a Torah scroll that was burned. The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah's exemption applies when one was not present at the moment of death.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that if one was present at the moment of death, he is obligated to tear.
A baraita is cited: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says one standing over the deceased at the moment of death must tear, comparing it to a Torah scroll that was burned.
The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah's exemption applies when one was not present at the moment of death.

items.text: Funeral of Rav Safra
items.text_en: Funeral of Rav Safra
items.desc_en: When Rav Safra died, the rabbis did not tear for him, saying they did not learn from him. Abaye objected: the baraita says 'a scholar who died,' not 'a teacher who died,' and his teachings are constantly in the study hall. They thought the obligation had passed, but Abaye cited a baraita that as long as they are engaged in the eulogy, they are obligated to tear. They considered tearing immediately, but Abaye cited that a scholar's honor is in his eulogy.

sub.desc_en: When Rav Safra died, the rabbis did not tear for him, saying they did not learn from him.
Abaye objects: the baraita says 'a scholar who died,' not 'a teacher who died,' and his teachings are constantly in the study hall.
The rabbis thought the obligation had passed.
Abaye cites a baraita: as long as they are engaged in the eulogy, they are obligated to tear.
They considered tearing immediately.
Abaye cites that a scholar's honor is in his eulogy, so they should tear during the eulogy, not immediately.

items.text: Funeral of Rav Huna: rulings by Rav Chisda
items.text_en: Funeral of Rav Huna: rulings by Rav Chisda
items.desc_en: When Rav Huna died, they considered placing a Torah scroll on his bier, but Rav Chisda forbade it based on Rav Huna's own practice. They considered lowering the bier through roofs, but Rav Chisda ruled that a scholar's honor is through the gate. They considered transferring him from bier to bier, but Rav Chisda ruled that a scholar's honor is on the first bier, citing a verse about the Ark.

sub.desc_en: The rabbis considered placing a Torah scroll on Rav Huna's bier, but Rav Chisda forbade it, citing Rav Huna's own practice of not sitting on a bed with a Torah scroll.
The rabbis considered lowering the bier through the roofs, but Rav Chisda ruled that a scholar's honor is through the gate.
The rabbis considered transferring Rav Huna from bier to bier, but Rav Chisda ruled that a scholar's honor is on the first bier, citing a verse about the Ark.

items.text: Eulogy for Rav Huna and objection
items.text_en: Eulogy for Rav Huna and objection
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba eulogized that Rav Huna was worthy of the Divine Presence but for Babylon. Rav Nachman bar Chisda (or Rav Chanan bar Chisda) objected with a verse that prophecy came to Ezekiel in Babylonia. His father slapped him, saying not to trouble the world, explaining that 'was' means it had already been.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba opens the eulogy for Rav Huna, stating that Rav Huna was worthy of the Divine Presence (שכינה) but for Babylon.

Rav Nachman bar Chisda (or some say Rav Chanan bar Chisda) objects by citing the verse 'הָיֹה הָיָה דְבַר ה׳ אֶל יְחֶזְקֵאל... בְּאֶרֶץ כַּשְׂדִּים' (Ezekiel 1:3), which shows that prophecy occurred in Babylonia, contradicting the claim that Babylon prevented the Divine Presence.

The father of Rav Nachman slaps him with a sandal and rebukes him for troubling the world, explaining that the word 'הָיָה' (was) in the verse indicates that the prophecy had already occurred before the exile, not that the Divine Presence was present in Babylonia.

items.text: Arrival of Rav Huna's coffin in Eretz Yisrael
items.text_en: Arrival of Rav Huna's coffin in Eretz Yisrael
items.desc_en: When they brought Rav Huna's coffin to Eretz Yisrael, Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi debated whether to go out. Some went out, some did not, based on conflicting baraitot about whether one stands in a row for a passing coffin. The Gemara resolves that it depends on whether the body is intact; Rav Huna's body was intact, but those who did not go out had not heard the resolution.

sub.desc_en: When Rav Huna's coffin was brought to Eretz Yisrael, Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi debated whether to go out to honor him, feeling unworthy.
They were told the coffin had arrived; Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi went out, while Rabbi Ila and Rabbi Chanina did not, with a variant report that Rabbi Ila went out but Rabbi Chanina did not.
The Gemara explains that those who went out relied on a baraita requiring standing in a row and reciting mourners' blessing and consolation for a passing coffin.

sub.text: Gemara's analysis of the opposing reason
sub.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the opposing reason
sub.desc_en: Those who did not go out relied on a conflicting baraita that for a passing coffin one does not stand in a row or recite mourners' blessing and consolation.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction: the first baraita applies when the body is intact, the second when it is not; Rav Huna's body was intact, but those who did not go out had not heard this resolution.

items.text: Burial of Rav Huna and Rav Chagga's merit
items.text_en: Burial of Rav Huna and Rav Chagga's merit
items.desc_en: They debated where to bury Rav Huna, as both he and Rabbi Chiya spread Torah in Israel. Rav Chagga offered to bring him in, citing his own merit of having studied before him without seminal emission and knowing that Rav Huna once fasted forty days for a tefillin strap. When he brought him in, Yehuda and Chizkiya were lying on either side of their father; Yehuda asked Chizkiya to rise for Rav Huna, and a pillar of fire rose. Rav Chagga was frightened but was not punished because he straightened the coffin.

sub.desc_en: The gemara raises the question of where to bury Rav Huna, noting that both he and Rabbi Chiya spread Torah in Israel.
Rav Chagga offers to bring Rav Huna in, citing his own merit of having studied before him without seminal emission and knowing that Rav Huna once fasted forty days for a tefillin strap.

When Rav Chagga brought Rav Huna in, Yehuda and Chizkiya were lying on either side of their father; Yehuda asked Chizkiya to rise for Rav Huna, a pillar of fire rose, and Rav Chagga was frightened but was not punished because he straightened the coffin.

items.text: Funeral of Rav Chisda
items.text_en: Funeral of Rav Chisda
items.desc_en: When Rav Chisda died, they considered placing a Torah scroll on his bier, but Rabbi Yitzchak objected based on his teacher's (Rav Huna's) ruling. They considered not rending their garments, but Rabbi Yitzchak bar Ami ruled that a scholar may rend once they turn their faces from behind the bier.

sub.desc_en: When Rav Chisda died, the community considered placing a Torah scroll on his bier, following the precedent of Rav Huna.
Rabbi Yitzchak objected, arguing that since Rav Chisda's own teacher (Rav Huna) had not permitted sitting on a bed with a Torah scroll, they should not do so for Rav Chisda.
The community then considered not rending their garments (or not closing the tear) for Rav Chisda.
Rabbi Yitzchak bar Ami ruled that for a scholar, once the mourners turn their faces from behind the bier, they may close the tear (שוללין).

items.text: Burial of Rabbah bar Huna and Rav Hamnuna
items.text_en: Burial of Rabbah bar Huna and Rav Hamnuna
items.desc_en: When Rabbah bar Huna and Rav Hamnuna died, they were brought up to Eretz Yisrael for burial.

sub.desc_en: The gemara reports that when Rabbah bar Huna and Rav Hamnuna died, they were brought up to Eretz Yisrael for burial.

items.text: Incident at the bridge: Rabbah bar Huna and the Arab
items.text_en: Incident at the bridge: Rabbah bar Huna and the Arab
items.desc_en: When Rabbah bar Huna and Rav Chisda reached a bridge, their camels stopped as each sage deferred to the other. An Arab passerby ruled that Rabbah bar Huna should enter first, but his camel kicked the Arab, breaking his teeth.

sub.desc_en: The camels stop at the bridge as Rabbah bar Huna and Rav Chisda defer to each other.
The Arab asks what is happening.
They explain that each sage is honoring the other by deferring entry.
The Arab rules that Rabbah bar Huna should enter first.
Rabbah bar Huna's camel passes and kicks the Arab, breaking his jaw and teeth.

items.text: Dirge for Rabbah bar Huna by a child
items.text_en: Dirge for Rabbah bar Huna by a child
items.desc_en: A child recited a poetic dirge for Rabbah bar Huna, comparing him to a shoot from Babylon and describing the joy of God receiving his pure soul.

sub.desc_en: A child recited a poetic dirge for Rabbah bar Huna, comparing him to a shoot from Babylon and describing the joy of God receiving his pure soul.

items.text: Dirge for Ravina
items.text_en: Dirge for Ravina
items.desc_en: A eulogizer recited a dirge for Ravina, comparing him to a palm tree and describing the mourning of women.

sub.desc_en: The eulogizer recites a dirge for Ravina, comparing him to a palm tree and describing the mourning of women who turn nights into days.

items.text: Rav Ashi's inquiry about eulogies: Bar Kippok and Bar Avin
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's inquiry about eulogies: Bar Kippok and Bar Avin
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi asked Bar Kippok what he said at a eulogy; Bar Kippok recited a dirge comparing the sage to a cedar and Leviathan. Bar Avin objected, saying he would not compare sages to a hook or flame, and recited a different dirge. The sages were offended, and their legs were twisted; they did not attend the eulogy. Rav Ashi concluded that neither Bar Kippok nor Bar Avin were fit to eulogize.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks Bar Kippok what he said at the eulogy, and Bar Kippok responds with a dirge comparing the sage to a cedar and Leviathan.
Bar Avin objects to comparing sages to a hook or flame, and recites a different dirge emphasizing mourning for the living rather than the lost.

sub.text: Narrative conclusion and Rav Ashi's ruling
sub.text_en: Narrative conclusion and Rav Ashi's ruling
sub.desc_en: The sages are offended and their legs are twisted; they do not attend the eulogy, and Rav Ashi concludes that neither Bar Kippok nor Bar Avin are fit to eulogize.

items.text: Rava's request for a dirge from Bar Avin
items.text_en: Rava's request for a dirge from Bar Avin
items.desc_en: When Rava came to the Diglat river, he asked Bar Avin to recite a dirge. Bar Avin recited a poetic plea for mercy, comparing the people to a woman estranged from her husband.

sub.desc_en: The gemara narrates that when Rava came to the Diglat river, he asked Bar Avin to recite a dirge.
Bar Avin recites a poetic dirge pleading for mercy, comparing the people to a woman estranged from her husband.

items.text: Mnemonic for names of sages
items.text_en: Mnemonic for names of sages
items.desc_en: A mnemonic lists the names of sages whose deaths and eulogies are discussed: Chanin, Yochanan, Zeira, Abba, Yaakov, Yosei, Shmuel, Chiyya, Menachem.

sub.desc_en: The gemara provides a mnemonic listing the names of sages whose deaths and eulogies will be discussed.

items.text: Dirge for Rabbi Chanin
items.text_en: Dirge for Rabbi Chanin
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanin, son-in-law of the Nasi, had no children; he prayed and had a son, but died on the day of the child's birth. A eulogizer recited a dirge about joy turning to sorrow, and he was named Chanin after his father.

sub.desc_en: Introduces Rabbi Chanin as the son-in-law of the Nasi who had no children and prayed successfully for a son.
Reports that on the very day his son was born, Rabbi Chanin died.
The eulogizer recites a dirge about joy turning to sorrow and the loss of Chanin's grace at the moment of his grace.
Concludes that they named the child Chanin after his father.

items.text: Dirge for Rabbi Yochanan by Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elazar
items.text_en: Dirge for Rabbi Yochanan by Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elazar
items.desc_en: When Rabbi Yochanan died, Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elazar eulogized him, comparing the day to the sun setting at noon, citing a verse about the day of Josiah.

sub.desc_en: The narrator reports that when Rabbi Yochanan died, Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elazar opened his eulogy.
Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elazar compares the day of Rabbi Yochanan's death to the sun setting at noon, citing the verse from Amos about the day of Josiah.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan (cited by Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elazar)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan (cited by Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elazar)
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elazar concludes by citing Rabbi Yochanan's own interpretation that the verse refers to the day of King Josiah's death.

items.text: Rabbi Ami's mourning for Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Rabbi Ami's mourning for Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ami sat shiva for thirty-seven days after Rabbi Yochanan's death. Rabbi Abba bar Chiyya bar Abba commented that Rabbi Ami did this for himself, citing Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that one sits only one day even for one's teacher of wisdom.

sub.desc_en: The gemara reports that when Rabbi Yochanan died, Rabbi Ami sat shiva for thirty-seven days.

sub.text: Rabbi Abba bar Chiyya bar Abba's comment
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abba bar Chiyya bar Abba's comment
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Chiyya bar Abba objects that Rabbi Ami's extended mourning was for his own reasons, citing Rabbi Yochanan's own ruling that one sits only one day even for one's teacher of wisdom.

items.text: Dirge for Rabbi Zeira
items.text_en: Dirge for Rabbi Zeira
items.desc_en: A eulogizer recited a dirge for Rabbi Zeira, comparing the land of Shinar to a woman who lost her precious vessel.

sub.desc_en: The eulogizer opens a dirge for Rabbi Zeira, lamenting that the land of Shinar (Babylon) has lost its precious vessel.

items.text: Miraculous signs at the deaths of various sages
items.text_en: Miraculous signs at the deaths of various sages
items.desc_en: At the deaths of several sages, miraculous signs occurred: pillars of Caesarea filled with water, drains of Tzippori flowed with blood, stars appeared by day, trees were uprooted, fire fell from heaven, statues moved, bridges were cut, walls were breached, hail fell, and rivers kissed each other.

sub.desc_en: The gemara lists miraculous signs at the deaths of Rabbi Avahu, Rabbi Yosei, Rabbi Yaakov, Rabbi Assi, Rabbi Chiyya, and Rabbi Menachem bar Yosei.
The gemara continues listing miraculous signs at the deaths of Rabbi Tanchum bar Chiyya, Rabbi Elyashiv, Rav Hamnuna, Rabbah and Rav Yosef, Abaye and Rava, and Rabbi Mesharshiya.

items.text: Beginning of a baraita
items.text_en: Beginning of a baraita
items.desc_en: The text introduces a baraita with the phrase 'the Sages taught', indicating the start of a new teaching.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a baraita with the standard formula 'תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן' (the Sages taught), signaling the beginning of a new tannaitic teaching.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: List of tears that may never be repaired
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: List of tears that may never be repaired
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the tears that may never be repaired: for one's father, mother, Torah teacher, Nasi, Av Beit Din, bad news, blasphemy, a burnt Torah scroll, cities of Judah, the Temple, and Jerusalem. It adds that one tears for the Temple and adds for Jerusalem.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the tears that may never be repaired, including for parents, Torah teacher, Nasi, Av Beit Din, bad news, blasphemy, a burnt Torah scroll, cities of Judah, the Temple, and Jerusalem.

items.text: Source for father, mother, and Torah teacher; and that the tear never heals
items.text_en: Source for father, mother, and Torah teacher; and that the tear never heals
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives the obligation to tear for father, mother, and Torah teacher from Elisha's cry 'Avi Avi' (father) and 'Rekhev Yisrael ufarashav' (teacher). Rav Yosef translates the verse to show the teacher's value. The permanence of the tear is derived from the verse 'vayachazek bivgadav vayikra'em lishnayim kera'im', implying the tear remains forever. Reish Lakish asks Rabbi Yochanan about Elijah being alive, and is answered that relative to Elisha, he was considered dead.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source for tearing over father, mother, and Torah teacher, citing Elisha's cry 'Avi Avi' and 'Rekhev Yisrael ufarashav'.
Rav Yosef translates the verse to show that the teacher is called 'Rekhev Yisrael ufarashav' because his prayers are more valuable to Israel than chariots and horsemen.
The Gemara asks for the source that the tear never heals, citing the verse 'vayachazek bivgadav vayikra'em lishnayim kera'im'.
The Gemara explains that the extra word 'lishnayim' teaches that the tears remain forever.

sub.text: Reish Lakish's question to Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Reish Lakish's question to Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish asks Rabbi Yochanan whether Elijah is alive, and Rabbi Yochanan answers that relative to Elisha, he was considered dead.

items.text: Source for Nasi, Av Beit Din, and bad news
items.text_en: Source for Nasi, Av Beit Din, and bad news
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives the obligation to tear for a Nasi, Av Beit Din, and bad news from David's tearing upon hearing of the deaths of Saul, Jonathan, and the people. Rav Bar Shabba asks Rav Kahana why not require tearing for all of them together, and is answered that the repeated word 'al' separates the categories.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the obligation to tear for a Nasi, Av Beit Din, and bad news, citing David's tearing upon hearing of the deaths of Saul, Jonathan, and the people.
The Gemara identifies Saul as the Nasi, Jonathan as the Av Beit Din, and 'the people of the Lord and the house of Israel' as bad news.
Rav Bar Shabba objects to Rav Kahana: why not require tearing for all of them together as one category?
Rav Kahana answers that the repeated word 'עַל' (upon) in the verse separates the categories, so each requires its own tear.

items.text: Challenge: Do we tear for bad news? Incident with Shapur and Samuel
items.text_en: Challenge: Do we tear for bad news? Incident with Shapur and Samuel
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether one tears for bad news, citing an incident where Samuel did not tear upon hearing that King Shapur killed 12,000 Jews in Caesarea. The answer is that the obligation applies only to a majority of the community, as in the biblical precedent. The Gemara then clarifies that Shapur did not actually kill Jews; rather, the Jews caused their own deaths due to a wall collapsing from the noise of the city's mixing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the Mishnah's ruling that one tears for bad news, citing an incident where Samuel did not tear upon hearing that King Shapur killed 12,000 Jews in Caesarea.
The Gemara resolves that the obligation to tear for bad news applies only to a majority of the community, as in the biblical precedent.
The Gemara questions whether Shapur actually killed Jews, citing his own claim that he never killed a Jew.
Rabbi Ammi explains that the Jews caused their own deaths when a wall collapsed from the noise of the city's mixing, so Shapur was not directly responsible.

items.text: Source for blasphemy and that the tear never heals
items.text_en: Source for blasphemy and that the tear never heals
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives the obligation to tear for blasphemy from the verse where Eliakim, Shebna, and Joach came to Hezekiah with torn garments. A baraita teaches that both the direct hearer and the one who hears from the hearer must tear, but witnesses are exempt because they already tore when they heard. The permanence of the tear is derived via a verbal analogy of 'keriah'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of tearing for blasphemy (ברכת השם), citing the verse where Eliakim, Shebna, and Joach came to Hezekiah with torn garments.
A baraita teaches that both the direct hearer of blasphemy and the one who hears from the hearer must tear, but witnesses are exempt because they already tore when they heard.
The Gemara objects: what does 'when they heard' mean? They are hearing now! The Gemara rejects this, citing the verse that only the king tore.
The Gemara derives that the tear for blasphemy never heals via a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) of the word 'קריעה' (tearing) from the verse about the king's tear.

items.text: Source for a burnt Torah scroll and related laws
items.text_en: Source for a burnt Torah scroll and related laws
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives the obligation to tear for a burnt Torah scroll from the story of Jehoiakim burning Jeremiah's scroll. It explains the verse 'shalosh delatot v'arba'ah' as referring to the first four chapters of Lamentations. Rabbi Helbo quotes Rav Huna that one who sees a torn Torah scroll must tear twice: once for the parchment and once for the writing. A story about Rabbi Abba and Rav Huna bar Chiya illustrates that this applies only when the scroll is torn by force, as per Samuel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the obligation to tear for a burnt Torah scroll, citing the verse about Jehoiakim burning Jeremiah's scroll.
The Gemara recounts the story of Jehoiakim's dialogue about the scroll of Lamentations and his burning of it.
The Gemara concludes from the verse that the officials should have torn their garments, implying the obligation to tear for a burnt scroll.
Rav Pappa suggests the tearing might be due to bad tidings, but Abaye rejects this because there were no bad tidings at that time.
Rabbi Helbo quotes Rav Huna that one who sees a torn Torah scroll must tear twice: once for the parchment and once for the writing.

sub.text: Story about Rabbi Abba and Rav Huna bar Chiya
sub.text_en: Story about Rabbi Abba and Rav Huna bar Chiya
sub.desc_en: A story illustrates that the obligation to tear for a torn scroll applies only when the tearing is done by force, as per Samuel's ruling.

items.text: Source for cities of Judah, Jerusalem, and the Temple; and the order of tearing
items.text_en: Source for cities of Judah, Jerusalem, and the Temple; and the order of tearing
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives the obligation to tear for cities of Judah from the verse about men from Shechem, Shiloh, and Samaria with torn garments. Rabbi Helbo quotes Ulla Bira'ah quoting Rabbi Elazar that one who sees the cities of Judah in ruin recites a verse and tears; similarly for Jerusalem and the Temple. A contradiction is raised between the Mishnah (tear for Temple and add for Jerusalem) and a baraita (tear separately for each), and is resolved by the order of encountering them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of tearing for cities of Judah, citing the verse about men from Shechem, Shiloh, and Samaria with torn garments.

sub.text: Rabbi Helbo quoting Ulla Bira'ah quoting Rabbi Elazar
sub.text_en: Rabbi Helbo quoting Ulla Bira'ah quoting Rabbi Elazar
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Helbo in the name of Ulla Bira'ah citing Rabbi Elazar states the halacha: one who sees the cities of Judah in ruin recites a verse and tears; similarly for Jerusalem and the Temple.
The Gemara raises a contradiction between the Mishnah (tear for Temple and add for Jerusalem) and a baraita (tear separately for each).

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing the order of encountering them: if one encounters the Temple first, he tears for it and adds for Jerusalem; if Jerusalem first, he tears separately for each.

items.text: Concluding baraita: Permitted repairs for these tears
items.text_en: Concluding baraita: Permitted repairs for these tears
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that for all these tears, one may sew them in a ladder-like pattern but not fully repair them. Rav Chisda begins to speak, but the text cuts off.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that for all these tears, one may sew them in a ladder-like pattern but not fully repair them.
Rav Chisda begins to speak, but the text cuts off before his statement is recorded.

items.text: Alexandrian stitching qualifies for keriah
items.text_en: Alexandrian stitching qualifies for keriah
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita stating that tearing from a sewn seam (איחוי) is valid, and Rav Chisda specifies that this refers to Alexandrian stitching.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that tearing from a sewn seam (איחוי) is valid for keriah, but not from other types of stitching.
Rav Chisda specifies that the valid seam is specifically Alexandrian stitching (איחוי אלכסנדרי).

items.text: Permitted to turn garment and stitch; seller must inform buyer
items.text_en: Permitted to turn garment and stitch; seller must inform buyer
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one may turn the garment upside down and stitch it, but Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar forbids stitching. The seller must inform the buyer that the garment was torn for mourning.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that one is permitted to turn the garment upside down and stitch it.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar forbids stitching and rules that the seller must inform the buyer that the garment was torn for mourning.

items.text: Size of initial tear and addition: Rabbi Meir vs. Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Size of initial tear and addition: Rabbi Meir vs. Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: A baraita records a dispute: Rabbi Meir says the initial tear must be a handbreadth and the addition three fingerbreadths; Rabbi Yehuda says the initial tear is three fingerbreadths and any addition suffices. Ulla rules like Rabbi Meir for the initial tear and like Rabbi Yehuda for the addition, and a baraita supports this with Rabbi Yosei's opinion.

sub.desc_en: A baraita records the dispute between Rabbi Meir (initial tear a handbreadth, addition three fingerbreadths) and Rabbi Yehuda (initial tear three fingerbreadths, addition any amount).
Ulla rules like Rabbi Meir for the initial tear and like Rabbi Yehuda for the addition, and a supporting baraita cites Rabbi Yosei's opinion that matches this compromise.

items.text: Adding a tear for a second death; one tear for multiple relatives
items.text_en: Adding a tear for a second death; one tear for multiple relatives
items.desc_en: Baraitot discuss cases of adding a tear when a second relative dies: if the lower tear was for the first death, the upper tear is added and the lower may be stitched, and vice versa. Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira says one tear suffices for all relatives except for father and mother, where no addition is made. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains the reason: they are not subject to addition.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states the rule for adding a tear when a second relative dies: if the lower tear was for the father and the upper for the son, the lower may be stitched but the upper may not.
The baraita gives the reverse case: if the lower tear was for the son and the upper for the father, the upper may be stitched but the lower may not.
The baraita rules that for multiple relatives other than parents, one tear suffices for all.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira says one tear suffices for all relatives, but for father and mother a separate tear is required because no addition may be made to the tear for parents.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains the reason for Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's ruling: the tear for father and mother is not subject to addition.

items.text: Shmuel rules like Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira; mourning and tearing are separate
items.text_en: Shmuel rules like Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira; mourning and tearing are separate
items.desc_en: Shmuel rules in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira. The Gemara questions this because Shmuel elsewhere rules leniently in mourning, but resolves that mourning and tearing are separate matters.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that the law follows Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira regarding tearing a single tear for all relatives except parents.
The Gemara objects that Shmuel elsewhere rules leniently in mourning, contradicting his current ruling.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between mourning practices (אבלות) and tearing (קריעה), which are separate halachic domains.

items.text: How far to tear and where to tear; exceptions for the High Priest
items.text_en: How far to tear and where to tear; exceptions for the High Priest
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the extent of the tear: until the navel or the heart, with a verse as a reminder. If the tear reaches the navel, one must distance three fingerbreadths and continue. If the garment is filled, one turns it. Tearing from the bottom or sides is invalid, except for the High Priest who tears from below.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how far one must tear, citing two opinions: until the navel or until the heart.
The Gemara provides a biblical verse as a mnemonic for tearing to the heart.
The Gemara rules that if the tear reaches the navel, one must distance three fingerbreadths and continue; if the garment is filled, one turns it to the back.
The Gemara rules that if the tear is filled from above, one turns it below; tearing from the bottom or sides is invalid.
The Gemara notes an exception: the High Priest tears from below.

items.text: Duration for tearing and adding: dispute between Rav Mattana and Mar Ukva
items.text_en: Duration for tearing and adding: dispute between Rav Mattana and Mar Ukva
items.desc_en: Rav Mattana and Mar Ukva dispute, both citing the father of Shmuel and Levi: one says one may tear for seven days and add after; the other says thirty days. Rabbi Zeira challenges both: the first because a woman may stitch immediately, and the second because for parents stitching is never permitted. The Gemara answers that those are exceptions due to honor.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute between Rav Mattana and Mar Ukva, both citing the father of Shmuel and Levi.
Rabbi Zeira challenges the first opinion (tear for seven days) by citing the rule that a woman may stitch immediately, implying the same should apply here.
The Gemara answers that the woman's case is an exception due to her honor, so it does not apply to the general rule.
Rabbi Zeira challenges the second opinion (tear for thirty days) by noting that for a parent, stitching is never permitted, so the same logic should apply.
The Gemara answers that the parent case is an exception due to the honor of father and mother, so it does not apply to the general rule.

items.text: Laws of borrowing a garment for mourning; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling
items.text_en: Laws of borrowing a garment for mourning; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling
items.desc_en: A baraita states that one who goes out in a torn garment before the dead robs the dead and the living. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel discusses a case where one borrows a garment to visit a sick father who dies: he tears, stitches, and pays for the tear; if he did not inform the owner, he may not touch it.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that one who goes out in a torn garment before the dead robs both the dead and the living.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel rules that one who borrows a garment to visit a sick father who dies must tear, stitch, and pay for the tear; if he did not inform the owner, he may not touch it.

items.text: Various laws: sick person, minor, in-laws, and conduct at the mourner's house
items.text_en: Various laws: sick person, minor, in-laws, and conduct at the mourner's house
items.desc_en: Baraitot teach: a sick person is not informed of a death lest his mind become confused; no tearing is done in his presence. Tearing is done for a minor due to grief, and for in-laws due to honor of the wife. Rav Pappa cites that a mourner should not hold a child lest he laugh. The Gemara discusses how to conduct the meal of comfort, with a story about Rava and Abba bar Marta.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that a sick person is not informed of a death and no tearing is done in his presence, lest his mind become confused.
The baraita adds that tearing is performed for a minor due to grief, and for in-laws due to the honor of the wife.

sub.text: Rav Pappa citing the baraita in Evel Rabbati
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa citing the baraita in Evel Rabbati
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa cites that a mourner should not hold a child lest he laugh and appear disgraceful before others.
The baraita teaches that the meal of comfort is not served on upright couches; if the visitor is intimate with the mourner, they serve on overturned couches, otherwise on upright ones.

sub.text: Story about Rava and Abba bar Marta
sub.text_en: Story about Rava and Abba bar Marta
sub.desc_en: The gemara recounts that when Rava was in mourning, Abba bar Marta visited and overturned his couch, prompting Rava to remark on the visitor's lack of sensitivity.
The gemara transitions to a new baraita about one who travels from place to place.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a mourner can reduce his business dealings, he should; otherwise, he may engage with others.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a mourner should reduce his business dealings if possible, otherwise he may engage with others.

items.text: When to overturn beds – dispute and precedent
items.text_en: When to overturn beds – dispute and precedent
items.desc_en: A baraita records a dispute: Rabbi Eliezer says beds are overturned from the moment the deceased leaves the house, while Rabbi Yehoshua says from when the grave is sealed. A story about Rabban Gamliel the Elder shows both opinions were followed in practice.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with the question of when to overturn beds, and records Rabbi Eliezer's opinion that it is from the moment the deceased leaves the house.
Rabbi Yehoshua gives a competing opinion that beds are overturned only from when the grave is sealed.

sub.text: Story about Rabban Gamliel the Elder
sub.text_en: Story about Rabban Gamliel the Elder
sub.desc_en: A precedent is cited: when Rabban Gamliel the Elder died, Rabbi Eliezer ordered overturning at departure and Rabbi Yehoshua at sealing, and the people followed both instructions.

items.text: When to right beds on Shabbat eve and after Shabbat
items.text_en: When to right beds on Shabbat eve and after Shabbat
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that beds are righted on Shabbat eve from mincha time onward. Rabba bar Huna adds that one may not sit on it until dark, and after Shabbat, even if only one day of mourning remains, one must overturn it again.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states the time for righting beds on Shabbat eve is from mincha (afternoon prayer) onward.
Rabba bar Huna adds that even after righting the bed, one may not sit on it until nightfall.
Rabba bar Huna rules that after Shabbat, even if only one day of mourning remains, one must overturn the bed again.

items.text: Which beds must be overturned
items.text_en: Which beds must be overturned
items.desc_en: A baraita states that all beds in the house must be overturned, even ten in ten places, and even five brothers when one dies. Exceptions include a bed designated for vessels and a dargesh, which is only to be stood upright. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says the dargesh's straps are loosened and it falls by itself.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that one who overturns his bed must overturn all beds in his house, even ten in ten places or five brothers when one dies.
The baraita adds exceptions: a bed designated for vessels need not be overturned, and a dargesh (a special bed) is only stood upright.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says the dargesh's straps are loosened and it falls by itself.

items.text: Definition of dargesh and related discussions
items.text_en: Definition of dargesh and related discussions
items.desc_en: Ulla defines dargesh as a 'bed of a goat' (a folding bed). Rabba objects based on a mishna about a king reclining on a dargesh. Rav Ashi deflects the objection. A further difficulty arises from the baraita that all beds must be overturned, but a dargesh is exempt. This is resolved by comparing it to a bed designated for vessels. Another difficulty from Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's statement about straps is resolved when Ravin reports that a dargesh is a 'bed of a tanner'. Rabbi Yirmeya distinguishes between a dargesh (woven from within) and a bed (woven on top). Finally, Rabbi Yaakov bar Acha rules in accordance with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the definition of the term 'dargesh'.
Ulla defines 'dargesh' as a 'bed of a goat' (a folding bed).
Rabba objects based on the mishna where a king reclines on a dargesh, questioning how a folding bed could be used for reclining.
Rav Ashi deflects the objection by noting that the king's reclining is for eating and drinking, which was not done earlier but is done now.
The Gemara raises a new difficulty: if a dargesh is a folding bed, why is it exempt from overturning, given the baraita that all beds must be overturned?
The Gemara resolves the difficulty by comparing the dargesh to a bed designated for vessels, which is also exempt from overturning.
The Gemara raises another difficulty: if a dargesh is a folding bed, why does Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel mention straps for it?
Ravin reports that a dargesh is a 'bed of a tanner' (a frame for stretching hides), which explains the straps.
Rabbi Yirmeya distinguishes between a dargesh (woven from within) and a bed (woven on top), supporting the tanner's bed interpretation.
Rabbi Yaakov bar Acha rules in accordance with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's view on the dargesh.

sub.text: Rabbi Yaakov bar Acha's additional statement
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yaakov bar Acha's additional statement
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov bar Acha further states, citing Rabbi Asi, that a bed whose legs protrude need only be stood upright, not overturned.

items.text: Sleeping on a chair or the ground does not fulfill the obligation
items.text_en: Sleeping on a chair or the ground does not fulfill the obligation
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that sleeping on a chair, a large bench, or the ground does not fulfill the obligation of overturning the bed. Rabbi Yochanan explains that one has not fulfilled the mitzvah of overturning the bed.

sub.desc_en: A baraita rules that sleeping on a chair, a large bench, or the ground does not fulfill the obligation of overturning the bed.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that the reason is that one has not performed the act of overturning the bed.

items.text: Sweeping, sprinkling, and bringing incense in the house of mourning
items.text_en: Sweeping, sprinkling, and bringing incense in the house of mourning
items.desc_en: A baraita permits sweeping, sprinkling, and washing vessels in the house of mourning, but forbids bringing incense and spices. A contradiction is raised from bar Kappara's teaching that one does not recite a blessing over incense or spices, implying they may be brought. The resolution distinguishes between the house of mourning (where they are not brought) and the house of comforters (where they are).

sub.desc_en: A baraita permits sweeping, sprinkling, and washing vessels in the house of mourning, but forbids bringing incense and spices.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from bar Kappara's teaching that one does not recite a blessing over incense or spices in the house of mourning, implying they may be brought.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between the house of mourning (where incense and spices are not brought) and the house of comforters (where they are brought).

items.text: Mishnah: How food is brought and conduct in the mourner's house
items.text_en: Mishnah: How food is brought and conduct in the mourner's house
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that food is brought to the house of mourning in baskets, not on trays or plates. During Chol Hamoed, the mourner's blessing is not recited, but the comforters stand in a row and console. The bier is not placed in the street to avoid encouraging eulogies, and women's biers are never placed in the street out of respect.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that food is brought to the mourner's house only in baskets, not on trays or plates, and that during Chol Hamoed the mourner's blessing is not recited, but comforters stand in a row and console, and the public is dismissed.
The Mishnah adds that the bier is not placed in the street to avoid encouraging eulogies, and women's biers are never placed in the street out of respect.

items.text: Gemara: Historical enactments for equality in mourning practices
items.text_en: Gemara: Historical enactments for equality in mourning practices
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts three enactments: originally the wealthy brought food in silver/gold baskets and the poor in peeled willow baskets, causing shame, so all were required to use willow baskets. Similarly, the wealthy were given white glass and the poor colored glass for drinks, so all were given colored glass. Also, the faces of the wealthy were uncovered and the poor covered due to famine-induced darkening, so all were covered. The text begins to describe a fourth enactment about carrying out the deceased on a dargesh.

sub.desc_en: The baraita recounts the first enactment: originally the wealthy brought food in silver/gold baskets and the poor in peeled willow baskets, causing shame, so all were required to use willow baskets for the dignity of the poor.

The baraita recounts the second enactment: originally the wealthy were given white glass and the poor colored glass for drinks, causing shame, so all were given colored glass for the dignity of the poor.

The baraita recounts the third enactment: originally the faces of the wealthy were uncovered and the poor covered due to famine-induced darkening, causing shame, so all were covered for the dignity of the poor.
The baraita begins to recount a fourth enactment about carrying out the wealthy on a dargesh (bier) and the poor on a simple bed, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Enactments to prevent shame of the poor and living
items.text_en: Enactments to prevent shame of the poor and living
items.desc_en: The Mishnah recounts three earlier practices that caused shame to the poor and to living people with similar conditions, and the subsequent enactments to treat everyone equally for the sake of dignity.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the first practice: all were buried in a winding sheet (כליכה), but the poor were shamed, so they enacted that everyone uses a winding sheet for the dignity of the poor.

The Mishnah recounts the second practice: incense (מוגמר) was placed under those who died of bowel disease, shaming the living with the same condition, so they enacted that it be placed under everyone for the dignity of the living afflicted.

The Mishnah recounts the third and fourth practices: vessels were immersed over dead menstruants and dead זבים (zavim), shaming the living, so they enacted immersion over all women and all people for the dignity of the living.

items.text: Rabban Gamliel's enactment regarding burial shrouds
items.text_en: Rabban Gamliel's enactment regarding burial shrouds
items.desc_en: The Gemara relates that initially, the expense of burial was so great that relatives would abandon the dead. Rabban Gamliel set a precedent by going out in simple linen garments, and the people followed. Rav Pappa notes the current custom is even with a cheap wrap.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara relates that initially, the expense of burying the dead was so burdensome that relatives would abandon the corpse and flee.
Rabban Gamliel set a precedent by going out in simple linen garments, and the people followed his practice.
Rav Pappa notes that the current custom is even with a cheap wrap worth one zuz.

items.text: Placing the bier in the street and eulogies for a Torah scholar
items.text_en: Placing the bier in the street and eulogies for a Torah scholar
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one does not place the bier in the street. Rav Pappa says there is no מועד in the presence of a Torah scholar, and certainly not on Chanukah and Purim. The Gemara qualifies this, and discusses a case where Rav Kahana eulogized Rav Zevid, explaining it was a day of hearing news, considered like being in his presence.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one does not place the bier in the street.
Rav Pappa rules that there is no מועד (festival restriction) in the presence of a Torah scholar, and certainly not on Chanukah and Purim.
The Gemara qualifies that Rav Pappa's ruling applies only in the scholar's presence, but not in his absence.
The Gemara objects: Did not Rav Kahana eulogize Rav Zevid of Nehardea at the mouth of the river (outside his presence)?
Rav Pappei resolves that it was a day of hearing the news (of the death), which is considered like being in his presence.

items.text: Actions of eulogy: beating the heart, clapping, and clapping with the foot
items.text_en: Actions of eulogy: beating the heart, clapping, and clapping with the foot
items.desc_en: Ulla explains the actions of eulogy: הספד is on the heart, טיפוח is with the hand, and קילוס is with the foot. A baraisa adds that one should not clap with a sandal but with a shoe, due to danger.

sub.desc_en: Ulla defines the three actions of eulogy: הספד (beating the heart), טיפוח (clapping with the hand), and קילוס (clapping with the foot), citing a verse for the first.
A baraita adds that one who performs קילוס should do so with a shoe (מנעל) rather than a sandal (סנדל), due to danger.

items.text: Laws of the mourner: nodding head, standing for Nasi, and saying 'sit'
items.text_en: Laws of the mourner: nodding head, standing for Nasi, and saying 'sit'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that once a mourner nods his head, others are no longer permitted to sit with him to console. He also says that everyone must stand for the Nasi except a mourner and a sick person, and that everyone is told to sit except a mourner and a sick person.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that once a mourner nods his head, others are no longer permitted to sit with him to console.
Rabbi Yochanan states that everyone must stand for the Nasi except a mourner and a sick person.
Rabbi Yochanan rules that everyone is told to sit except a mourner and a sick person.

items.text: Laws of the first day: eating bread, work prohibition, and the story of Rav Hamnuna
items.text_en: Laws of the first day: eating bread, work prohibition, and the story of Rav Hamnuna
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav says a mourner is forbidden to eat his own bread on the first day, based on Ezekiel. Rabba and Rav Yosef would exchange meals. Rav Yehuda also says that if a dead person is in the city, all residents are forbidden from work. Rav Hamnuna excommunicated people working when a corpse was in the city, but permitted them when told it was a burial society.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav states that a mourner is forbidden to eat his own bread on the first day, deriving this from the verse to Ezekiel.
The gemara notes that Rabba and Rav Yosef would exchange meals with each other to avoid eating their own bread while mourning.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav states that when a dead person is in the city, all residents are forbidden from performing work.
Rav Hamnuna arrived at a town, heard the shofar for a deceased person, saw people working, and excommunicated them for violating the work prohibition.

sub.text: Rav Hamnuna's response to the townspeople
sub.text_en: Rav Hamnuna's response to the townspeople
sub.desc_en: When told that a burial society (חבורתא) was handling the deceased, Rav Hamnuna permitted the workers, as the prohibition only applies when no one else is attending to the burial.

items.text: Excessive grief and the limits of mourning
items.text_en: Excessive grief and the limits of mourning
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav says that one who is excessively distressed over his dead will weep for another. The story of a woman who wept excessively for her son is told, and Rav Huna warned her, leading to the death of all her sons and herself. The verse 'Do not weep for the dead' is interpreted to mean not excessively, with set times: three days for weeping, seven for eulogy, thirty for ironing and haircutting.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav states that one who is excessively distressed over his dead will weep for another.

sub.text: Story about a woman and Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Story about a woman and Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: A story is told of a woman who wept excessively for her son; Rav Huna warned her, and when she ignored him, all her sons died.
Rav Huna then told the woman to prepare provisions for herself, and she died.
The verse 'Do not weep for the dead' is interpreted to mean not excessively, with set times: three days for weeping, seven for eulogy, thirty for ironing and haircutting.
After these set times, the Holy One, Blessed be He, says that one should not be more merciful toward the dead than He is.

items.text: Weeping for one who dies childless, and the concept of a repeated sin
items.text_en: Weeping for one who dies childless, and the concept of a repeated sin
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda interprets 'weep for the one who goes' as one who dies without children. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi only attended the house of mourning for such a person. Rav Huna says it refers to one who commits a sin and repeats it. The Gemara explains Rav Huna's view: a repeated sin becomes permitted to him. Rabbi Levi describes the mourner's feelings: the first three days like a sword between his thighs, from three to seven like opposite him in a corner, thereafter like passing him in the market.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda interprets the verse 'weep for the one who goes' as referring to one who dies without children.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi only attended the house of mourning for one who died without children, citing the same verse.
Rav Huna interprets the verse as referring to one who commits a sin and repeats it.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rav Huna's view
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rav Huna's view
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rav Huna's reasoning: a repeated sin becomes permitted to him, though the Gemara corrects that it only becomes like permitted.
Rabbi Levi describes the mourner's feelings: the first three days like a sword between his thighs, from three to seven like opposite him in a corner, thereafter like passing him in the market.

items.text: The death of Miriam and the atonement of righteous deaths
items.text_en: The death of Miriam and the atonement of righteous deaths
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the proximity of Miriam's death to the parah adumah, teaching that the death of the righteous atones. Rabbi Elazar adds that Miriam died by a kiss, like Moses, but the phrase 'by the mouth of the Lord' was omitted out of respect.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether only a living woman is exempt from the mourning practices, while other women are obligated.
Rabbi Elazar answers that even other women are exempt, citing the verse about Miriam's death and burial being juxtaposed.
Rabbi Elazar adds that Miriam died by a kiss (נשיקה), like Moses, but the phrase 'by the mouth of the Lord' was omitted out of respect.
Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Elazar explain that the juxtaposition of Miriam's death to the red heifer (פרה אדומה) and Aaron's death to the priestly garments teaches that the death of the righteous atones.

items.text: Categories of death by duration of illness
items.text_en: Categories of death by duration of illness
items.desc_en: The Tannaim classify death based on how long one was ill: sudden death (chatufah), one day (dechufah), two days (dechuyah), three (ge'arah), four (nezifah), five (normal death). Rabbi Chanin derives the five-day period from a verse. The Gemara then discusses death at specific ages: 50 (karet), 52 (Samuel), 60 (death by heaven), 70 (old age), 80 (strength).

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma opens by defining sudden death as 'חטופה' (snatched) and death after one day of illness as 'דחופה' (pushed).
Rabbi Chananya ben Gamliel identifies death after one day as 'מיתת מגפה' (death by plague), citing Ezekiel's prophecy about his wife's death.
The Tanna Kamma continues the classification: two days is 'דחויה' (pushed off), three is 'גערה' (rebuke), four is 'נזיפה' (reproof), and five is the normal death of every person.
Rabbi Chanin derives the five-day period from the verse 'הן קרבו ימיך למות' (Behold your days approach to die), counting 'הן' as one, 'קרבו' as two, and 'ימיך' as two, totaling five.
The Gemara states that death at 50 is 'מיתת כרת' (death by karet), and at 52 is the death of Samuel the Ramathite.
Mar Zutra derives that death at 60 is 'מיתה בידי שמים' (death by heaven) from the verse 'תבא בכלח אלי קבר', where 'בכלח' has a gematria of 60.
The Gemara states that 70 is old age and 80 is strength, citing Psalms; Rabbah clarifies that karet applies from 50 to 60, and the omission of 51-59 is due to the honor of Samuel.

items.text: Rav Yosef's celebration at age sixty
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's celebration at age sixty
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef made a feast for the rabbis when he turned sixty, saying he had escaped karet. Abaye questioned whether he had escaped karet of days, and Rav Yosef told him to at least take half the credit.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef, upon turning sixty, made a feast for the rabbis, declaring he had escaped karet (premature death).
Abaye questions whether Rav Yosef has escaped karet of days (death within a year) as well as karet of years (death before sixty).
Rav Yosef concedes the point and tells Abaye to at least take partial credit for his escape.

items.text: Rav Huna's sudden death and the exception for the strong
items.text_en: Rav Huna's sudden death and the exception for the strong
items.desc_en: Rav Huna died suddenly, and the rabbis were distressed. A pair of amoraim taught that sudden death is only considered bad if one has not reached the age of strength (eighty), but if one has, it is a death by a kiss.

sub.desc_en: The gemara reports that Rav Huna died suddenly, and the rabbis were distressed.
A pair of amoraim taught that sudden death is only considered bad if one has not reached the age of strength (eighty), but if one has, it is a death by a kiss.

items.text: Life, children, and sustenance depend on mazal, not merit
items.text_en: Life, children, and sustenance depend on mazal, not merit
items.desc_en: Rava argues that life, children, and sustenance depend on mazal (fortune), not merit, citing the examples of Rabbah and Rav Chisda. He then recounts his own requests from heaven: the wisdom of Rav Huna and the wealth of Rav Chisda were granted, but the humility of Rabbah bar Rav Huna was not.

sub.desc_en: Rava opens by asserting that life, children, and sustenance depend on mazal (fortune), not merit.

sub.text: Rava's evidence from Rabbah and Rav Chisda
sub.text_en: Rava's evidence from Rabbah and Rav Chisda
sub.desc_en: Rava supports his claim by contrasting the fates of Rabbah and Rav Chisda: both were righteous, yet Rav Chisda lived long, had many weddings, and had abundant food, while Rabbah died young, had many funerals, and lacked bread.
Rava concludes by recounting his own requests from heaven: granted the wisdom of Rav Huna and the wealth of Rav Chisda, but denied the humility of Rabbah bar Rav Huna.

items.text: Stories of rabbis confronting the Angel of Death
items.text_en: Stories of rabbis confronting the Angel of Death
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts several episodes where the Angel of Death appeared to various rabbis. Rav Se'orim, Rava, Rabbi Elazar, Rav Sheshet, Rav Ashi, Rav Chisda, and Rabbi Chiya each had encounters, often using their Torah knowledge or cunning to delay or avoid death.

sub.desc_en: Rav Se'orim, Rava's brother, sees the Angel of Death dozing and asks Rava to command him not to torment; Rava notes that since his mazal (fortune) has been surrendered, the Angel ignores him.

Rava, sitting before Rav Nachman, sees the Angel dozing and asks him to command the Angel; Rav Nachman responds that the Angel considers him an important person, and the Angel replies with a cryptic phrase about who is truly important.

Rav Nachman asks to see the Angel, who appears and describes his suffering as like removing a thread from milk; Rav Nachman says he would not want to return to this world because of the Angel's great fear.
Rabbi Elazar, while eating תרומה (priestly portion), tells the Angel that he is eating sacred food and thus cannot be taken; the Angel passes by, and the moment passes.
The Angel appears to Rav Sheshet in the marketplace; Rav Sheshet rebukes him for appearing in a public place like an animal, and the Angel comes to his house instead.

Rav Ashi asks the Angel for a thirty-day delay to review his Talmud; the Angel grants it, explaining that the delay is because the foot of a mortal is pressing, and one kingdom does not touch another even by a hair's breadth.
The Angel could not overcome Rav Chisda because his mouth never stopped studying; the Angel sat on a cedar in the study hall, the cedar cracked, Rav Chisda fell silent, and the Angel overcame him.

The Angel could not approach Rabbi Chiya, so he disguised himself as a poor man asking for bread; when Rabbi Chiya showed compassion, the Angel revealed himself, showed a rod of fire, and Rabbi Chiya surrendered his soul.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Laws of mourning practices during festivals
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Laws of mourning practices during festivals
items.desc_en: The Mishnah distinguishes between עינון (wailing in unison), טפוח (clapping), and קינון (lamenting with a leader). Women may wail during the festival but not clap; Rabbi Yishmael permits clapping for those near the bier. On Rosh Chodesh, Chanukah, and Purim, both wailing and clapping are permitted but not lamenting. Once the dead is buried, all mourning practices cease.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that women may wail (מענות) during the festival but may not clap (מטפחות).
Rabbi Yishmael permits clapping for women who are near the bier.
The Mishnah rules that on Rosh Chodesh, Chanukah, and Purim, both wailing and clapping are permitted, but lamenting (קינון) is not.
The Mishnah states that once the dead is buried, all mourning practices cease.
The Mishnah defines עינון (wailing) as all women responding in unison, and קינון (lamenting) as one woman speaking and all responding after her.
The Mishnah cites a verse (Jeremiah 9:19) to support the definition of lamenting.
The Mishnah concludes with a future-oriented verse (Isaiah 25:8) promising the end of death and sorrow.

items.text: Gemara: Examples of wailing and lamentation formulas
items.text_en: Gemara: Examples of wailing and lamentation formulas
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the wailing formula is. Rav and Rava provide examples from the women of Shakhnetziv, including various Aramaic dirges that express grief and the finality of death.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the formula for wailing (עִינּוּי) is.
Rav provides a wailing formula: 'Woe to the departed, woe to the bundle.'

sub.text: Rava's citation of the women of Shakhnetziv
sub.text_en: Rava's citation of the women of Shakhnetziv
sub.desc_en: Rava cites the women of Shakhnetziv who recite a dirge about a bone stuck in the throat, expressing the futility of efforts to save the deceased.

sub.text: Rava's additional citations of the women of Shakhnetziv
sub.text_en: Rava's additional citations of the women of Shakhnetziv
sub.desc_en: Rava continues citing the women of Shakhnetziv, who recite several Aramaic dirges about the finality of death, the futility of worldly pursuits, and the equivalence of all deaths.

items.text: Baraita: Rabbi Meir on the lesson from visiting mourners
items.text_en: Baraita: Rabbi Meir on the lesson from visiting mourners
items.desc_en: A baraita quotes Rabbi Meir expounding on the verse 'Better to go to a house of mourning...' — the living should take to heart that they too will be mourned, buried, carried, and lifted. An alternative version emphasizes humility: one who does not lift himself will be lifted.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Meir expounds the verse 'Better to go to a house of mourning...' — the living should take to heart that they too will be mourned, buried, carried, and lifted.
An alternative version emphasizes humility: one who does not lift himself will be lifted, citing the verse 'For it is good that it be said to you, Come up here...'

items.text: Story: Four elders console Rabbi Yishmael after his sons' death
items.text_en: Story: Four elders console Rabbi Yishmael after his sons' death
items.desc_en: When Rabbi Yishmael's sons died, four elders (Rabbi Tarfon, Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah, and Rabbi Akiva) came to console him. Each elder opened with a verse and a kal vachomer argument comparing the sons' merit to biblical figures (Nadav and Avihu, Aviyah ben Yeravam, Zedekiah, and Ahab), concluding that the sons deserved even greater honor.

sub.desc_en: The baraita introduces the story of four elders entering to console Rabbi Yishmael after his sons' death, with Rabbi Tarfon instructing them not to interrupt each other and Rabbi Akiva speaking last.
Rabbi Yishmael opens with a lament, saying his sins multiplied and his grief overwhelmed him, troubling his teachers twice.

Rabbi Tarfon consoles Rabbi Yishmael with a kal vachomer (a fortiori) argument: if Nadav and Avihu, who performed only one mitzvah, were mourned, then Rabbi Yishmael's sons deserve even greater mourning.

items.text: Rava's questions to Rabbah bar Mari on apparent contradictions
items.text_en: Rava's questions to Rabbah bar Mari on apparent contradictions
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rabbah bar Mari about contradictions in the fates of Zedekiah and Josiah: how could Zedekiah die in peace yet be blinded, and how could Josiah die in peace yet be shot by archers? Rabbah bar Mari answers with Rabbi Yochanan's explanations: Zedekiah saw Nebuchadnezzar's death in his lifetime, and Josiah's peace was that the Temple was not destroyed in his days.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rabbah bar Mari about the contradiction in Zedekiah's fate: the verse says he will die in peace, yet his eyes were blinded.

sub.text: Rabbah bar Mari's answer citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar Mari's answer citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Mari answers that Rabbi Yochanan explained: Zedekiah died in peace because Nebuchadnezzar died during his lifetime.
Rava asks about the contradiction in Josiah's fate: the verse promises he will be gathered to his grave in peace, yet he was shot by archers and his body was riddled like a sieve.

sub.text: Rabbah bar Mari's answer citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar Mari's answer citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Mari answers that Rabbi Yochanan explained: Josiah's peace was that the Temple was not destroyed in his days.

items.text: Laws of consolation and seating: mourner and groom at the head
items.text_en: Laws of consolation and seating: mourner and groom at the head
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that consolers may not speak until the mourner opens first, citing Job. Rabbi Avahu derives that the mourner sits at the head from a verse. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak corrects the reading to 'yinnachem'. Mar Zutra learns from 'mirzach seruchim'. Rabbi Chama bar Chanina derives that a groom sits at the head from 'k'chatan y'chahen pe'er', and the priest's precedence is from 'v'kidashto'. Rabbi Chanina concludes that death is as painful as the parting of the soul from the body.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that consolers may not speak until the mourner opens first, citing Job.
Rabbi Avahu derives from a verse that the mourner sits at the head.
The Gemara objects that the verse 'יְנַחֵם' implies others console, not the mourner leading.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak corrects the reading to 'יִנָּחֵם' (he will be consoled), resolving the objection.
Mar Zutra learns from 'מִרְזַח סְרוּחִים' that the mourner becomes a leader over the mourners.
Rabbi Chama bar Chanina derives from 'כְּחָתָן יְכַהֵן פְּאֵר' that a groom sits at the head, via a verbal analogy with the priest.
The Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael derives the priest's precedence from 'וְקִדַּשְׁתּוֹ', applying to all matters of sanctity.
Rabbi Chanina concludes that the departure of the soul from the body is as painful as the parting of the soul from the body.

items.text: Opening dispute on the metaphor for death
items.text_en: Opening dispute on the metaphor for death
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and an earlier opinion about the metaphor for the moment of death: one compares it to a bird in the throat, the other to a plug in the throat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with an anonymous statement comparing the moment of death to a bird in the throat (כְּצִיפּוֹרֵי בְּפִי הַוֶּושֶׁט).
Rabbi Yochanan offers an alternative metaphor: the moment of death is like a plug (פִּטּוּרֵי) in the throat, contrasting with the bird metaphor.

items.text: Proper farewell formulations for the dead and the living
items.text_en: Proper farewell formulations for the dead and the living
items.desc_en: Rabbi Levi bar Chayta teaches that one who takes leave of the dead should say 'Go in peace' (בְּשָׁלוֹם), while one who takes leave of the living should say 'Go to peace' (לְשָׁלוֹם). Prooftexts are provided from the Torah and from the contrasting outcomes of David's and Jethro's farewells.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Levi bar Chayta teaches the proper farewell formulations: for the dead say 'go in peace' (בְּשָׁלוֹם), for the living say 'go to peace' (לְשָׁלוֹם).
The rule for the dead is supported by the verse 'you shall come to your fathers in peace' (בְּשָׁלוֹם).
The rule for the living is supported by contrasting outcomes: David said 'go in peace' (בְּשָׁלוֹם) to Absalom who was hanged, while Jethro said 'go to peace' (לְשָׁלוֹם) to Moses who succeeded.

items.text: Merit of moving from synagogue to study hall
items.text_en: Merit of moving from synagogue to study hall
items.desc_en: Rabbi Levi teaches that one who goes from the synagogue to the study hall, or vice versa, merits to receive the Divine Presence, citing the verse 'They go from strength to strength, they appear before God in Zion.'

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Levi teaches that one who goes from the synagogue to the study hall or vice versa merits to receive the Divine Presence, citing the verse 'They go from strength to strength, they appear before God in Zion.'

items.text: Torah scholars have no rest even in the World to Come
items.text_en: Torah scholars have no rest even in the World to Come
items.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi in the name of Rav teaches that Torah scholars have no rest even in the World to Come, as they continually go from strength to strength, citing the same verse.

sub.text: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi in the name of Rav teaches that Torah scholars have no rest even in the World to Come, citing the verse 'יֵלְכוּ מֵחַיִל אֶל חָיִל יֵרָאֶה אֶל אֱלֹהִים בְּצִיּוֹן' (they go from strength to strength, each will appear before God in Zion).
